orderingVariable: COURSE ORDER — 4 stages that run alongside the versatility list's stages (a chunk in Stage N is learned during versatility Stage N). The most common idioms first; each stage mixes several topics; within a topic, chunks run from the most common idioms to less common ones.
whyThatVariable: Selected on how commonly each idiom is said in everyday conversation: counted in 3.17M lines of Japanese film and TV subtitles (OpenSubtitles 2018) and corrected by native judgement where foreign-film subtitles over-count dramatic lines and under-count casual Japanese talk.

conventions.romaji: kotoba's stored spelling: modified Hepburn, lowercase, no macrons, long vowels as spelled (sou, koohii), wa/o/e particles, っ before ch = t.
conventions.register: romaji = the plain form as people say it; polite = its desu/masu form, or null when there is no register difference.
conventions.meaning: english = what the idiom means; literal = word for word; englishIdiom = a close English idiom when a natural one exists, else null (the list is chosen on Japanese commonness, not English equivalents).
conventions.parts: noun / particle / verb for noun + verb idioms (te / o / kasu), else null.
conventions.measured: count = occurrences in the subtitle corpus; source = pairs (the noun + verb pair on dictionary forms, any inflection, particle or none) or phrase (the written forms of the idiom). null = too rare in films to count.
conventions.listLinks: ids of items in 20-list-versatile.json that the idiom builds on.
conventions.contrastGroup: idioms sharing a group name are learned side by side.

stages.name: Stage 1
stages.summary: Tell someone to knock it off, say you're angry or not in the mood, offer or ask for help, call people kind, clever or loose-lipped, say something makes no sense, and talk about luck, bad times and getting fired.

stages.name: Stage 2
stages.summary: Say you're at your wit's end or shaken up, call people skilled, immature or easygoing, point out hypocrisy, say what's too much to handle, and talk about who you click with, who's a burden and getting the short end.

stages.name: Stage 3
stages.summary: Say you feel better or need to cool off, describe stubborn or two-faced people, let things go or hold a grudge, keep a secret, and talk about being busy, hunches, getting carried away and wasted effort.

stages.name: Stage 4
stages.summary: Say you're down, embarrassed or moved, talk about couples, connections and who's under whose thumb, call out lies and say you warned them, and say whether a gamble or a purchase was worth it.

blocks.label: Enough already
blocks.rationale: Outbursts telling someone they have gone too far, from 'knock it off' to 'fine, do what you want'.
blocks.interference: kanben shite vs katte ni shite (both -te pleas: spare me vs do as you like); ii kagen ni shite vs ni mo hodo ga aru (both 'too far').

items.use: Snapped at someone whose behaviour has gone on too long, usually as mou ii kagen ni shite!, and men often use the rough ii kagen ni shiro. It's a different thing from the adjective ii kagen na (sloppy, half-baked), as in ii kagen na hito.
items.politeJa: いい加減にしてください

example.romaji: nankai onaji koto iwaseru no? ii kagen ni shite.
example.ja: 何回同じこと言わせるの？いい加減にして。
example.english: How many times do I have to tell you? Enough already.

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro ii kagen ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: そろそろいい加減にしてください。
examplePolite.english: That's quite enough now.

items.notes: Rough: ii kagen ni shiro; short plain version: mou ii.

items.english: give me a break, spare me
items.use: The groan when something is too much or happening again: mou kanben shite yo. Men also say kanben shite kure, or the rough kanben shiro. Kanben shite kudasai can be a real plea to be excused.

example.romaji: sono hanashi, mou kanben shite.
example.ja: その話、もう勘弁して。
example.english: Spare me that story already.

examplePolite.romaji: sono hanashi wa mou kanben shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: その話はもう勘弁してください。
examplePolite.english: Please, let's not go over that again.

items.notes: Male casual: kanben shite kure; rough: kanben shiro.

items.english: no way, you've got to be kidding
items.englishIdiom: you've got to be kidding me
items.use: An indignant refusal or outburst at something outrageous: joudan ja nai yo! (rough male: joudan ja nee). Uso! reacts to surprising news, but joudan ja nai rejects what's being asked or done. It can also simply mean 'I'm not joking' (joudan ja nai, honki da yo); the indignant one is snapped out on its own.

example.romaji: mata zangyou? joudan ja nai yo.
example.ja: また残業？冗談じゃないよ。
example.english: Overtime again? You've got to be kidding.

examplePolite.romaji: mata zangyou desu ka? joudan ja nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: また残業ですか？冗談じゃないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Overtime again? You can't be serious.

items.notes: Softer disbelief: joudan deshou? (you're joking, right?).

items.use: Ends an argument when you give up on persuading someone: mou ii, katte ni shite. The rough male katte ni shiro is the form films use most, and katte ni sureba (go ahead, then) is colder. Douzo gokatte ni is the polite, icy version. Suki ni shite is the friendly 'do as you like'.

example.romaji: mou ii, katte ni shite.
example.ja: もういい、勝手にして。
example.english: Forget it. Do whatever you want.

examplePolite.romaji: wakarimashita. jaa, katte ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: わかりました。じゃあ、勝手にしてください。
examplePolite.english: Fine. Suit yourself, then.

items.notes: Rough: katte ni shiro (72 of the 107 hits; katte ni shite itself is 15). Colder: katte ni sureba. Polite and icy: douzo gokatte ni.

items.use: Attaches to a noun or adjective as an exasperated rebuke: baka ni mo hodo ga aru, shitsurei ni mo hodo ga aru, usually ending in yo or daro. It's also used playfully for praise: kawaii ni mo hodo ga aru (way too cute).

example.romaji: joudan ni mo hodo ga aru yo.
example.ja: 冗談にも程があるよ。
example.english: A joke's a joke, but that's too far.

examplePolite.romaji: joudan ni mo hodo ga arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 冗談にも程がありますよ。
examplePolite.english: That's taking the joke much too far.

items.notes: The frame varies: joudan, gaman, shitsurei, baka ni mo hodo ga aru.

blocks.label: Lending a hand
blocks.rationale: Offering and giving help, from a quick hand to joining forces.
blocks.interference: te o kasu (a quick hand) vs chikara o kasu (back something bigger) share kasu; chikara ni naru (be there for someone) vs chikara o awaseru (join forces) share chikara.

items.english: help out, give someone a hand
items.use: The everyday ask or offer for a quick bit of hands-on help, usually chotto te kashite (give me a hand). chikara o kasu is backing for something bigger, and chikara ni naru is any support ('anything I can do'). Also an accomplice's help: hanzai ni te o kasu (help with a crime).

example.romaji: kore omoi kara, chotto te kashite.
example.ja: これ重いから、ちょっと手貸して。
example.english: This is heavy, give me a hand.

examplePolite.romaji: kore omoi node, chotto te o kashite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これ重いので、ちょっと手を貸してもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: This is heavy, could you give me a hand?

items.notes: Plain alternative: tetsudau (tetsudatte = help me).

items.use: The go-to offer of support when someone is struggling, mostly in the potential: chikara ni nareru koto attara itte, or chikara ni narenakute gomen. It covers any help at all; te o kasu is a quick hand and chikara o kasu is backing something big.

example.romaji: nanka chikara ni nareru koto attara itte ne.
example.ja: なんか力になれることあったら言ってね。
example.english: If there's anything I can do, just say.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika chikara ni nareru koto ga attara, itte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何か力になれることがあったら、言ってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: If there's anything I can do, just say.

items.english: lend your support, help (with something big)
items.use: The serious ask for backing on a project, a cause or a hard situation: chikara o kashite hoshii (I need your help). Bigger than te o kasu (a quick hand); chikara ni naru is offering support yourself.

example.romaji: kono purojekuto, chikara kashite kurenai?
example.ja: このプロジェクト、力貸してくれない？
example.english: Would you help me out on this project?

examplePolite.romaji: kono purojekuto ni, zehi chikara o kashite itadakemasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: このプロジェクトに、ぜひ力を貸していただけませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you be willing to help us with this project?

items.notes: chie o kasu = help someone think something through.

items.use: The rallying line for a team, class, family or workplace facing something hard, usually minna de chikara o awasete (all of us together). Heard in pep talks and speeches as much as in chat; te o kumu is two sides forming an alliance.

example.romaji: minna de chikara awasete ganbarou!
example.ja: みんなで力合わせて頑張ろう！
example.english: Let's all pull together!

examplePolite.romaji: minna de chikara o awasete ganbarimashou.
examplePolite.ja: みんなで力を合わせて頑張りましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's all pull together and do our best.

blocks.label: Giving it everything
blocks.rationale: Four ways to say you are putting everything into something, from the everyday isshou kenmei to the dramatic shinu ki de.
blocks.interference: isshou kenmei is ordinary effort and shinu ki de is life-or-death; kiai o ireru means psyching yourself up, and nani ga nandemo means 'whatever it takes'.

items.english: as hard as one can, with all one's might
items.literal: a whole life, staking one's life
items.use: The everyday way to say someone tried their hardest, mostly as an adverb before a verb: isshou kenmei ganbatta, isshou kenmei hataraite iru. It also works before nouns (isshou kenmei na hito) and describes the manner of effort, where ganbaru is the effort itself.

example.romaji: isshou kenmei ganbatta n da kedo na
example.ja: 一生懸命頑張ったんだけどな
example.english: I really did try my hardest, though.

examplePolite.romaji: isshou kenmei ganbatta n desu kedo ne
examplePolite.ja: 一生懸命頑張ったんですけどね
examplePolite.english: I really did try my hardest, though.

items.notes: Older spelling 一所懸命 (issho kenmei, literally staking one's life on one plot of land) means the same.

items.english: no matter what, at all costs
items.use: Shows firm resolve to get something done, usually before a deadline or goal: nani ga nandemo maniawaseru, nani ga nandemo katsu. Stronger than zettai, and always about someone's will.

example.romaji: nani ga nandemo kyoujuu ni owaraseru
example.ja: 何が何でも今日中に終わらせる
example.english: I'm finishing it today, no matter what.

examplePolite.romaji: nani ga nandemo kyoujuu ni owarasemasu
examplePolite.ja: 何が何でも今日中に終わらせます
examplePolite.english: I'll finish it today, no matter what.

items.notes: Plain alternative: zettai (definitely).

items.english: get fired up; put real effort into
items.use: Rallying yourself or a team before a game, exam or big day: yoshi, kiai irete ikou! Also kiai irete + verb for doing something with real effort (kiai irete tsukutta), and aimed at someone else it can mean shaking them into shape (kiai o irete yaru).

example.romaji: yoshi, kiai irete ikou
example.ja: よし、気合入れていこう
example.english: Right, let's get fired up and go!

examplePolite.romaji: yoshi, kiai o irete ikimashou
examplePolite.ja: よし、気合を入れていきましょう
examplePolite.english: Right, let's get fired up and go!

items.notes: Not trying hard enough: kiai ga tarinai.

items.english: all-out, as if your life depended on it
items.englishIdiom: like your life depends on it
items.use: Pep-talk exaggeration before a verb of effort: shinu ki de ganbaru, shinu ki de benkyou shiro. Sounds intense, so friends often use it half-jokingly about exams and deadlines.

example.romaji: kondo no shiken, shinu ki de ganbaru
example.ja: 今度の試験、死ぬ気で頑張る
example.english: I'm going all-out for the next exam.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo no shiken, shinu ki de ganbarimasu
examplePolite.ja: 今度の試験、死ぬ気で頑張ります
examplePolite.english: I'm going all-out for the next exam.

items.notes: Softer: isshou kenmei.

blocks.label: Kind or nasty
blocks.rationale: How someone treats others, good or bad: thoughtful, trusting, really nasty, teasingly mean.
blocks.interference: hito ga ii and hito ga warui are not opposites: warui is a teasing 'that's mean', while tachi ga warui is truly nasty. ki ga kiku can be mistaken for the literal ki ga tsuku (notice).

items.english: thoughtful, attentive; (of a remark or gift) clever, apt
items.use: Praise for someone who does what's needed before being asked, like refilling drinks: ki ga kiku ne! (kiku here means 'work well', not 'listen'). Before a noun it often describes words or gifts: ki no kiita koto ga ienai (I can't think of anything clever to say). To a boss, skip the praise and just say thank you.

example.romaji: ki ga kiku ne, arigatou!
example.ja: 気が利くね、ありがとう！
example.english: That's so thoughtful, thanks!

examplePolite.romaji: ki ga kikimasu ne, arigatou gozaimasu!
examplePolite.ja: 気が利きますね、ありがとうございます！
examplePolite.english: How thoughtful of you, thank you!

items.notes: Opposite: ki ga kikanai (thoughtless).

items.english: good-natured and trusting (often too much so)
items.englishIdiom: too nice for one's own good
items.use: Said with fondness and worry about someone who trusts everyone or can't refuse, often as hito ga yosugiru (way too nice). Not the same as ii hito (a nice person): the idiom hints at naive; hito ga warui is not its opposite but means sly.

example.romaji: mata hikiuketa no? hito ga yosugiru yo.
example.ja: また引き受けたの？人が良すぎるよ。
example.english: You said yes again? You're too nice.

examplePolite.romaji: mata hikiuketa n desu ka? hito ga yosugimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: また引き受けたんですか？人が良すぎますよ。
examplePolite.english: You took that on again? You're too kind for your own good.

items.notes: Single word: ohitoyoshi (a soft touch, too trusting).

items.english: nasty, vicious, hard to deal with
items.use: For something nasty or hard to deal with: a cruel prank, a scam, a cold that won't go away, or a person who hurts others on purpose (tachi warui yo, tachi no warui joudan); a mean drunk is nomu to tachi ga warui. Much stronger than hito ga warui, which is only playful slyness.

example.romaji: sono joudan, tachi warui yo.
example.ja: その冗談、たち悪いよ。
example.english: That joke's just nasty.

examplePolite.romaji: sono joudan wa tachi ga warui desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: その冗談はたちが悪いですよ。
examplePolite.english: That's a rather nasty joke.

items.notes: Also written タチが悪い or 質が悪い; tachi alone is someone's nature (sou iu tachi = that's how I am).

items.use: A mild, often fond complaint when someone teased you, kept a secret or let you worry for nothing: mou, hito ga warui naa. Not the opposite of hito ga ii, and far lighter than tachi ga warui or seikaku ga warui (nasty).

example.romaji: nan da, shitteta no? hito ga warui naa.
example.ja: なんだ、知ってたの？人が悪いなあ。
example.english: You knew all along? That's sneaky.

examplePolite.romaji: shitteta n desu ka? hito ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 知ってたんですか？人が悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: You knew? That's a bit sneaky of you.

blocks.label: Having an idea
blocks.rationale: Knowing or not knowing who, why or what: the two most-said idioms of the topic (357, 251) plus the 'I know full well' answer.
blocks.interference: kentou mo tsukanai (not even a guess) and kokoroatari ga nai (nothing comes to mind) both come out as 'no idea'; hyaku mo shouchi is 'I know', usually followed by a 'but'.

items.english: have an idea who, why or where
items.literal: a match in the mind exists
items.use: Asked when something is lost, missing or odd and you want leads. You'll mostly hear it as a question, kokoroatari wa? or nanka kokoroatari aru?, and the answer is often zenzen nai. It means you know a possible cause from your own experience, while kentou ga tsuku is making a rough guess.

example.romaji: doko de nakushita ka, kokoroatari aru?
example.ja: どこでなくしたか、心当たりある？
example.english: Any idea where you lost it?

examplePolite.romaji: doko de nakushita ka, kokoroatari wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どこでなくしたか、心当たりはありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have any idea where you lost it?

items.notes: Negative: kokoroatari ga nai (no idea at all). Related: omoi ataru fushi ga aru (something comes to mind that might explain it).

items.use: The standard answer when you can't even guess who, where or how much: zenzen kentou mo tsukanai, or casually kentou tsukanai. The positive kentou ga tsuku means 'I can roughly guess'. Don't confuse it with kentou suru (look into, consider).

example.romaji: doko ni aru ka kentou mo tsukanai.
example.ja: どこにあるか見当もつかない。
example.english: I have no idea where it could be.

examplePolite.romaji: doko ni aru ka kentou mo tsukimasen.
examplePolite.ja: どこにあるか見当もつきません。
examplePolite.english: I have no idea where it could be.

items.notes: Positive: kentou ga tsuku (have a rough idea).

items.use: Said defensively when someone points out a risk or downside you've already weighed, often as sonna koto wa hyaku mo shouchi da, or to concede a point before going ahead or asking a favour: muri na onegai na no wa hyaku mo shouchi desu ga...

example.romaji: abunai no wa hyaku mo shouchi da yo. demo yaru.
example.ja: 危ないのは百も承知だよ。でもやる。
example.english: I know full well it's risky. I'm doing it anyway.

examplePolite.romaji: abunai no wa hyaku mo shouchi desu. demo yarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 危ないのは百も承知です。でもやります。
examplePolite.english: I know full well it's risky. I'm doing it anyway.

items.notes: Plain alternative: wakatteru tte (I know, I know).

blocks.label: Gains and windfalls
blocks.rationale: Good things coming your way, from simply getting hold of something to luck that falls in your lap.
blocks.interference: te ni ireru (you get it) vs te ni hairu (it comes to you) is a transitive/intransitive pair; tanabota is unearned luck, negatte mo nai is a chance better than you'd hoped for.

items.use: Said when you finally get something hard to come by, like tickets, a rare item or information. You mostly hear the past, te ni ireta. You are the one doing the getting; with te ni hairu, the thing itself is the subject.

example.romaji: yatto chiketto te ni ireta yo
example.ja: やっとチケット手に入れたよ
example.english: I finally got my hands on tickets.

examplePolite.romaji: yatto chiketto o te ni iremashita
examplePolite.ja: やっとチケットを手に入れました
examplePolite.english: I finally got hold of the tickets.

items.notes: Everyday alternatives: getto suru (casual); toreta (managed to get, for tickets and seats).

items.english: be obtainable, come into one's hands
items.use: The partner of te ni ireru, with the thing as the subject. You hear it most in the negative, nakanaka te ni hairanai (hard to get hold of), in questions like doko de te ni hairu no? (where can you get it?), and in the cheer yatto te ni haitta! (got it at last!).

example.romaji: kore, nakanaka te ni hairanai n da yo
example.ja: これ、なかなか手に入らないんだよ
example.english: This is really hard to get hold of.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, nakanaka te ni hairanai n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: これ、なかなか手に入らないんですよ
examplePolite.english: This is really hard to get hold of.

items.notes: Formal word: nyuushu (obtaining), as in nyuushu konnan (hard to get).

items.englishIdiom: kill two birds with one stone
items.use: Said casually about any double win, for example walking to work saves money and gets you exercise: isseki nichou jan. It comes up more lightly and more often than the English, usually as a cheerful aside.

example.romaji: sore isseki nichou jan
example.ja: それ一石二鳥じゃん
example.english: That's two birds with one stone!

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa isseki nichou desu ne
examplePolite.ja: それは一石二鳥ですね
examplePolite.english: That kills two birds with one stone.

items.notes: Formal near-synonym: ikkyo ryoutoku.

items.english: better than you could have hoped for, most welcome
items.literal: not (to be had) even by wishing
items.use: Almost always before a noun: negatte mo nai chansu / hanashi (a chance you couldn't have hoped for), or as sore wa negatte mo nai koto da. Also said on its own as a delighted reply to an offer. Said when an offer or a bit of luck is better than you'd dared to hope.
items.politeJa: 願ってもないことです

example.romaji: sore, negatte mo nai chansu jan!
example.ja: それ、願ってもないチャンスじゃん！
example.english: You couldn't ask for a better chance!

examplePolite.romaji: negatte mo nai ohanashi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 願ってもないお話です。
examplePolite.english: That's more than I could have hoped for.

items.literal: shelf rice-cake (a rice cake falling off the shelf)
items.use: Said when something good lands in your lap without effort, like a ticket from someone's cancellation or a rival dropping out: tanabota da! It's the clipped, everyday form of the saying tana kara botamochi.

example.romaji: tanabota datta ne
example.ja: 棚ぼただったね
example.english: That just fell into your lap, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: tanabota deshita ne
examplePolite.ja: 棚ぼたでしたね
examplePolite.english: That was a lucky windfall.

items.notes: Full saying: tana kara botamochi.

blocks.label: Saying it
blocks.rationale: The core 'say it' idioms: mentioning something, voicing it, and 'needless to say'.
blocks.interference: kuchi ni suru and kuchi ni dasu both mean say aloud; kuchi ni suru is also formal 'eat or drink', while kuchi ni dasu stresses finally voicing what was held in.

items.use: Uttering or mentioning a word, name or topic, a touch more formal than iu: sono namae, nido to kuchi ni suru na (never mention that name again). It also means eating or drinking: kyou wa mada nani mo kuchi ni shite nai (I haven't had a thing today). Unlike kuchi ni dasu, finally voicing what you'd kept inside, there's no sense of holding back. It's the mouth twin of mimi ni suru.

example.romaji: sono namae, ano hito no mae de wa kuchi ni shinai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: その名前、あの人の前では口にしないほうがいいよ。
example.english: Better not mention that name in front of her.

examplePolite.romaji: sono namae wa, ano kata no mae de wa kuchi ni shinai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: その名前は、あの方の前では口にしないほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's best not to mention that name in front of her.

items.english: needless to say, it goes without saying; (X wa iu made mo naku) not to mention X
items.literal: no need to go as far as saying it
items.use: Comes before a point everyone already knows, as iu made mo nai kedo... (needless to say...), or as a reply: iu made mo nai desho (that goes without saying). Its most frequent form is iu made mo naku, which after a noun means 'not to mention': eigo wa iu made mo naku, chuugokugo mo perapera (she's fluent in Chinese, not to mention English). It sounds a little formal and is heard most in speeches and announcements; friends often just say mochiron.
items.politeJa: 言うまでもありません

example.romaji: iu made mo nai kedo, kore naisho ne.
example.ja: 言うまでもないけど、これ内緒ね。
example.english: Needless to say, this stays between us.

examplePolite.romaji: iu made mo arimasen ga, kore wa naisho de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 言うまでもありませんが、これは内緒でお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Needless to say, please keep this to yourself.

items.notes: Pattern: X made mo nai (no need even to X), as in miru made mo nai. Plain alternatives: mochiron, atarimae.

items.english: say out loud, put into words, mention
items.literal: put it out into the mouth
items.use: Saying aloud what you've been thinking or feeling, often in the negative about feelings kept inside: kuchi ni dasanai to tsutawaranai yo (if you don't say it, they won't know). Also mentioning a name or subject you shouldn't: sono namae, kuchi ni dasu na (don't mention that name). Only the particle separates it from kuchi o dasu (to meddle); kuchi ni suru is a slightly more formal near-synonym.

example.romaji: omotteru dake ja dame, kuchi ni dasanai to.
example.ja: 思ってるだけじゃダメ、口に出さないと。
example.english: Just thinking it isn't enough. You have to say it.

examplePolite.romaji: omotteru dake ja dame desu yo, kuchi ni dasanai to.
examplePolite.ja: 思ってるだけじゃダメですよ、口に出さないと。
examplePolite.english: Just thinking it won't do. You have to say it.

blocks.label: Getting angry
blocks.rationale: Shades of anger, from mild dislike and disgust to snapping; a natural six.
blocks.interference: katto naru vs kachin to kuru (both sound words: snap vs stung by a remark); hara ga tatsu vs atama ni kuru (belly vs head for the same anger).

items.use: The anger you feel inside about a person or thing. In casual speech ga drops (maji hara tatsu). Okoru is showing anger or telling someone off, and hara o tateru is the 'get angry over it' form, heard mostly in sonna koto de hara o tateru na (don't get angry over that).

example.romaji: nanka jibun ni hara tatsu.
example.ja: なんか自分に腹立つ。
example.english: I'm kind of mad at myself.

examplePolite.romaji: jibun ni hara ga tachimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 自分に腹が立ちました。
examplePolite.english: I was angry with myself.

items.notes: Plain alternatives: mukatsuku, iraira suru.

items.use: Mostly an outburst about what someone did: atama kita! or honto atama kuru. It's stronger and more sudden than hara ga tatsu. Not 'go to one's head' (getting conceited is choushi ni noru).

example.romaji: ano hito no taido, maji atama kuru.
example.ja: あの人の態度、マジ頭来る。
example.english: That person's attitude really pisses me off.

examplePolite.romaji: ano taido ni wa atama ni kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの態度には頭に来ました。
examplePolite.english: That attitude made me really angry.

items.notes: Plain one-word alternative: mukatsuku.

items.english: don't like, rubs you the wrong way
items.use: Blunt dislike of a person or how they act, often vague with nanka or doumo: aitsu, nanka ki ni kuwanai. You'll also hear nani ga ki ni kuwanai n da? (what's your problem with it?). The softer form is ki ni iranai, and the plain word is kirai.

example.romaji: aitsu, nanka ki ni kuwanai na.
example.ja: あいつ、なんか気に食わないな。
example.english: Something about that guy rubs me the wrong way.

items.notes: Softer: ki ni iranai; plain word: kirai.

items.use: A sudden flash of anger that makes you act without thinking. You'll mostly hear it in the apology tsui katto natte (I just snapped). It's short-lived, unlike the lingering hara ga tatsu.

example.romaji: gomen, tsui katto natchatta.
example.ja: ごめん、ついカッとなっちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, I just snapped.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, tsui katto natte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ついカッとなってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I lost my temper.

items.notes: Plain slang alternative: kireru (snap).

items.use: A rough reaction to a nasty story, an unfair ending or a bully: munakuso warui hanashi da na. Kimochi warui is gut-level 'gross, creepy'; munakuso warui is moral disgust at something unfair or cruel.

example.romaji: ano nyuusu, maji de munakuso warui.
example.ja: あのニュース、マジで胸くそ悪い。
example.english: That news is seriously sickening.

items.notes: Slang short form: munakuso.

items.use: The sharp flash of irritation at a remark or tone, mostly in the past: ima no, chotto kachin to kita. It's milder than atama ni kuru, and it's set off by words rather than events.

example.romaji: ima no iikata, chotto kachin to kita.
example.ja: 今の言い方、ちょっとカチンときた。
example.english: The way you just said that kind of got to me.

examplePolite.romaji: ano iikata ni wa chotto kachin to kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの言い方にはちょっとカチンときました。
examplePolite.english: The way he put it rubbed me up the wrong way.

blocks.label: Dealing with people
blocks.rationale: How you treat someone: obey them, take them on, speak to them, count on them.
blocks.interference: iu koto o kiku (obey) vs kuchi o kiku (be on speaking terms) both end in kiku; aite ni suru (bother with) vs ate ni suru (count on) differ by one sound.

items.use: Parents, teachers and dog owners say it daily, usually without o: zenzen iu koto kikanai (won't listen at all). Also for a body or machine that won't cooperate (karada ga iu koto kikanai). It's obeying, not just hearing someone out (hanashi o kiku).

example.romaji: uchi no ko, zenzen iu koto kikanai no.
example.ja: うちの子、全然言うこと聞かないの。
example.english: My kid won't listen to a word I say.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no ko, zenzen iu koto o kikanai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちの子、全然言うことを聞かないんです。
examplePolite.english: My kid won't listen to a word I say.

items.notes: Parents' command: iu koto kikinasai.

items.english: deal with, take on (an opponent); (negative) ignore, not bother with
items.use: Two everyday uses. In the negative it means ignoring someone: aite ni shinakute ii (just ignore him), daremo aite ni shite kurenai (nobody pays me any attention), aite ni sarenai (get brushed off). In the positive it means dealing with or taking someone on: kodomo o aite ni suru shigoto (a job dealing with kids), dare o aite ni shiteru to omotteru no? (who do you think you're dealing with?). Don't confuse it with ate ni suru (count on).

example.romaji: anna yatsu, aite ni shinakute ii yo.
example.ja: あんなやつ、相手にしなくていいよ。
example.english: Just ignore a guy like that.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito no koto wa, aite ni shinakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの人のことは、相手にしなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Just ignore him.

items.notes: aite o suru (with o) = keep someone company, play with (kids).

items.english: speak to someone, be on speaking terms
items.use: Mostly negative, after a fight: mou kuchi kikanai (I'm not speaking to you), kuchi kiite kurenai (she won't talk to me); also namaiki na kuchi o kiku na (don't talk back). The kiku is 利く (work), so it isn't iu koto o kiku (obey).

example.romaji: kenka shite kara, kanojo ga kuchi kiite kurenai.
example.ja: 喧嘩してから、彼女が口きいてくれない。
example.english: Since our fight, she won't speak to me.

examplePolite.romaji: kenka shite kara, kanojo ga kuchi o kiite kurenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 喧嘩してから、彼女が口をきいてくれないんです。
examplePolite.english: Since our fight, she won't speak to me.

items.notes: Also kuchi o kiite morau = get someone to put in a good word.

items.use: Mostly in warnings and complaints: anmari ate ni shinaide (don't count on me too much), ano hito wa ate ni naranai (he's unreliable). Also for forecasts and promises; not aite ni suru (bother with someone).

example.romaji: anmari ate ni shinaide ne.
example.ja: あんまり当てにしないでね。
example.english: Don't count on me too much, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: amari ate ni shinaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: あまり当てにしないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please don't count on me too much.

items.notes: ate ni naranai = unreliable; plain alternative: tayoru.

blocks.label: Work and breaks
blocks.rationale: The arc of a workload: a mountain to do, no end in sight, a good place to stop, and a breather.
blocks.interference: kiri ga nai and kiri ga ii share kiri with opposite meanings: 'there's no end to it' versus 'a good point to stop'.

items.use: Everyday exaggeration for a huge amount, most often of work or things to do: yaru koto ga yama hodo aru. Yama hodo also goes before other verbs (yama hodo katta, iitai koto ga yama hodo aru).

example.romaji: yaru koto ga yama hodo aru n da yo
example.ja: やることが山ほどあるんだよ
example.english: I've got tons to do.

examplePolite.romaji: yaru koto ga yama hodo aru n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: やることが山ほどあるんですよ
examplePolite.english: I've got tons to do.

items.notes: Plain alternative: takusan aru, ippai aru.

items.english: take a breather, have a short break
items.use: Pausing after a stretch of work or a rush (chotto hitoiki tsukou), or feeling the pressure lift (yatto hitoiki tsuketa, I can finally breathe). Not yasumi o toru, which is taking days off.

example.romaji: chotto hitoiki tsukou ka
example.ja: ちょっと一息つこうか
example.english: Shall we take a breather?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto hitoiki tsukimashou ka
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと一息つきましょうか
examplePolite.english: Shall we take a breather?

items.notes: Also hitoiki ireru (take a short break); hotto hitoiki = a sigh of relief.

items.use: Said when something could go on forever, so you have to stop somewhere, usually after a -tara clause: ittara kiri ga nai (I could go on and on), ki ni shitara kiri ga nai. Not kiri ga ii, which is a good place to stop.

example.romaji: ki ni shidashitara kiri ga nai yo
example.ja: 気にしだしたらキリがないよ
example.english: Once you start worrying, there's no end to it.

examplePolite.romaji: ki ni shidashitara kiri ga nai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 気にしだしたらキリがないですよ
examplePolite.english: Once you start worrying, there's no end to it.

items.notes: Casually kiri nai; kiri ga arimasen is the formal, written-sounding version.

items.english: at a good stopping point; a nice round number
items.use: At work or study, a natural place to stop: kiri no ii tokoro de yasumou. Also a round number (kiri ga ii kara sen'en de ii yo); not kiri ga nai, which is endless.

example.romaji: kiri ga ii kara, kyou wa koko made ni shiyou
example.ja: キリがいいから、今日はここまでにしよう
example.english: Good place to stop, let's call it a day.

examplePolite.romaji: kiri ga ii node, kyou wa koko made ni shimashou
examplePolite.ja: キリがいいので、今日はここまでにしましょう
examplePolite.english: This is a good place to stop, let's call it a day.

items.notes: Also kugiri ga ii, same meaning.

blocks.label: Talk and secrets
blocks.rationale: The kuchi set for how someone talks: all talk, keeps secrets, sharp-tongued, blabs, smooth talker.
blocks.interference: kuchi ga katai (discreet) and kuchi ga karui (blabs) differ by one sound. kuchi ga warui (harsh) contrasts with kuchi ga umai (smooth). kuchi ni au (to one's taste) is in Tastes and likeness.

items.use: About someone who promises or boasts and never follows through, like a friend who always says he'll quit smoking: aitsu, kuchi dake da kara. Kuchi bakkari means the same, and kuchi dake ja nai (it's not just talk) defends someone.

example.romaji: aitsu, kuchi dake da kara.
example.ja: あいつ、口だけだから。
example.english: He's all talk.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, kuchi dake desu kara ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人、口だけですからね。
examplePolite.english: He's all talk, you know.

items.notes: Also kuchi bakkari, kuchisaki dake.

items.use: Reassurance when a secret is shared: kare wa kuchi ga katai kara daijoubu, or about yourself, watashi, kuchi katai kara. The pair to kuchi ga karui (can't keep a secret).

example.romaji: daijoubu, watashi, kuchi katai kara.
example.ja: 大丈夫、私、口堅いから。
example.english: Don't worry, I can keep a secret.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu, watashi, kuchi wa katai desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫です、私、口は堅いですから。
examplePolite.english: Don't worry, I won't tell anyone.

items.notes: Opposite: kuchi ga karui (can't keep a secret).

items.english: sharp-tongued, blunt to the point of rude
items.use: About how someone talks, not who they are, often defended in the same breath: kuchi wa warui kedo ne wa ii. Also an apology for your own bluntness: kuchi ga warukute gomen. Not kuchi ga karui (can't keep a secret).

example.romaji: gomen, kuchi ga warukute.
example.ja: ごめん、口が悪くて。
example.english: Sorry, I've got a sharp tongue.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kuchi ga warukute.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、口が悪くて。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I can be blunt.

items.use: A warning not to tell someone something, or a jab after a secret got out: ano ko, kuchi karui kara. The pair to kuchi ga katai; not kuchi ga warui (sharp-tongued).

example.romaji: ano ko, kuchi karui kara iwanai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: あの子、口軽いから言わない方がいいよ。
example.english: Better not tell her, she can't keep a secret.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa kuchi ga karui node, iwanai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は口が軽いので、言わない方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: She can't keep a secret, so better not tell her.

items.notes: Opposite: kuchi ga katai (can keep a secret).

items.english: smooth-talking, good with words (often of flattery or sales talk)
items.use: A warning about a salesperson or charmer who talks people round (kuchi ga umai kara ki o tsukete), or a laughing reply to a compliment: mata, kuchi ga umai n da kara. Not umai alone (tasty, good at).

example.romaji: kare, kuchi ga umai kara ki o tsukete.
example.ja: 彼、口がうまいから気をつけて。
example.english: He's a smooth talker, so watch out.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa kuchi ga umai node, ki o tsukete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は口がうまいので、気をつけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: He's a smooth talker, so do be careful.

items.notes: Also kuchi ga jouzu; written 口が上手い too. To someone's face in polite speech: mata, ojouzu desu ne / okuchi ga ojouzu desu ne.

blocks.label: Eyes on it
blocks.rationale: Where your eyes are held: not taking them off, setting them on someone, things catching them, being glued, keeping watch.
blocks.interference: me ni tsuku (it catches your eye) vs me o tsukeru (you single someone out): the particle flips who acts; me o hanasu na (don't look away) and me o hikaraseru (keep a sharp eye) both mean watching closely.

items.use: Said about kids, pets, bags or a suspect. It's mostly a warning (me o hanasu na, me o hanasanaide: don't let them out of your sight) or appears in chotto me o hanashita suki ni (the moment I looked away). Hanasu here is 離す (let go), not 話す (talk), and me o sorasu means looking away to avoid someone's eyes.

example.romaji: chotto me o hanashita suki ni inaku natta.
example.ja: ちょっと目を離した隙にいなくなった。
example.english: I looked away for a second and they were gone.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto me o hanashita suki ni inaku narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと目を離した隙にいなくなりました。
examplePolite.english: I looked away for a second and they were gone.

items.notes: Can't-look-away form: me ga hanasenai (gripping, or needs constant watching).

items.english: have your eye on; single someone out
items.use: Used for something or someone you want, like a bag, a house or a promising newcomer: zutto me o tsuketeta. The passive me o tsukerareta means you got on someone's bad side, and ii tokoro ni me o tsuketa ne praises someone for spotting the right point or angle. It's different from me ni tsuku, where the thing itself catches your eye.

example.romaji: zutto kono baggu ni me o tsuketeta n da.
example.ja: ずっとこのバッグに目をつけてたんだ。
example.english: I've had my eye on this bag for ages.

examplePolite.romaji: zutto kono baggu ni me o tsukete ita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: ずっとこのバッグに目をつけていたんです。
examplePolite.english: I've had my eye on this bag for ages.

items.notes: Plain alternative: nerau (go after, aim for).

items.use: The thing is the subject: a sign, a stain, a typo, someone's flaws. It often sounds slightly negative (warui toko bakari me ni tsuku). Hitome ni tsuku means being seen by other people. Me o tsukeru is different: you set your eyes on something you want.

example.romaji: kare no warui toko bakkari me ni tsuku.
example.ja: 彼の悪いとこばっかり目につく。
example.english: All I notice are his bad points.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no warui tokoro bakari me ni tsukimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の悪いところばかり目につきます。
examplePolite.english: All I notice are his bad points.

items.notes: Plain alternative: medatsu (stand out).

items.english: be glued to (a screen, a sight)
items.use: Said when your eyes or attention are stuck on something: a match on TV, a stunning view, someone gorgeous. It's usually said without naru, as X ni kugizuke (da/datta), and me ga kugizuke means your eyes were fixed on it. It also means stuck in place: ichinichijuu desuku ni kugizuke datta (chained to my desk all day).

example.romaji: minna terebi ni kugizuke datta yo.
example.ja: みんなテレビに釘付けだったよ。
example.english: Everyone was glued to the TV.

examplePolite.romaji: minna terebi ni kugizuke deshita yo.
examplePolite.ja: みんなテレビに釘付けでしたよ。
examplePolite.english: Everyone was glued to the TV.

items.use: Said of someone watching for trouble or rule-breaking: parents, teachers, a strict boss, the police. You'll hear it in the -teru form. Me ga hanasenai is needing to watch; me o hikaraseru is standing guard.

example.romaji: buchou ga me o hikaraseteru kara, sumaho tsukaenai.
example.ja: 部長が目を光らせてるから、スマホ使えない。
example.english: The boss is watching like a hawk, so no phones.

examplePolite.romaji: buchou ga me o hikaraseteru node, sumaho wa tsukaemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 部長が目を光らせてるので、スマホは使えませんね。
examplePolite.english: The boss is watching like a hawk, so no phones.

blocks.label: A rough time
blocks.rationale: Going through something bad, from one nasty experience to one blow after another.
blocks.interference: hidoi me ni au (an awful time) vs itai me ni au (paying for a mistake) share me ni au; ma ga warui (bad timing) sounds like ma ga sashita (a sudden lapse) in Getting carried away.

items.literal: meet a terrible eye (me = an experience)
items.use: How people tell any bad-experience story, from a ruined trip to being cheated. It is almost always in the past: hidoi me ni atta. Here me means 'experience', not 'eye'.

example.romaji: kinou hidoi me ni atta yo
example.ja: 昨日ひどい目に遭ったよ
example.english: I had an awful time yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou hidoi me ni aimashita yo
examplePolite.ja: 昨日ひどい目に遭いましたよ
examplePolite.english: I had an awful time yesterday.

items.notes: Stronger variant: sanzan na me ni atta; making someone suffer is hidoi me ni awaseru.

items.english: get hurt; get burned (pay for a mistake)
items.literal: meet a painful eye (me = an experience)
items.use: Three uses: a threat of harm (itai me ni aitakunakattara damatte ro, if you don't want to get hurt, shut up), a warning about consequences (amaku miteru to itai me ni au yo) and a look back (mukashi itai me ni atta). hidoi me is about having a bad time; itai me is about getting hurt or paying for a mistake.

example.romaji: amaku miteru to itai me ni au yo
example.ja: 甘く見てると痛い目に遭うよ
example.english: Take it lightly and you'll get burned.

examplePolite.romaji: amaku miteru to itai me ni aimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: 甘く見てると痛い目に遭いますよ
examplePolite.english: If you underestimate it, you'll get burned.

items.notes: Same meaning: itai me o miru; the threat 'you'll pay for this' is itai me ni awaseru zo.

items.english: it's no joke, it's seriously bad
items.use: A reaction to something that is past being funny, like dangerous heat, a huge bill or a prank gone wrong: kore wa share ni naranai. Casual speech shortens it to share ni nannai.

example.romaji: kono atsusa, share ni nannai yo
example.ja: この暑さ、シャレになんないよ
example.english: This heat is no joke.

examplePolite.romaji: kono atsusa wa share ni narimasen ne
examplePolite.ja: この暑さはシャレになりませんね
examplePolite.english: This heat is seriously no joke.

items.notes: Casual: share ni nannai; plain alternative: yabai.

items.use: Said when something happens at just the wrong moment, like walking in on an argument: ma ga warui naa. It also describes someone with a knack for bad timing. Before a noun it's ma no warui, and ma no warui koto ni means 'as (bad) luck would have it'. It isn't un ga warui, which means bad luck in general.

example.romaji: ma no warui koto ni, choudo kachou ga kita n da yo
example.ja: 間の悪いことに、ちょうど課長が来たんだよ
example.english: As luck would have it, the boss showed up right then.

examplePolite.romaji: ma no warui koto ni, choudo kachou ga kita n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 間の悪いことに、ちょうど課長が来たんですよ
examplePolite.english: As luck would have it, the boss showed up just then.

items.notes: Plain alternative: taimingu ga warui.

items.use: The bad-day summary when one blow lands on top of another: kyou wa fundari kettari da. Said about your own luck or, very often, in sympathy after a friend lists their mishaps (sore wa fundari kettari datta ne, what a run of bad luck).
items.politeJa: 踏んだり蹴ったりです

example.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni fundari kettari da yo.
example.ja: 今日は本当に踏んだり蹴ったりだよ。
example.english: Today's been one thing after another.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni fundari kettari deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当に踏んだり蹴ったりでした。
examplePolite.english: Today was one thing after another.

items.notes: Plain alternative: tsuitenai (I'm out of luck).

blocks.label: Hearing
blocks.rationale: The mimi idioms for hearing about something and for listening.
blocks.interference: mimi ni suru (you hear it) vs mimi ni hairu (word reaches you) vs komimi ni hasamu (you catch it in passing); mimi o kasu is listening, and is mostly said in the negative.

items.use: A slightly more formal way to say you hear a word, name or rumour in passing: saikin yoku mimi ni suru (you hear it a lot lately), hajimete mimi ni shita (first I've heard of it). It's hearing by chance, not listening on purpose (that's kiku); news reaching you is mimi ni hairu.

example.romaji: sono hanashi, saikin yoku mimi ni suru yo ne.
example.ja: その話、最近よく耳にするよね。
example.english: You hear about that a lot lately, don't you?

examplePolite.romaji: sono hanashi, saikin yoku mimi ni shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: その話、最近よく耳にしますね。
examplePolite.english: You hear about that a lot these days.

items.notes: Plain alternative: kiku (sono hanashi kiita).

items.english: heed, give someone a hearing (mostly 'won't listen'); lean in so I can whisper
items.use: Mostly negative, about ignoring advice or pleas: dare no iu koto ni mo mimi o kasanai (won't listen to anyone), ano hito no hanashi ni mimi o kasu na (don't listen to him). In casual talk, chotto mimi kashite means 'come here, let me whisper something'. Ordinary 'listen' is still kiku.

example.romaji: chotto mimi kashite.
example.ja: ちょっと耳貸して。
example.english: Come here, let me whisper something.

examplePolite.romaji: buchou, sukoshi wa genba no koe ni mo mimi o kashite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 部長、少しは現場の声にも耳を貸してください。
examplePolite.english: Please listen to the people on the ground for once.

items.english: reach someone's ears, get word of
items.use: News or a rumour reaching someone, often someone it shouldn't: buchou no mimi ni haittara yabai (if this gets back to the boss, we're in trouble). Unlike mimi ni suru, the news is the subject; you just end up knowing. In the negative it can also mean you can't take in what's said: hanashi ga zenzen mimi ni haitte konai (I can't take in a word).

example.romaji: sono uwasa, mou mimi ni haitteru yo.
example.ja: その噂、もう耳に入ってるよ。
example.english: That rumour's already reached me.

examplePolite.romaji: sono ken wa mou buchou no mimi ni haitte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: その件はもう部長の耳に入っています。
examplePolite.english: The manager has already heard about that.

items.notes: At work, the transitive form tells a superior something: omimi ni irete okitai koto ga arimasu (there's something I'd like you to know).

items.english: happen to hear, catch wind of
items.literal: pinch it in the ear, just a little (ko-: slightly)
items.use: Almost always in the past as a gossip opener: komimi ni hasanda n da kedo... (I happened to hear that...). It signals you heard it in passing and aren't sure it's true, which is softer than saying who told you.

example.romaji: komimi ni hasanda n da kedo, tanaka-san yameru no?
example.ja: 小耳に挟んだんだけど、田中さん辞めるの？
example.english: I happened to hear something. Is Tanaka quitting?

examplePolite.romaji: komimi ni hasanda n desu kedo, tanaka-san ga yameru tte hontou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 小耳に挟んだんですけど、田中さんが辞めるって本当ですか？
examplePolite.english: I happened to hear something. Is it true Tanaka is leaving?

blocks.label: In the mood
blocks.rationale: Being willing or not to do something: change your mind, feel like it, not keen, feel bad doing it.
blocks.interference: All ki ga + verb: ki ga noranai (not in the mood) vs ki ga susumanai (reluctant), ki ga muku is the positive.

items.use: Mostly in the past (ki ga kawatta, I changed my mind) and in ki ga kawaranai uchi ni (before I change my mind). It's about plans and intentions; a changed opinion is kangae ga kawaru.

example.romaji: yappari ikanai. ki ga kawatta.
example.ja: やっぱり行かない。気が変わった。
example.english: Actually, I'm not going. I changed my mind.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ki ga kawatte, yappari ikanai koto ni shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、気が変わって、やっぱり行かないことにしました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I changed my mind and decided not to go after all.

items.notes: ki ga kawattara oshiete = let me know if you change your mind.

items.use: A soft way to say you'd rather not, often to turn something down: chotto ki ga susumanai n da kedo. Almost always negative. Ki ga noranai is about your mood right now, while ki ga susumanai is reluctance about the thing itself.

example.romaji: ano nomikai, ki ga susumanai n da yo ne.
example.ja: あの飲み会、気が進まないんだよね。
example.english: I'm not too keen on that drinking party.

examplePolite.romaji: sono hanashi wa chotto ki ga susumimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: その話はちょっと気が進みませんね。
examplePolite.english: I'm a little reluctant about that idea.

items.notes: Blunter one-word alternative: iya.

items.use: Not having the mood or energy for something right now: kyou wa ki ga noranai. Ki ga susumanai is reluctance about the thing itself, and the positive ki ga noru is much rarer.

example.romaji: kyou wa nanka ki ga noranai.
example.ja: 今日はなんか気が乗らない。
example.english: I'm just not feeling it today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa chotto ki ga noranai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はちょっと気が乗らないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm just not in the mood today.

items.notes: Also said: kinori shinai (from the noun kinori).

items.use: Mostly heard as ki ga muitara (whenever you feel like it), the no-pressure invitation, and as ki ga mukanai (don't feel like it). Also ki ga muita toki ni (when the mood takes me).

example.romaji: ki ga muitara asobi ni kite ne.
example.ja: 気が向いたら遊びに来てね。
example.english: Come over whenever you feel like it.

examplePolite.romaji: ki ga muitara, itsu demo asobi ni kite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 気が向いたら、いつでも遊びに来てくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Drop by any time you feel like it.

items.use: Said when doing something feels like imposing or taking too much: zenbu ogotte morau no wa ki ga hikeru. Ki ga susumanai is plain reluctance, while ki ga hikeru is reluctance out of guilt or modesty.

example.romaji: zenbu ogotte morau no wa ki ga hikeru yo.
example.ja: 全部おごってもらうのは気が引けるよ。
example.english: I'd feel bad letting you pay for everything.

examplePolite.romaji: zenbu gochisou ni naru no wa ki ga hikemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 全部ごちそうになるのは気が引けます。
examplePolite.english: I'd feel bad letting you treat me to all of it.

items.notes: Plain alternatives: moushiwakenai, warui (I feel bad).

blocks.label: Butting in
blocks.rationale: Getting your hand, mouth or neck into someone else's business, plus the retort to it.
blocks.interference: te o dasu (lay a finger on, get mixed up in) vs kuchi o dasu (butt in) swap only the body part; kao o dasu (show up) is in At a get-together.

items.english: hit, lay a finger on; get into (drugs, stocks); make a move on (someone)
items.use: Mostly heard as a warning or in a fight: te o dasu na (hands off), saki ni te o dashita (threw the first punch). It also means getting into something new (kabu ni te o dasu) or making a move on someone. Literally it's also 'hold out your hand' (te o dashite). Don't mix it up with kuchi o dasu (butt in) or kao o dasu (show up).

example.romaji: saki ni te dashita no wa mukou da yo.
example.ja: 先に手出したのは向こうだよ。
example.english: They're the ones who threw the first punch.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni te o dashita no wa mukou desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 先に手を出したのは向こうですよ。
examplePolite.english: They're the ones who threw the first punch.

items.notes: Noun: tedashi (tedashi suru na = keep out of it).

items.use: A complaint or warning about interfering in someone's decisions: kuchi dasanaide (stay out of it), oya ga sugu kuchi o dasu. Unlike kuchi o hasamu (cut into a conversation), it's meddling in what isn't yours to decide.

example.romaji: kore wa watashi no mondai da kara, kuchi dasanaide.
example.ja: これは私の問題だから、口出さないで。
example.english: This is my problem, so stay out of it.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa watashi no mondai desu kara, kuchi o dasanaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これは私の問題ですから、口を出さないでください。
examplePolite.english: This is my problem, so please stay out of it.

items.notes: Noun: kuchidashi (kuchidashi shinaide).

items.use: The snappy comeback to advice nobody asked for, usually yokei na osewa da (yo). Said to friends, family or rivals, never to someone above you; osewa here is sarcastic, unlike thankful osewa ni naru.

example.romaji: yokei na osewa da yo. hottoite.
example.ja: 余計なお世話だよ。ほっといて。
example.english: None of your business. Leave me alone.

items.notes: Variant: ookina osewa (da).

items.english: poke your nose in, get mixed up in
items.use: A warning or complaint about getting involved in what isn't yours: yokei na koto ni kubi tsukkomu na. Unlike kuchi o dasu (butting in with advice), you actually wade in.

example.romaji: yokei na koto ni kubi tsukkomanai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 余計なことに首突っ込まないほうがいいよ。
example.english: Better not stick your nose in other people's business.

examplePolite.romaji: yokei na koto ni wa kubi o tsukkomanai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 余計なことには首を突っ込まないほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's better not to get mixed up in other people's business.

blocks.label: Smart or crazy
blocks.rationale: What someone's head is like: off its hinges, sharp, a quick thinker, quick to pick things up.
blocks.interference: atama ga kireru (sharp) is easy to confuse with plain kireru (snap) and with atama ga okashii (crazy). atama no kaiten ga hayai (fast thinker) and nomikomi ga hayai (fast learner) both end in ga hayai.

items.use: A blunt jab at someone acting crazy: atama okashii n ja nai? (ga is often dropped in speech), or about a third person, ano hito atama okashii yo. About yourself, atama okashiku narisou (I'm going to lose my mind) is a safe everyday complaint. Harsher than dou ka shiteru (you're not yourself).

example.romaji: atama okashii n ja nai?
example.ja: 頭おかしいんじゃない？
example.english: Are you out of your mind?

items.notes: About yourself: atama okashiku narisou (I'm going to lose my mind); for just 'weird', hen.

items.literal: the head cuts well (like a blade)
items.use: Said admiringly of a sharp strategist, lawyer or boss, or warily of an opponent: hannin wa atama ga kireru; before a noun, atama no kireru hito. Not kireru alone, which means snap or lose it (ano hito sugu kireru).

example.romaji: ano bengoshi, kanari atama kireru yo.
example.ja: あの弁護士、かなり頭切れるよ。
example.english: That lawyer's really sharp.

examplePolite.romaji: ano bengoshi-san wa atama ga kiremasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの弁護士さんは頭が切れますよ。
examplePolite.english: That lawyer is very sharp.

items.notes: Plain: atama ga ii (smart); kireru alone = snap, lose your temper.

items.polite: atama no kaiten ga hayai desu
items.use: Praise for someone who thinks and answers fast, like a sharp debater or a friend with quick comebacks: atama no kaiten hayai ne. Different from atama ga ii (smart, does well at school); the opposite is atama no kaiten ga osoi.
items.kana: あたまのかいてんがはやい

example.romaji: kare, atama no kaiten hayai yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、頭の回転速いよね。
example.english: He's a really quick thinker.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa atama no kaiten ga hayai desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は頭の回転が速いですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's very quick-witted, isn't he?

items.notes: Close: atama ga kireru (sharp, brilliant) and nomikomi ga hayai (a quick learner).

items.use: Praise for a new hire, student or kid who picks up a task fast: nomikomi hayai ne! The opposite nomikomi ga warui (slow on the uptake) is often said of yourself: nomikomi ga warukute sumimasen. It's about learning; atama no kaiten ga hayai is about thinking on your feet.

example.romaji: nomikomi hayai ne! mou oboeta no?
example.ja: 飲み込み早いね！もう覚えたの？
example.english: You're a quick learner! You've got it already?

examplePolite.romaji: nomikomi ga hayai desu ne! mou oboeta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 飲み込みが早いですね！もう覚えたんですか？
examplePolite.english: You pick things up fast! You've learned it already?

items.notes: Opposite: nomikomi ga warui (slow to pick things up).

blocks.label: Doesn't add up
blocks.rationale: Judging whether something makes sense, from baffling to logical but it still won't sit right.
blocks.interference: suji ga tooru (it holds together) vs tsujitsuma ga awanai (the details clash); wake ga wakaranai (makes no sense) vs nani ga nan da ka wakaranai (lost about what's going on); fu ni ochinai is a feeling that persists even when the logic works.

items.english: makes no sense at all, baffling
items.use: Your reaction when a situation, a rule or someone's behaviour is baffling or absurd; casually wake wakannai. In quick reactions it swaps freely with imi wakannai, but only wake works before a noun: wake no wakannai koto iwanaide (don't talk nonsense). Aimed at what the listener just said, it's blunt even in polite form.

example.romaji: kono ruuru, chotto wake wakannai yo ne.
example.ja: このルール、ちょっとわけわかんないよね。
example.english: This rule doesn't make any sense, does it?

examplePolite.romaji: kono ruuru, chotto wake ga wakarimasen yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: このルール、ちょっと訳が分かりませんよね。
examplePolite.english: This rule doesn't make any sense, does it?

items.notes: Before a noun: wake no wakaranai hito (a weirdo); slangy one word: imifu (makes no sense).

items.english: make sense, be fair and logical
items.use: Often negative, about a demand, an excuse or a way of doing things that isn't logical or fair: sore wa suji ga tooranai (that's not right). The positive is suji ga tootteru or suji no tootta hanashi (a reasonable argument). Tsujitsuma ga awanai is different: a story that contradicts itself.

example.romaji: sore ja suji ga tooranai yo.
example.ja: それじゃ筋が通らないよ。
example.english: That doesn't make sense, and it isn't fair.

examplePolite.romaji: sore de wa suji ga toorimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: それでは筋が通りませんよ。
examplePolite.english: That doesn't make sense, and it isn't fair.

items.notes: Related: suji o toosu (do it properly, through the right channels).

items.literal: the seams and hems don't meet
items.use: Said when a story, an alibi or an excuse contradicts itself: hanashi no tsujitsuma ga awanai. It's mostly negative, and tsujitsuma o awaseru means patching a story so it fits. Fu ni ochinai is about your own feeling of not being convinced.

example.romaji: sore, sakki no hanashi to tsujitsuma awanai jan.
example.ja: それ、さっきの話とつじつま合わないじゃん。
example.english: That doesn't match what you said earlier.

examplePolite.romaji: sore, sakki no ohanashi to tsujitsuma ga aimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: それ、さっきのお話とつじつまが合いませんね。
examplePolite.english: That doesn't match what you said earlier.

items.notes: Plain alternative: mujun shiteru (it's contradictory).

items.romaji: nani ga nan da ka wakaranai
items.polite: nani ga nan da ka wakarimasen
items.english: have no idea what's going on
items.use: Said when too much happens at once or something comes out of nowhere and you're lost. It's often cut short to nani ga nan da ka. Wake ga wakaranai judges something as absurd; this one is just being lost.
items.ja: 何が何だか分からない
items.kana: なにがなんだかわからない
items.politeJa: 何が何だか分かりません

example.romaji: kyuu ni sonna koto iwarete mo, nani ga nan da ka wakannai yo.
example.ja: 急にそんなこと言われても、何が何だか分かんないよ。
example.english: You can't just spring that on me. I've no idea what's going on.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni sonna koto o iwarete mo, nani ga nan da ka wakarimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 急にそんなことを言われても、何が何だか分かりませんよ。
examplePolite.english: You can't just spring that on me. I've no idea what's going on.

items.notes: Casual: nani ga nan da ka wakannai, or just nani ga nan da ka.

items.english: can't quite accept it, doesn't sit right
items.use: Said when an explanation or a result leaves you unconvinced, even if you can't say why: nanka fu ni ochinai. It's almost always negative and about your own feeling, unlike tsujitsuma ga awanai, where the story itself contradicts.

example.romaji: setsumei wa kiita kedo, nanka fu ni ochinai.
example.ja: 説明は聞いたけど、なんか腑に落ちない。
example.english: I heard the explanation, but something doesn't sit right.

examplePolite.romaji: setsumei wa kikimashita kedo, dou mo fu ni ochinai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 説明は聞きましたけど、どうも腑に落ちないんです。
examplePolite.english: I heard the explanation, but something just doesn't sit right.

items.notes: Plain alternative: nattoku dekinai (I'm not convinced).

blocks.label: Out of a job
blocks.rationale: Being fired, firing someone, or leaving a shady line of work behind.
blocks.interference: kubi ni naru (you get fired) vs kubi ni suru (you fire someone); ashi o arau is quitting by choice, not being fired.

items.use: The everyday way to say you or someone else lost a job. It is nearly always in the past (kubi ni natta), or just kubi da. It is not for quitting by choice, which is yameru.

example.romaji: kare, kaisha kubi ni natta rashii yo
example.ja: 彼、会社クビになったらしいよ
example.english: Apparently he got fired.

examplePolite.romaji: kare, kaisha o kubi ni natta rashii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 彼、会社をクビになったらしいですよ
examplePolite.english: I hear he was let go from his company.

items.notes: A bare kubi! means 'You're fired!'; the formal word is kaiko sareru.

items.use: The boss's side of firing. You hear it as a threat (kubi ni suru zo) or in the passive from the person who lost the job (kubi ni sareta). Use kubi ni naru for a plain 'got fired' that doesn't say who did it.

example.romaji: tenchou ni kubi ni sareta
example.ja: 店長にクビにされた
example.english: The manager fired me.

examplePolite.romaji: tenchou ni kubi ni saremashita
examplePolite.ja: 店長にクビにされました
examplePolite.english: The manager let me go.

items.notes: Formal equivalent: kaiko suru (dismiss).

items.english: go straight, quit a shady life
items.use: Said about leaving crime, gambling or a dubious job for good, and jokingly about any bad habit: X kara ashi o arau. It does not mean 'wash one's hands of', which is te o hiku.

example.romaji: pachinko kara wa mou ashi o aratta yo
example.ja: パチンコからはもう足を洗ったよ
example.english: I've quit pachinko for good.

examplePolite.romaji: pachinko kara wa mou ashi o araimashita
examplePolite.ja: パチンコからはもう足を洗いました
examplePolite.english: I've given up pachinko for good.

items.notes: Plain alternative: yameru (quit).

blocks.label: About the talk
blocks.rationale: Four fixed hanashi remarks about where a discussion stands.
blocks.interference: hanashi ga chigau (not what we agreed) vs hanashi wa betsu (a separate matter); hanashi ni naranai (hopeless) vs hanashi ga hayai (that makes it easy).

items.english: that's not what we agreed; that's a different matter
items.use: The complaint when the terms or plan turn out different from what you were told: chotto, hanashi ga chigau ja nai (hey, that's not what you said). It also means 'that's a different matter': sore to kore to wa hanashi ga chigau (those are two different things), akaji ni naru nara hanashi ga chigau (if we'd lose money, that changes things). There it overlaps with hanashi wa betsu.

example.romaji: e, kyuuryou sagaru no? hanashi ga chigau yo.
example.ja: え、給料下がるの？話が違うよ。
example.english: What, my pay's going down? That's not what we agreed.

examplePolite.romaji: e, kyuuryou ga sagaru n desu ka? hanashi ga chigaimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: え、給料が下がるんですか？話が違いますよ。
examplePolite.english: My pay is going down? That's not what we agreed.

items.use: Dismisses an offer, an excuse or someone's performance as too poor to even talk about: kono nedan ja hanashi ni naranai (at this price, forget it). Said of a person, ano hito ja hanashi ni naranai means there's no reasoning with them.

example.romaji: ichiman en? sore ja hanashi ni naranai yo.
example.ja: 一万円？それじゃ話にならないよ。
example.english: Ten thousand yen? That's not even worth discussing.

examplePolite.romaji: ichiman en desu ka? sore ja hanashi ni narimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 一万円ですか？それじゃ話になりませんよ。
examplePolite.english: Ten thousand yen? That's out of the question.

items.notes: Casual: hanashi ni nannai.

items.use: Follows a condition that changes your answer: X nara hanashi wa betsu da (if it's X, that changes things), typically when an offer gets better. hanashi ga chigau can say the same thing (X nara hanashi ga chigau), but its everyday use is the complaint that a deal was changed on you.

example.romaji: ogori nara hanashi wa betsu da yo.
example.ja: おごりなら話は別だよ。
example.english: If it's your treat, that's a different story.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuuryou ga agaru nara hanashi wa betsu desu kedo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 給料が上がるなら話は別ですけどね。
examplePolite.english: If the pay went up, that'd be a different story.

items.english: that makes it easy, that saves explaining
items.use: Said when the other person already knows or agrees, so you can skip the explaining: sore nara hanashi ga hayai (well, that makes it easy). Said of a person, it means they catch on fast. It has nothing to do with talking fast, which is hayakuchi.

example.romaji: shitteru nara hanashi ga hayai ne.
example.ja: 知ってるなら話が早いね。
example.english: If you already know, that makes it easy.

examplePolite.romaji: gozonji nara hanashi ga hayai desu.
examplePolite.ja: ご存じなら話が早いです。
examplePolite.english: If you already know, that makes things easier.

items.notes: Also: hanashi wa hayai.

blocks.label: Owing favours
blocks.rationale: Asking for, accepting and owing favours.
blocks.interference: kari ga aru (I owe you one) is a debt to repay while on ni kiru (I'm deeply grateful) is thanks; okotoba ni amaete accepts an offer, isshou no onegai begs for one.

items.use: Said when someone has done you a favour you haven't repaid: ano hito ni wa kari ga aru. kari ga dekita (now I owe you) and kari o kaesu (pay it back) go with it; it's mostly favours, since a money debt is usually shakkin ga aru.

example.romaji: ano hito ni wa kari ga aru kara, kotowarenai.
example.ja: あの人には借りがあるから、断れない。
example.english: I owe him one, so I can't say no.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito ni wa kari ga aru node, kotowarenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの人には借りがあるので、断れないんです。
examplePolite.english: I owe him one, so I can't say no.

items.notes: Flip side: kashi ga aru / kore de kashi hitotsu ne (now you owe me one). Even again: kore de kashikari nashi.

items.english: I'll gladly take you up on that
items.englishIdiom: I'll take you up on that
items.use: The fixed way to accept an offer (a ride, a treat, staying over) after first holding back: jaa, okotoba ni amaete. Said to hosts, seniors and colleagues, and jokingly to friends.
items.politeJa: お言葉に甘えさせていただきます

example.romaji: ii no? jaa, okotoba ni amaete!
example.ja: いいの？じゃあ、お言葉に甘えて！
example.english: Really? Well, if you insist!

examplePolite.romaji: ii n desu ka? jaa, okotoba ni amaesasete itadakimasu.
examplePolite.ja: いいんですか？じゃあ、お言葉に甘えさせていただきます。
examplePolite.english: Are you sure? Then I'll gladly take you up on it.

items.english: please, I'm begging you (just this once)
items.use: The dramatic plea among friends and siblings, or from kids to parents, often with hands pressed together: isshou no onegai! To a teacher or senior it's isshou no onegai desu. Everyone uses it again and again despite the name, which is half the joke.
items.kana: いっしょうのおねがい

example.romaji: isshou no onegai! konkai dake okane kashite.
example.ja: 一生のお願い！今回だけお金貸して。
example.english: I'm begging you! Lend me some money just this once.

examplePolite.romaji: isshou no onegai desu! konkai dake minogashite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 一生のお願いです！今回だけ見逃してください。
examplePolite.english: I'm begging you! Just let it slide this once.

items.english: I owe you big, I'm really grateful
items.use: A heartfelt, slightly old-school thank-you when someone bails you out, mostly men among friends: warui na, on ni kiru yo. kari ga aru describes the debt; this is the thanks you say on the spot.

example.romaji: warui na, on ni kiru yo.
example.ja: 悪いな、恩に着るよ。
example.english: Thanks, man. I owe you big.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou ni tasukarimashita. on ni kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 本当に助かりました。恩に着ます。
examplePolite.english: You really saved me. I owe you big.

items.notes: on o kaesu = repay a kindness; onkisegamashii = making a big show of a favour.

blocks.label: Wrong words
blocks.rationale: Shutting down what someone said, and walking back what you said yourself.
blocks.interference: baka iwanaide (don't talk nonsense) vs engi demo nai (don't jinx it); kotoba no aya (just a figure of speech) vs kokoro ni mo nai koto o iu (said in anger, not meant).

items.english: don't be silly, don't talk nonsense
items.use: Brushes off a ridiculous idea, or reassures someone who is putting themselves down: baka iwanaide, sonna wake nai desho (don't be silly, of course not). The rougher, mostly male form is baka iu na. In polite speech it becomes baka na koto iwanaide kudasai, which is still quite direct.
items.politeJa: バカなこと言わないでください

example.romaji: baka iwanaide, sonna wake nai desho.
example.ja: バカ言わないで、そんなわけないでしょ。
example.english: Don't be silly, of course not.

examplePolite.romaji: baka na koto iwanaide kudasai yo, sonna wake nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: バカなこと言わないでくださいよ、そんなわけないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Don't be silly, that's not true at all.

items.notes: Rougher, mostly male: baka iu na; baka ie (nonsense!, a flat rebuttal).

items.english: just a figure of speech, not meant literally
items.use: The standard backpedal when someone takes your words too literally or too hard: ima no wa kotoba no aya da yo (that was just a way of putting it). Aya is the pattern woven into cloth.

example.romaji: gomen, ima no wa kotoba no aya da yo.
example.ja: ごめん、今のは言葉のあやだよ。
example.english: Sorry, that was just a figure of speech.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima no wa kotoba no aya desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今のは言葉のあやです。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I didn't mean that literally.

items.romaji: kokoro ni mo nai koto o iu
items.polite: kokoro ni mo nai koto o iimasu
items.literal: say things that aren't even in your heart
items.use: Mostly in apologies after a fight: kokoro ni mo nai koto itchatta (I said things I didn't mean). The phrase kokoro ni mo nai also goes with flattery you don't mean: kokoro ni mo nai oseji.
items.ja: 心にもないことを言う
items.kana: こころにもないことをいう
items.politeJa: 心にもないことを言います

example.romaji: tsui katto natte, kokoro ni mo nai koto itchatta.
example.ja: ついカッとなって、心にもないこと言っちゃった。
example.english: I lost my temper and said things I didn't mean.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui katto natte, kokoro ni mo nai koto o itte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ついカッとなって、心にもないことを言ってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I lost my temper and said something I didn't mean.

items.english: don't say such ominous things, perish the thought
items.use: The quick rebuke when someone mentions death, illness, an accident or failure, even as a joke: engi demo nai koto iwanaide (don't say things like that). Engi is luck or omen, as in engi ga ii / engi ga warui.

example.romaji: chotto, engi demo nai koto iwanaide yo.
example.ja: ちょっと、縁起でもないこと言わないでよ。
example.english: Hey, bite your tongue! Don't say things like that.

examplePolite.romaji: engi demo nai koto iwanaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: 縁起でもないこと言わないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Please don't say such ominous things.

blocks.label: Having someone's back
blocks.rationale: Caring about someone, urging them on and taking their side.
blocks.interference: ki ni kakeru (look out for someone) sounds like ki ni kakaru / ki ni suru elsewhere; senaka o osu (push them to go for it) vs kata o motsu (take their side).

items.english: be concerned about, look out for (someone)
items.use: Warm concern for how a person is doing, heard most as thanks: itsumo ki ni kakete kurete arigatou (thanks for always looking out for me). Not ki ni suru (mind, worry about), which is fretting over a thing.

example.romaji: itsumo ki ni kakete kurete, arigatou ne.
example.ja: いつも気にかけてくれて、ありがとうね。
example.english: Thanks for always looking out for me.

examplePolite.romaji: itsumo ki ni kakete itadaite, arigatou gozaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: いつも気にかけていただいて、ありがとうございます。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for always looking out for me.

items.notes: Intransitive partner: ki ni kakaru (weigh on your mind), e.g. sore ga zutto ki ni kakatteta.

items.english: encourage someone to go for it
items.use: Thanking or describing someone who gave you the courage to act, usually -te kureta: ano hito ga senaka o oshite kureta. Different from kata o motsu, which is taking someone's side in a dispute.

example.romaji: tomodachi ga senaka oshite kureta n da.
example.ja: 友達が背中押してくれたんだ。
example.english: My friend gave me the push I needed.

examplePolite.romaji: tomodachi ga senaka o oshite kureta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 友達が背中を押してくれたんです。
examplePolite.english: My friend gave me the push I needed.

items.use: A staple of arguments and family fights, usually a complaint about unfair favouring: dotchi no kata motsu no? (whose side are you on?). Different from senaka o osu, which is encouraging someone to act.

example.romaji: nande itsumo ano ko no kata motsu no?
example.ja: なんでいつもあの子の肩持つの？
example.english: Why do you always take her side?

examplePolite.romaji: doushite itsumo ano hito no kata o motsu n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どうしていつもあの人の肩を持つんですか？
examplePolite.english: Why do you always take her side?

blocks.label: Not yourself
blocks.rationale: Someone, or your own head, not working the way it usually does.
blocks.interference: dou ka shiteru (you've lost it) and dou iu kaze no fukimawashi (what's got into you, often at sudden kindness) both open with dou; atama ga mawaranai blurs with kuchi ga mawaranai and the busy list's te ga mawaranai.

items.english: be out of one's mind, not be oneself
items.use: Said to someone acting crazy (anta dou ka shiteru yo: you've lost it), or about yourself in the past as an apology: gomen, dou ka shiteta (sorry, I wasn't myself). Also about a situation: kono atsusa, dou ka shiteru (this heat is crazy). Don't confuse it with the question dou ka shita? (is something wrong?). Atama ga okashii is the harsher 'you're crazy'.

example.romaji: gomen, sakki wa dou ka shiteta.
example.ja: ごめん、さっきはどうかしてた。
example.english: Sorry, I wasn't myself earlier.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sakki wa dou ka shite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、さっきはどうかしていました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I wasn't myself earlier.

items.notes: Plain alternative: okashii yo (you're acting weird).

items.use: The everyday excuse when you're tired, hungry or hungover: nebusoku de atama mawannai. Casual speech squashes it to mawannai. Atama ga masshiro ni naru is different: your mind goes blank in a panic.

example.romaji: nebusoku de atama mawannai.
example.ja: 寝不足で頭回んない。
example.english: I'm too short on sleep to think straight.

examplePolite.romaji: nebusoku de atama ga mawarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 寝不足で頭が回りません。
examplePolite.english: I'm too short on sleep to think straight.

items.notes: Positive: atama ga yoku mawaru (quick-witted). Don't confuse with kuchi ga mawaranai (can't get the words out).

items.polite: dou iu kaze no fukimawashi desu ka
items.english: what's brought this on? (someone acting out of character)
items.literal: what kind of turn of the wind
items.use: A teasing question when someone does something out of character, like cooking, paying or cleaning, or turns up or calls out of the blue: dou iu kaze no fukimawashi de koko e? About someone else: dou iu kaze no fukimawashi ka, kare ga tetsudatte kureta (for some reason, he helped out).
items.ja: どういう風の吹き回し
items.kana: どういうかぜのふきまわし
items.politeJa: どういう風の吹き回しですか

example.romaji: ogotte kureru nante, dou iu kaze no fukimawashi?
example.ja: おごってくれるなんて、どういう風の吹き回し？
example.english: You're treating me? What's gotten into you?

examplePolite.romaji: senpai ga ogotte kureru nante, dou iu kaze no fukimawashi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 先輩がおごってくれるなんて、どういう風の吹き回しですか？
examplePolite.english: You're treating me? What's gotten into you?

blocks.label: Learning a skill
blocks.rationale: Progress on something new: start on it, get the knack, hit a wall, keep adding up, until it is yours.
blocks.interference: mi ni tsukeru and te o tsukeru share tsukeru: mi means making a skill your own, while te means starting on a task (or touching food or money).

items.english: pick up (a skill or habit); wear
items.use: How people talk about gaining skills, knowledge and habits through practice: eigo o mi ni tsuketai, shuukan o mi ni tsukeru; the intransitive mi ni tsuku (it sticks) is just as common. With clothes and accessories it means wear or carry on you, a more formal ring than kiru.

example.romaji: shigoto shinagara mi ni tsuketa n da
example.ja: 仕事しながら身につけたんだ
example.english: I picked it up on the job.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto shinagara mi ni tsuketa n desu
examplePolite.ja: 仕事しながら身につけたんです
examplePolite.english: I picked it up on the job.

items.notes: Intransitive: renshuu shinai to mi ni tsukanai (it won't stick without practice).

items.english: start on (a task); touch (food); dip into (money)
items.use: Two everyday shapes: doko kara te o tsukereba ii ka wakaranai (don't know where to start) and mada zenzen te tsuketenai (haven't even started). The thing takes ni, and it also covers food and money: gohan ni te o tsuketenai (hasn't touched the food), chokin ni te o tsukeru (dip into savings), kaisha no kane ni te o tsukeru (help yourself to company money). In speech the o often drops.

example.romaji: repooto, mada zenzen te tsuketenai
example.ja: レポート、まだ全然手つけてない
example.english: I haven't even started on the report.

examplePolite.romaji: repooto, mada zenzen te o tsuketenai n desu
examplePolite.ja: レポート、まだ全然手をつけてないんです
examplePolite.english: I haven't even started on the report.

items.notes: Plain alternative: hajimeru (start). With a person as the object it means something else: onna ni te o tsukeru is taking a woman in your charge as a lover (drama talk; everyday speech says te o dasu).

items.english: get the knack, get the feel of it
items.use: Said whenever a skill, sport, game or job starts to click: yatto kotsu tsukanda!, and while it is happening, kotsu ga tsukamete kita (I'm getting the hang of it). The o often drops in casual speech, and kotsu alone is the trick to something (kotsu o oshiete, tell me the trick).

example.romaji: yatto kotsu tsukanda kamo
example.ja: やっとコツつかんだかも
example.english: I think I've finally got the hang of it.

examplePolite.romaji: yatto kotsu o tsukanda ki ga shimasu
examplePolite.ja: やっとコツをつかんだ気がします
examplePolite.english: I think I've finally got the hang of it.

items.notes: Plain alternative: kotsu ga wakatte kita (it's starting to click) or dekiru you ni natta (I can do it now).

items.english: hit a wall, stop making progress
items.use: How learners, athletes and workers describe a plateau or obstacle, usually as -teru (stuck now) or -ta: ima chotto kabe ni butsukatteru. The same words describe literally walking into a wall.

example.romaji: nihongo, ima kabe ni butsukatteru n da
example.ja: 日本語、今壁にぶつかってるんだ
example.english: I've hit a wall with my Japanese right now.

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo, ima kabe ni butsukatte iru n desu
examplePolite.ja: 日本語、今壁にぶつかっているんです
examplePolite.english: I've hit a wall with my Japanese right now.

items.notes: Getting past it: kabe o koeru / norikoeru.

items.romaji: chiri mo tsumoreba yama to naru
items.literal: even dust, piled up, becomes a mountain
items.use: Said about saving small change, daily study or small habits that build up, and about small costs that add up. Often only the first half is said (chiri mo tsumoreba...).
items.ja: 塵も積もれば山となる
items.kana: ちりもつもればやまとなる

example.romaji: chiri mo tsumoreba yama to naru tte ne
example.ja: 塵も積もれば山となるってね
example.english: Little things add up, as they say.

examplePolite.romaji: chiri mo tsumoreba yama to naru tte iimasu kara ne
examplePolite.ja: 塵も積もれば山となるって言いますからね
examplePolite.english: Little things add up, as they say.

items.notes: Slang short form: chiritsumo.

blocks.label: Skill and judgement
blocks.rationale: How capable someone is: a poor judge, skilled hands, shrewd, savvy.
