blocks.interference: miru me ga nai (poor judge, criticism) and nukeme ga nai (shrewd, praise) share 'ga nai' but are opposite in tone. youryou ga ii can hint at cutting corners; ude ga ii never does.

items.english: be a poor judge (of people or things)
items.use: Mostly about picking the wrong partner or hiring the wrong person (otoko o miru me ga nai), and as praise, miru me aru ne (you've got a good eye). Not me ga nai, which means you can't resist something.

example.romaji: watashi tte, otoko o miru me nai naa.
example.ja: 私って、男を見る目ないなあ。
example.english: I'm such a bad judge of men.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, otoko o miru me ga nai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私、男を見る目がないんですよね。
examplePolite.english: I'm just a poor judge of men.

items.notes: Praise form: miru me ga aru (have a good eye).

items.use: Praise for a professional's skill, such as a doctor, cook, hairdresser or mechanic: ano isha, ude ii yo, or before a noun ude no ii shokunin. For everyday 'good at', jouzu is the plain word; ude ga ii judges someone's work as a pro.

example.romaji: ano biyoushi-san, ude ii yo.
example.ja: あの美容師さん、腕いいよ。
example.english: That hairdresser's really good.

examplePolite.romaji: ano biyoushi-san wa ude ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの美容師さんは腕がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: That hairdresser is very skilled.

items.notes: Ude ga agaru = get better at it; plain single word: jouzu (good at).

items.use: Grudging admiration for someone who covers every angle or grabs every advantage, like a coworker who has already booked the good meeting room: nukeme nai na, with ga dropped. Sharper than youryou ga ii, and it can hint at calculating.

example.romaji: ano hito, honto nukeme nai yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、ほんと抜け目ないよね。
example.english: She really never misses a trick, does she?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa hontou ni nukeme ga nai desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は本当に抜け目がないですよね。
examplePolite.english: She really never misses a chance, does she?

items.notes: Adverb: nukeme naku (shrewdly, without missing a thing).

items.english: savvy, gets things done the smart way
items.use: About someone who gets results with little effort or knows how to stay on the boss's good side, said with admiration or a little envy. The opposite youryou ga warui (clumsy, inefficient) is often said about yourself; not the same as atama ga ii (smart).

example.romaji: kare, honto youryou ii yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、ほんと要領いいよね。
example.english: He really knows how to work things.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa hontou ni youryou ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は本当に要領がいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's really good at getting things done efficiently.

items.notes: Opposite: youryou ga warui (inefficient, clumsy at it).

blocks.label: At wit's end
blocks.rationale: Worn down by a situation: driven crazy, stifled, sick of it, lost, reckless.
blocks.interference: iki ga tsumaru vs iyake ga sasu (similar sound, stifled vs sick of it); tohou ni kureru (at a loss) vs yake ni naru (reckless).

items.literal: the mind feels about to go haywire
items.use: Exaggerated distress, whether frustration (kono oto, ki ga kuruisou), worry, longing or being cooped up (aitakute ki ga kuruisou datta). Ki demo kurutta no? (have you lost your mind?) is mostly a dubbed-film line; in real talk it's atama okashii n ja nai? Ki ga kuruu touches on mental illness, so TV avoids it, and atama ga okashiku narisou is the softer everyday swap.

example.romaji: tonari no kouji, urusakute ki ga kuruisou.
example.ja: 隣の工事、うるさくて気が狂いそう。
example.english: The construction next door is so loud it's driving me crazy.

examplePolite.romaji: hikkoshi to shigoto ga kasanatte, ki ga kuruisou deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 引っ越しと仕事が重なって、気が狂いそうでした。
examplePolite.english: Moving house and work all hit at once. I thought I'd lose my mind.

items.notes: Softer: atama ga okashiku narisou. Film line: ki demo kurutta no? = have you lost your mind? (most of the 257 hits are ki ga kurutta / ki demo kurutta; the -sou headword itself is 54).

items.literal: night falls on the way ahead
items.use: Being stranded with no idea what to do next, mostly as a state and when telling the story afterwards: saifu nakushite tohou ni kureteta. On the spot people just say dou shiyou. It's helpless rather than upset; yake ni naru is giving up and doing something rash.

example.romaji: shuuden nogashite, eki de tohou ni kureteta.
example.ja: 終電逃して、駅で途方に暮れてた。
example.english: I missed the last train and was stuck at the station with no idea what to do.

examplePolite.romaji: saifu o nakushite, tohou ni kurete imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 財布をなくして、途方に暮れていました。
examplePolite.english: I'd lost my wallet and was completely at a loss.

items.notes: Not kureru 'give': this kureru is 'grow dark', as in hi ga kureru.

items.use: Doing something rash and self-destructive after a breakup, a failure or bad news because nothing seems to matter, mostly said about someone: furarete yake ni natteru, yake ni natte zenbu nonjatta. The line you say to them is yake ni naranaide (don't do anything stupid). Tohou ni kureru is being stuck and helpless; yake ni naru is throwing caution to the wind.

example.romaji: ikkai shippai shita kurai de, yake ni naranaide yo.
example.ja: 一回失敗したくらいで、ヤケにならないでよ。
example.english: Don't go off the rails just because you failed once.

examplePolite.romaji: yake ni naranaide, mou ichido kangaete mimashou.
examplePolite.ja: ヤケにならないで、もう一度考えてみましょう。
examplePolite.english: Don't do anything rash. Let's think it over again.

items.notes: Different word by ear: the adverb yake ni (awfully, oddly), heard more often: yake ni shizuka da na = it's awfully quiet. yakekuso (desperate, all-or-nothing); yakezake (drinking to drown it).

items.use: A complaint about a tense or controlling home, office or relationship: ano ie, iki ga tsumaru, often as iki ga tsumarisou. It can also be literal, not being able to breathe.

example.romaji: jikka ni zutto iru to, iki ga tsumaru.
example.ja: 実家にずっといると、息が詰まる。
example.english: Being at my parents' the whole time is suffocating.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kaigi, iki ga tsumarisou deshita.
examplePolite.ja: あの会議、息が詰まりそうでした。
examplePolite.english: That meeting was so tense I could barely breathe.

items.notes: Single word: ikigurushii (stifling).

items.english: get fed up, be sick of it
items.literal: a feeling of dislike creeps in
items.englishIdiom: be sick and tired of it
items.use: Said about a job, a place, a routine or yourself, often as iyake ga sashite kita (I'm getting sick of it): shigoto ni iyake ga sasu. Akiru is being bored of something; iyake ga sasu is real dislike.

example.romaji: mainichi onaji koto no kurikaeshi de, iyake ga sashite kita.
example.ja: 毎日同じことの繰り返しで、嫌気がさしてきた。
example.english: Same thing every day. I'm getting sick of it.

examplePolite.romaji: shoujiki, ima no shigoto ni iyake ga sashite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 正直、今の仕事に嫌気がさしています。
examplePolite.english: Honestly, I'm fed up with my job.

items.notes: Plain word: unzari suru (be fed up).

blocks.label: Making a move
blocks.rationale: Moves and timing against the other side: acting, having no other option, getting in first or being beaten to it.
blocks.interference: te o utsu (take action, settle for) vs sente o utsu (move first); saki o kosareru is the losing end of sente o utsu, and hayai mono gachi is the rule behind both.

items.english: take action; settle for (a price or compromise)
items.literal: strike a hand (a move in go; a clap that seals a deal)
items.use: It has two uses: dealing with a problem (nanka te o utanai to, we have to do something), and agreeing on terms while haggling (kono hen de te o utou, let's call it a deal). Don't confuse it with te o dasu (hit, meddle).

example.romaji: hayaku nanka te o utanai to
example.ja: 早くなんか手を打たないと
example.english: We need to do something about it, fast.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku nanika te o utanai to ikemasen ne
examplePolite.ja: 早く何か手を打たないといけませんね
examplePolite.english: We need to take some action soon.

items.notes: Literal twin: te o utsu = clap one's hands (everyday clapping is te o tataku). Related: utsu te ga nai (nothing more can be done); formal: taisaku o toru.

items.use: Said when you're out of options and have to go with the one that's left: hoka ni te wa nai, kore shika te ga nai. The same te (move, option) appears in utsu te ga nai (nothing more can be done). It sounds a little dramatic; in casual talk people more often say kore shika nai.

example.romaji: shouganai yo, hoka ni te ga nai n da kara
example.ja: しょうがないよ、他に手がないんだから
example.english: Can't be helped, there's no other way.

examplePolite.romaji: shouganai desu yo, hoka ni te ga nai n desu kara
examplePolite.ja: しょうがないですよ、他に手がないんですから
examplePolite.english: It can't be helped; there's no other option.

items.notes: Variants: kore shika te ga nai (this is the only way); utsu te ga nai (nothing more to try).

items.english: act first, get in before the other side
items.literal: play the first move (as in go)
items.use: Said about heading off a problem or a rival before they move, like complaints, a competitor or a parent's objection. Mostly advice (sente o utte okou) or past (sente o utareta, they got in first). It shares te (a move) with te o utsu.

example.romaji: monku iwareru mae ni sente utte okou.
example.ja: 文句言われる前に先手打っておこう。
example.english: Let's get in first, before they complain.

examplePolite.romaji: kujou ga kuru mae ni, sente o utte okimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 苦情が来る前に、先手を打っておきましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's act before any complaints come in.

items.notes: Opposite feeling: saki o kosareru (someone beat you to it).

items.literal: have someone pass you to the front
items.use: The groan when someone else gets there first: the last item, a seat, a confession, a promotion, a rival company's launch. Mostly past and often without o: saki kosareta! For getting in first on purpose, say sente o utsu.

example.romaji: aa, saki kosareta!
example.ja: あー、先越された！
example.english: Argh, someone beat me to it!

examplePolite.romaji: tasha ni saki o kosarete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 他社に先を越されてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: Another company beat us to it.

items.notes: Rarer active form: saki o kosu (get there ahead of someone).

items.use: Said about the last snack, good seats, sale items or a free spot: hayai mono gachi da yo! It's often a playful call to grab something before others do.

example.romaji: nokori wa hayai mono gachi da yo
example.ja: 残りは早い者勝ちだよ
example.english: The rest is first come, first served.

examplePolite.romaji: nokori wa hayai mono gachi desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 残りは早い者勝ちですよ
examplePolite.english: The rest is first come, first served.

items.notes: Casual: hayai mon gachi.

blocks.label: Straight or soft
blocks.rationale: Talking things out directly with someone, set against softening it or being brutally blunt.
blocks.interference: hanashi o tsukeru (settle a matter) vs hara o watte hanasu (open up honestly); oburaato ni tsutsumu (soften it) vs mi mo futa mo nai (brutally blunt); tantou chokunyuu = get to the point, men to mukatte = to someone's face.

items.english: settle it by talking to someone, sort it out with them
items.use: Going to someone, often the other side or the person in charge, and settling a problem or getting their OK by talking: ore ga hanashi tsukete kuru (I'll go sort it out with them). Crime dramas give it a hint of muscle, but everyday use is just arranging things.

example.romaji: ooya-san ni wa watashi ga hanashi tsuketoku ne.
example.ja: 大家さんには私が話つけとくね。
example.english: I'll sort it out with the landlord.

examplePolite.romaji: ooya-san ni wa watashi kara hanashi o tsukete okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 大家さんには私から話をつけておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll get it settled with the landlord myself.

items.notes: Once settled: hanashi ga tsuita (it's been sorted out).

items.use: Goes with what you say, or can't say, directly to the person, usually in the negative: men to mukatte wa ienai. It's about complaints, thanks or confessions, not just meeting in person (that's chokusetsu au).

example.romaji: sonna koto, men to mukatte ienai yo.
example.ja: そんなこと、面と向かって言えないよ。
example.english: I can't say that to her face.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna koto, men to mukatte iemasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなこと、面と向かって言えませんよ。
examplePolite.english: I couldn't say that to her face.

items.use: Announces that you're about to say or ask something directly: tantou chokunyuu ni iu to / kiku kedo... (to put it plainly / I'll just ask). It sounds a bit formal, so friends often say zubari instead.
items.kana: たんとうちょくにゅう

example.romaji: tantou chokunyuu ni kiku kedo, kanojo iru?
example.ja: 単刀直入に聞くけど、彼女いる？
example.english: I'll just come out and ask: got a girlfriend?

examplePolite.romaji: tantou chokunyuu ni kikimasu kedo, kanojo wa imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 単刀直入に聞きますけど、彼女はいますか？
examplePolite.english: I'll get straight to the point: do you have a girlfriend?

items.notes: Casual alternative: zubari.

items.literal: split the belly open and talk
items.use: An invitation to drop the politeness and say what you really think, usually as hara (o) watte hanasou (let's talk honestly): to clear the air after friction, to get closer, or between rivals laying their cards on the table. The hara (belly) is where your true intentions are kept.

example.romaji: ikkai chanto hara watte hanasou yo.
example.ja: 一回ちゃんと腹割って話そうよ。
example.english: Let's sit down and have a proper heart-to-heart.

examplePolite.romaji: ichido, hara o watte hanashimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 一度、腹を割って話しませんか？
examplePolite.english: Why don't we sit down and talk frankly sometime?

items.notes: Casual speech often drops the o: hara watte hanasou.

items.literal: wrap it in edible starch film
items.use: About softening a blunt message, often as a request: mou chotto oburaato ni tsutsunde (put it more gently). The negative oburaato ni tsutsumazu ni iu means saying it straight out. Oburaato is the thin film once used to swallow bitter medicine.
items.politeJa: オブラートに包みます

example.romaji: mou chotto oburaato ni tsutsunde yo.
example.ja: もうちょっとオブラートに包んでよ。
example.english: Could you put it a bit more gently?

examplePolite.romaji: mou chotto oburaato ni tsutsunde moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: もうちょっとオブラートに包んでもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you phrase that a little more gently?

items.polite: mi mo futa mo nai desu
items.english: brutally blunt, put so baldly there's nothing left to say
items.use: A reaction to a remark so blunt or bleak that it kills the conversation, usually sore o itcha mi mo futa mo nai (if you say that, there's nothing left to talk about). Typical triggers are harsh truths like 'it all comes down to money'. Also mi mo futa mo nai iikata (a brutally blunt way of putting it).

example.romaji: sore o itcha, mi mo futa mo nai yo.
example.ja: それを言っちゃ、身も蓋もないよ。
example.english: Well, if you put it that bluntly, there's nothing left to say.

examplePolite.romaji: sore o itcha, mi mo futa mo nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それを言っちゃ、身も蓋もないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Putting it that way leaves nothing to discuss.

blocks.label: Squaring up
blocks.rationale: Rough lines in a confrontation: blaming both sides, brushing off, challenging, picking a fight.
blocks.interference: dotchi mo dotchi (both as bad) vs shitta kotcha nai (not my problem) are both casual put-downs; kenka o uru (pick a fight) vs teki ni mawasu (make an enemy) in Bad blood; keep shitta kotcha nai and nanisama no tsumori casual only.

items.english: both as bad as each other
items.englishIdiom: six of one and half a dozen of the other
items.use: The verdict on a quarrel or a couple's fight where neither side is innocent: sore wa dotchi mo dotchi da yo. Also for two equally poor choices. It refuses to take sides, unlike kata o motsu.

example.romaji: sore wa dotchi mo dotchi da yo.
example.ja: それはどっちもどっちだよ。
example.english: You're both as bad as each other.

examplePolite.romaji: maa, dotchi mo dotchi desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: まあ、どっちもどっちですよね。
examplePolite.english: Well, they're both as bad as each other.

items.english: not my problem, I couldn't care less
items.literal: (it's) not a thing I know about
items.use: A rough brush-off when someone's trouble lands on you: sonna no shitta kotcha nai (that's not my problem). Said in anger or bluster, more often by men; the milder version is kankei nai.

example.romaji: sonna no, ore no shitta kotcha nai yo.
example.ja: そんなの、俺の知ったこっちゃないよ。
example.english: That's not my problem.

items.notes: Also the retort shitta koto ka! (like I care!), and aimed at the listener: omae no shitta kotcha nai (none of your business). Cold polite form: watashi no shitta koto de wa arimasen. Plain alternative: kankei nai.

items.english: who do you think you are
items.englishIdiom: who do you think you are
items.use: An angry retort to someone acting superior or bossy, said to their face or, more often, behind their back: ano hito, nanisama no tsumori? It's harsh, so keep it for real anger or venting.

example.romaji: ano hito, ittai nanisama no tsumori?
example.ja: あの人、いったい何様のつもり？
example.english: Who does she think she is?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, ittai nanisama no tsumori na n deshou ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人、いったい何様のつもりなんでしょうね。
examplePolite.english: Who does she think she is?

items.notes: Short form: nanisama? / nanisama da yo.

items.use: Confronting someone provocative, usually kenka utteru no? (are you looking for a fight?), half-joking among friends, rough with strangers. The other side is kenka o kau (take up the challenge).

example.romaji: nani sore, kenka utteru no?
example.ja: 何それ、喧嘩売ってるの？
example.english: What's that supposed to mean, you looking for a fight?

examplePolite.romaji: sore, kenka utteru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それ、喧嘩売ってるんですか？
examplePolite.english: Are you trying to pick a fight with me?

items.notes: Accepting: kenka o kau (sono kenka, katta = you're on).

blocks.label: Careful or careless
blocks.rationale: How much attention you give something: looking it over and minding others vs underrating it or putting it second.
blocks.interference: amaku miru (underrate someone or something) vs kangae ga amai (your own plan is naive): both built on amai; me o toosu is a once-through read, not a close inspection.

items.use: Used for documents, emails and menus, and means going through it once, not studying it. You'll mostly hear it in requests like me o tooshite oite (have a look over this) and in ichiou me o tooshita (I've had a look). At work: ome o tooshite itadakemasu ka (could you look this over?).

example.romaji: kore, ato de me o tooshitoite.
example.ja: これ、あとで目を通しといて。
example.english: Have a look over this later.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, ato de me o tooshite oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これ、あとで目を通しておいてください。
examplePolite.english: Please have a look over this later.

items.notes: Plain alternative: zatto miru (have a quick look).

items.use: Said about an opponent, a task, a cold or the weather that turns out tougher than you thought: amaku miteta (I underestimated it). It's also a warning: amaku miru na, amaku minai hou ga ii. Don't confuse it with amai (soft on someone) or oome ni miru (let it slide); kangae ga amai judges a whole plan as naive.

example.romaji: shiken, chotto amaku miteta.
example.ja: 試験、ちょっと甘く見てた。
example.english: I kind of underestimated the exam.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken o chotto amaku mite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 試験をちょっと甘く見ていました。
examplePolite.english: I kind of underestimated the exam.

items.notes: Slangy one word: nameru (namen na yo = don't underestimate me).

items.english: be attentive; look out for others
items.use: Said with approval of someone who notices what everyone needs (mawari ni ki o kubaru), or about keeping an eye on details or your health. The noun kikubari is just as common: kikubari ga dekiru hito. It's close to ki o tsukau (go out of your way for someone) and ki ga kiku (be thoughtful); ki o mawasu is thinking ahead too much.

example.romaji: kanojo, itsumo mawari ni ki o kubatteru yo ne.
example.ja: 彼女、いつも周りに気を配ってるよね。
example.english: She's always looking out for everyone, isn't she.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo wa itsumo mawari ni ki o kubatte imasu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女はいつも周りに気を配っていますよね。
examplePolite.english: She's always looking out for everyone, isn't she.

items.notes: Noun form: kikubari (kikubari ga dekiru = attentive).

items.use: Said as X wa ni no tsugi to rank what matters less: your own priorities (mitame wa ni no tsugi, jibun no koto wa ni no tsugi) or, critically, someone else's (kazoku wa ni no tsugi). Also ni no tsugi ni suru (put X second) and ni no tsugi ni naru (end up coming second).

example.romaji: kare no baai, kazoku wa ni no tsugi na n da yo.
example.ja: 彼の場合、家族は二の次なんだよ。
example.english: With him, his family always comes second.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no baai, kazoku wa ni no tsugi na n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の場合、家族は二の次なんですよ。
examplePolite.english: With him, his family always comes second.

items.notes: Plain alternative: atomawashi (put off till later).

items.english: be naive, not think it through
items.use: A blunt judgement on a plan that ignores how hard things are, usually from someone more experienced: sonna no kangae ga amai yo. Amaku miru is underestimating one task or opponent.

example.romaji: ichinichi de owaru? sore wa kangae ga amai yo.
example.ja: 一日で終わる？それは考えが甘いよ。
example.english: Done in a day? That's naive.

examplePolite.romaji: ichinichi de owaru n desu ka? sore wa chotto kangae ga amai to omoimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 一日で終わるんですか？それはちょっと考えが甘いと思いますよ。
examplePolite.english: Done in a day? I think that's a bit naive.

items.notes: Past misjudgement: yomi ga amakatta (I misread it).

blocks.label: Against the clock
blocks.rationale: Time running out or slipping away: over in no time, stalling for time, and a deadline finally lighting a fire.
blocks.interference: none

items.english: in no time, over in a flash
items.literal: the time it takes to say 'ah'
items.englishIdiom: in the blink of an eye
items.use: Said all the time about time flying (atto iu ma datta ne) and about things happening fast (atto iu ma ni owatta). Takes ni before a verb and da / datta at the end; iu is pronounced yuu.

example.romaji: ichinen tte atto iu ma da ne
example.ja: 一年ってあっという間だね
example.english: A year goes by in no time, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: ichinen tte atto iu ma desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 一年ってあっという間ですね
examplePolite.english: A year goes by in no time, doesn't it.

items.notes: Plain alternative: sugu (right away).

items.use: Delaying on purpose so you or someone else can get ready or act, at work, in a game or in a crisis: chotto jikan kasegou. Not jikan o tsubusu, which is filling spare time.

example.romaji: mada junbi dekitenai kara, chotto jikan kasegou
example.ja: まだ準備できてないから、ちょっと時間稼ごう
example.english: We're not ready yet, so let's stall a bit.

examplePolite.romaji: mada junbi ga dekite inai node, sukoshi jikan o kasegimashou
examplePolite.ja: まだ準備ができていないので、少し時間を稼ぎましょう
examplePolite.english: We're not ready yet, so let's stall for a little while.

items.notes: Noun: jikan kasegi (a stalling tactic).

items.english: finally feel the pressure of a deadline
items.use: Describes finally getting going because a deadline or exam is close, about yourself or a procrastinator: shiri ni hi ga tsuite yatto yaridashita. In speech ketsu ni hi ga tsuku (rough) is most common; oshiri ni hi ga tsuku is the softer, polite-friendly version.

example.romaji: shiri ni hi ga tsuite, yatto yaridashita
example.ja: 尻に火がついて、やっとやり出した
example.english: Once the pressure was on, I finally got going.

examplePolite.romaji: oshiri ni hi ga tsuite, yatto yaridashimashita
examplePolite.ja: お尻に火がついて、やっとやり出しました
examplePolite.english: Once the pressure was on, I finally got going.

items.notes: Causing it: shiri o tataku (push someone to get moving).

blocks.label: Immature
blocks.rationale: Faults you scold someone for: selfish, too old for this, dithering, quitting after three days.
blocks.interference: ii toshi shite and ii kagen ni shite (mood) are both scolding lines that start with ii. jibun katte (selfish) can be mixed up with katte ni shite (suit yourself).

items.use: The standard complaint about someone who does what suits them and ignores everyone else: jibun katte da yo, jibun katte na hito. When apologising for your own request, people drop jibun: katte na onegai desu ga... Not the same as katte ni (without asking).

example.romaji: ano hito, honto jibun katte da yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、ほんと自分勝手だよね。
example.english: He's so selfish, isn't he?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa hontou ni jibun katte desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は本当に自分勝手ですよね。
examplePolite.english: He really is selfish, isn't he?

items.notes: Single words: wagamama (selfish, spoilt), jikochuu (self-centred, slang).

items.english: at your age (you should know better)
items.use: A jab at a grown-up acting childish or silly: ii toshi shite nani yatteru no? Also said about yourself with embarrassment (ii toshi shite naichatta, I cried, at my age); the o of ii toshi o shite is usually dropped.

example.romaji: ii toshi shite, nani yatteru no?
example.ja: いい年して、何やってるの？
example.english: What are you doing, at your age?

items.notes: Also written いい歳して; rougher: ii toshi koite.

items.english: indecisive, can't make up one's mind
items.use: About someone who takes forever to choose, at a menu, between two partners or at work, very often yourself: yuujuu fudan de kimerarenai. One of the four-character phrases people really say aloud.

example.romaji: watashi, yuujuu fudan da kara kimerarenai.
example.ja: 私、優柔不断だから決められない。
example.english: I'm so indecisive, I can't choose.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, yuujuu fudan na node kimerarenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 私、優柔不断なので決められないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm indecisive, so I can't make up my mind.

items.notes: Plain way: nakanaka kimerarenai (I just can't decide).

items.english: someone who gives up after a few days
items.use: Self-mockery about diets, diaries, the gym and New Year resolutions that didn't last: mata mikka bouzu da. Mostly about yourself; mikka bouzu de owaru = it didn't stick.

example.romaji: daietto, mata mikka bouzu datta.
example.ja: ダイエット、また三日坊主だった。
example.english: My diet lasted three days again.

examplePolite.romaji: daietto wa mata mikka bouzu deshita.
examplePolite.ja: ダイエットはまた三日坊主でした。
examplePolite.english: My diet only lasted a few days again.

items.notes: Plain way: sugu yamechau (I always quit right away).

blocks.label: Shock and nerves
blocks.rationale: Creepy, scary or overwhelming moments, and bracing yourself for them.
blocks.interference: kimi ga warui (creepy) vs shinzou ni warui (gave me a scare): both '... warui'.

items.use: For anything eerie or unsettling, like a silent house, a stranger staring or a fixed smile. You'll mostly hear kimi warui (no ga). Kimochi warui is broader (gross, nauseating), while kimi ga warui only means eerie. Same sound as kimi ga warui 'it's your fault' (kimi = you), but the creepy one is said about a thing or person, not to someone.

example.romaji: nanka kono heya, kimi warui ne.
example.ja: なんかこの部屋、気味悪いね。
example.english: This room is kind of creepy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono heya, chotto kimi ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この部屋、ちょっと気味が悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: This room is a bit creepy, isn't it?

items.notes: Single-word alternative: bukimi (eerie).

items.use: Mostly negative, when news or a big moment comes too fast: mada kokoro no junbi ga dekitenai. Kokoro no junbi wa ii? asks if someone is ready to hear something. Plain junbi ga dekiru is being ready in practical terms.
items.kana: こころのじゅんびができる

example.romaji: chotto matte, mada kokoro no junbi ga dekitenai.
example.ja: ちょっと待って、まだ心の準備ができてない。
example.english: Wait, I'm not ready for this yet.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni iwarete mo, mada kokoro no junbi ga dekitenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 急に言われても、まだ心の準備ができてないんです。
examplePolite.english: This is so sudden. I'm just not ready for it yet.

items.notes: Also: kokoro no junbi o suru (brace yourself).

items.english: gave me a scare, too nerve-racking
items.englishIdiom: nearly give someone a heart attack
items.use: A joking complaint after a scare, or about a nail-biting game or film: bikkuri shita, shinzou ni warui yo. It isn't a statement about health here.

example.romaji: kyuu ni dete konaide yo, shinzou ni warui.
example.ja: 急に出てこないでよ、心臓に悪い。
example.english: Don't jump out like that, you nearly gave me a heart attack.

examplePolite.romaji: mou, shinzou ni warui desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: もう、心臓に悪いですよ。
examplePolite.english: Goodness, you nearly gave me a heart attack.

items.use: How people describe freezing up from nerves or shock in an exam, speech or interview, nearly always in the past: kinchou shite atama ga masshiro ni natta. You'll also hear atama no naka ga masshiro.
items.kana: あたまがまっしろになる
items.politeJa: 頭が真っ白になります

example.romaji: kinchou shite atama masshiro ni natta.
example.ja: 緊張して頭真っ白になった。
example.english: I got so nervous my mind went blank.

examplePolite.romaji: kinchou shite atama ga masshiro ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 緊張して頭が真っ白になりました。
examplePolite.english: I was so nervous my mind went blank.

blocks.label: The short end
blocks.rationale: Coming off worse: stuck with a chore, playing into someone's hands, taking the blame, drawing the worst lot.
blocks.interference: hame ni naru (stuck doing it) shares hame with hame o hazusu (let loose) in Getting carried away; binbou kuji o hiku is about being the unlucky one, hame ni naru about the chore itself.

items.english: end up having to do something unpleasant
items.literal: come to a hame (a tight spot)
items.use: The everyday grumble about getting stuck with a chore or a bad outcome: after a plain verb (zangyou suru hame ni natta) or konna (konna hame ni naru nante). Mostly past, or as a warning (... suru hame ni naru yo). Only for results you didn't want.

example.romaji: kekkyoku hitori de katazukeru hame ni natta
example.ja: 結局一人で片付ける羽目になった
example.english: I ended up stuck cleaning up alone.

examplePolite.romaji: kekkyoku hitori de katazukeru hame ni narimashita
examplePolite.ja: 結局一人で片付ける羽目になりました
examplePolite.english: I ended up having to clean up by myself.

items.notes: Neutral alternative: ... koto ni natta (it turned out that ...).

items.literal: the (dice) cup one has in mind
items.use: Almost always X no omou tsubo da: if you react, you're doing just what the other side wants. People use it to talk someone out of taking the bait, as in sore ja aite no omou tsubo da yo.

example.romaji: okottara aitsu no omou tsubo da yo
example.ja: 怒ったらあいつの思うつぼだよ
example.english: Get angry and you play right into his hands.

examplePolite.romaji: okottara aite no omou tsubo desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 怒ったら相手の思うつぼですよ
examplePolite.english: If you get angry, that's exactly what they want.

items.notes: Usually with aite (the other side): aite no omou tsubo.

items.english: falsely accuse, pin it on someone
items.use: Mostly heard from the person who was wrongly blamed: nureginu o kiserareta (I was falsely accused), or just nureginu da! (I didn't do it!). It works for small blame at school or work, not only for crimes.

example.romaji: nureginu o kiserareta n da yo
example.ja: 濡れ衣を着せられたんだよ
example.english: I got blamed for something I didn't do.

examplePolite.romaji: nureginu o kiserareta n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 濡れ衣を着せられたんですよ
examplePolite.english: I was blamed for something I didn't do.

items.notes: The bare noun is common: nureginu da! (that's a false accusation!).

items.english: be the one who loses out, get stuck with the worst job or the raw deal
items.use: The grumble when you end up the one who loses out, often stuck with the job, role or seat nobody wanted, through bad luck or being too nice: mata binbou kuji hiichatta. hame ni naru is about the chore itself; binbou kuji is about being the unlucky one.

example.romaji: mata binbou kuji hiichatta yo.
example.ja: また貧乏くじ引いちゃったよ。
example.english: Ugh, I drew the short straw again.

examplePolite.romaji: mata binbou kuji o hiite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: また貧乏くじを引いてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I drew the short straw again.

blocks.label: Look who's talking
blocks.rationale: Calling out someone's nerve or hypocrisy, and admitting your own.
blocks.interference: yoku iu yo and ii dokyou shiteru both come out as 'you've got some nerve': yoku iu yo scoffs at a remark, ii dokyou shiteru is a veiled warning; kotchi no serifu throws their words back, hito no koto ienai turns it on yourself, tana ni ageru describes the hypocrisy.

items.english: you've got some nerve, look who's talking
items.use: A retort when someone says something cheeky, shameless or hypocritical: yoku iu yo, jibun datte... (you've got a nerve, when you...). Among friends it's often half-laughing. It's a different thing from plain yoku iu (people often say), which has no retort tone. Even as yoku iimasu ne it is a jab: say it to equals or about a third person, never to a boss.

example.romaji: yoku iu yo, jibun datte okureta kuse ni.
example.ja: よく言うよ、自分だって遅れたくせに。
example.english: Look who's talking. You were late too!

examplePolite.romaji: yoku iimasu ne. sochira datte okurete kita ja nai desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: よく言いますね。そちらだって遅れてきたじゃないですか。
examplePolite.english: That's rich. You were late too, weren't you?

items.notes: Variant: yoku ieru ne (how can you even say that).

items.english: that's my line; I should be the one saying that
items.use: Throws someone's complaint or accusation straight back at them: sore wa kotchi no serifu da yo. You hear it in arguments and teasing, for example after 'you're late' or 'you're annoying'.

example.romaji: osoi tte, sore kotchi no serifu da yo.
example.ja: 遅いって、それこっちのセリフだよ。
example.english: 'You're late'? That's my line!

examplePolite.romaji: osoi tte, sore wa kotchi no serifu desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 遅いって、それはこっちのセリフですよ。
examplePolite.english: 'Late'? I should be the one saying that.

items.notes: Formal: kochira no serifu desu.

items.english: you've got some nerve (usually a sarcastic warning)
items.use: A sarcastic warning to someone who has just done or said something bold or cheeky, half-joking among friends or mock-threatening from a senior. Unlike yoku iu yo, which calls out hypocrisy, it's about daring to do something. It can also be grudging admiration: ii dokyou da, ki ni itta (you've got guts, I like that).

example.romaji: watashi no purin tabeta no? ii dokyou shiteru ja nai.
example.ja: 私のプリン食べたの？いい度胸してるじゃない。
example.english: You ate my pudding? You've got some nerve.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi no purin, tabeta n desu ka? ii dokyou shitemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私のプリン、食べたんですか？いい度胸してますね。
examplePolite.english: You ate my pudding? You've got some nerve.

items.notes: Just as common, and blunter: ii dokyou da (na), with na rougher and mostly male.

items.english: ignore one's own faults while criticising others
items.englishIdiom: the pot calling the kettle black
items.use: Almost always jibun no koto wa tana ni agete..., calling out someone who criticises others for what they do themselves. It's also an admission: jibun no koto wa tana ni agete iu kedo (I know I'm no better, but...). Not to be confused with tanaage ni suru (shelve a plan or problem).

example.romaji: jibun no koto wa tana ni agete, hito no monku bakkari.
example.ja: 自分のことは棚に上げて、人の文句ばっかり。
example.english: He ignores his own faults and just complains about everyone else.

examplePolite.romaji: buchou tte, jibun no koto wa tana ni agete, hito no monku bakari desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 部長って、自分のことは棚に上げて、人の文句ばかりですよね。
examplePolite.english: The boss ignores his own faults and just complains about everyone else, doesn't he?

items.english: I'm not one to talk, I'm no better myself
items.use: Softens your own complaint by admitting you do the same thing: watashi mo hito no koto ienai kedo... Turned on someone else, hito no koto ieru? is the jab 'are you really one to talk?'
items.politeJa: 人のことは言えません

example.romaji: maa, watashi mo hito no koto ienai kedo ne.
example.ja: まあ、私も人のこと言えないけどね。
example.english: Well, I'm not one to talk.

examplePolite.romaji: maa, watashi mo hito no koto wa iemasen kedo ne.
examplePolite.ja: まあ、私も人のことは言えませんけどね。
examplePolite.english: Well, I'm hardly one to talk.

blocks.label: Clicking and fancying
blocks.rationale: Whether two people get on, and whether someone is into you.
blocks.interference: ki ga au (get along) vs ki ga aru (fancy someone) differ by one sound, and ki o hiku (catch their eye) is a third ki frame; myaku ga aru (there's a chance) is the sign, not the feeling.

items.use: For friends, colleagues or partners you naturally click with (ki ga au hito), often negative too (joushi to ki ga awanai). The au is 合う (fit), not 会う (meet); don't confuse it with ki ga aru (be into someone).

example.romaji: kanojo to wa nanka ki ga au n da yo ne.
example.ja: 彼女とはなんか気が合うんだよね。
example.english: I just click with her somehow.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo to wa nanka ki ga au n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女とはなんか気が合うんですよね。
examplePolite.english: I just click with her somehow.

items.notes: Negative ki ga awanai = just don't get on. Near-twin: uma ga au.

items.use: Gossip about who fancies whom, always X ni ki ga aru: ano ko, kimi ni ki ga aru yo. Without ni it means being willing (yaru ki ga aru); don't confuse it with ki ga au (get along).

example.romaji: kare, zettai kimi ni ki ga aru yo.
example.ja: 彼、絶対君に気があるよ。
example.english: He's definitely into you.

examplePolite.romaji: kare, zettai satou-san ni ki ga arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼、絶対佐藤さんに気がありますよ。
examplePolite.english: He's definitely into you, Ms Sato.

items.notes: Negative ki ga nai = not interested.

items.english: catch someone's attention or interest (often romantic)
items.use: Dating talk about winning someone's interest, usually heard as wanting or trying to: kare no ki o hikitakute (because I wanted his attention), ki o hikou to shite. Also a child acting up to be noticed, or drawing attention away as a decoy: boku ga ki o hiku kara, nigete (I'll distract them, you run). ki ga aru is already being into someone, and myaku ari is them liking you back.

example.romaji: kare no ki o hikitakute, wazato sokkenaku shiteru no.
example.ja: 彼の気を引きたくて、わざとそっけなくしてるの。
example.english: I'm playing it cool on purpose to get his attention.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no ki o hikitakute, wazato sokkenaku shite iru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の気を引きたくて、わざとそっけなくしているんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm playing it cool on purpose to get his attention.

items.notes: Not hiku on its own, slang for being put off (sore wa hiku), nor ki o hikishimeru (brace yourself). ki o hiite miru = sound out how someone feels.

items.english: there's a chance (they like you back)
items.use: Dating talk reading someone's signals: sore, myaku ari da yo (you've got a shot), or the letdown myaku nashi ka (no chance, then). Also outside romance for a deal or lead that still has hope: kono hanashi, myaku ari da na. ki ga aru is someone actually being into you.

example.romaji: henji sugu kuru n desho? sore, myaku ari da yo.
example.ja: 返事すぐ来るんでしょ？それ、脈ありだよ。
example.english: He texts back right away? You've got a shot.

examplePolite.romaji: henji ga hayai nara, myaku ari desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 返事が早いなら、脈ありですよ。
examplePolite.english: If he replies fast, you've got a shot.

items.notes: Opposite: myaku nashi (no chance). Plain myaku ga aru / myaku ga nai is usually a doctor checking a pulse; mada myaku wa aru = there's still hope (any situation).

blocks.label: Mind elsewhere
blocks.rationale: Attention stuck on one thing or scattered, so you're not really present.
blocks.interference: ki ga chiru (scattered by your surroundings) vs ki o torareru (pulled away by one thing); atama kara hanarenai (can't stop thinking of it) and atama ga ippai (room for nothing else) both mean preoccupied; uwa no sora is how it looks from outside.

items.englishIdiom: can't get it out of my head
items.use: For a song, a worry, a scene or a person that keeps coming back, with the thing as the subject: ano kotoba ga atama kara hanarenai. It's almost always negative. Atama ni ukabu is a thought popping up once.
items.kana: あたまからはなれない

example.romaji: ano kyoku ga atama kara hanarenai.
example.ja: あの曲が頭から離れない。
example.english: I can't get that song out of my head.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kyoku ga atama kara hanaremasen.
examplePolite.ja: あの曲が頭から離れません。
examplePolite.english: I can't get that song out of my head.

items.use: The everyday complaint when noise, a phone or someone talking breaks your focus: urusakute ki ga chiru, ki ga chiru kara yamete. It's the annoying kind of distraction; ki o torareru names the one thing that pulled you away. Ki ga magireru is the welcome kind that takes your mind off worries.

example.romaji: mawari ga urusakute ki ga chiru.
example.ja: 周りがうるさくて気が散る。
example.english: It's so noisy around here I can't focus.

examplePolite.romaji: mawari ga urusakute ki ga chirimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 周りがうるさくて気が散ります。
examplePolite.english: It's so noisy around here I can't focus.

items.notes: Opposite: shuuchuu suru (focus).

items.english: be distracted by, have your mind on something else
items.use: Explaining a slip: you were caught up in one thing (X ni ki o torarete) and missed or forgot something else, as in sumaho ni ki o torarete norisugoshita. Ki ga chiru is losing focus to noise or interruptions; ki o torareru names the one thing that took your attention.

example.romaji: sumaho ni ki o torarete, norisugoshichatta.
example.ja: スマホに気を取られて、乗り過ごしちゃった。
example.english: I was so caught up in my phone I missed my stop.

examplePolite.romaji: sumaho ni ki o torarete, norisugoshite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: スマホに気を取られて、乗り過ごしてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I was so caught up in my phone I missed my stop.

items.english: can think of nothing else, preoccupied
items.use: Said as X no koto de atama ga ippai: an exam, a crush, money or a sick parent fills your head and leaves no room for anything else. Shika atama ni nai is the teasing version about someone else.

example.romaji: ima wa shiken no koto de atama ga ippai.
example.ja: 今は試験のことで頭がいっぱい。
example.english: Right now the exam is all I can think about.

examplePolite.romaji: ima wa shiken no koto de atama ga ippai na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今は試験のことで頭がいっぱいなんです。
examplePolite.english: Right now the exam is all I can think about.

items.notes: Overwhelmed: mou ippai ippai (I'm at my limit, can't take any more).

items.use: Said of someone who nods along but isn't listening, often because they're in love or worried: sakki kara uwa no sora da yo. It works like a na-adjective: uwa no sora de kiku (half listen).

example.romaji: nee, kiiteru? sakki kara uwa no sora da yo.
example.ja: ねえ、聞いてる？さっきから上の空だよ。
example.english: Hey, are you listening? You've been miles away.

examplePolite.romaji: ano, kiitemasu? sakki kara uwa no sora desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの、聞いてます？さっきから上の空ですね。
examplePolite.english: Um, are you listening? You've been miles away.

blocks.label: Too much to handle
blocks.rationale: Something beyond you: out of control, daunting, too heavy a responsibility, or an opponent you cannot match.
blocks.interference: ha ga tatanai and tachiuchi dekinai both mean 'no match for' (ha is also used for a problem you can't crack, tachiuchi for rivals); te ni oenai means out of control, and ni ga omoi means too much responsibility.

items.english: more than one can handle, out of control
items.literal: can't bear it in one's hands
items.use: Said of a kid, pet, person or problem beyond your control or skill: ano ko wa te ni oenai, watashi no te ni wa oenai. Only ever said in the negative (te ni ou is not used); not ha ga tatanai, which is being outmatched by a strong opponent or a hard problem.

example.romaji: uchi no inu, mou te ni oenai yo
example.ja: うちの犬、もう手に負えないよ
example.english: Our dog is out of control now.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no inu, mou te ni oenai n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: うちの犬、もう手に負えないんですよ
examplePolite.english: Our dog is out of control now.

items.notes: Plain alternative: muri (mou muri).

items.english: daunting, too much to take on
items.use: Very common modern way to say something feels too daunting to try, socially or in skill: hitori de yakiniku wa haadoru ga takai. Usually about yourself and often softened with chotto; the ga often drops.

example.romaji: hitori yakiniku wa chotto haadoru takai na
example.ja: 一人焼肉はちょっとハードル高いな
example.english: Yakiniku on my own? That's a bit daunting.

examplePolite.romaji: hitori yakiniku wa chotto haadoru ga takai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 一人焼肉はちょっとハードルが高いですね
examplePolite.english: Yakiniku on my own? That's a bit daunting.

items.notes: Expectations: haadoru o ageru (raise the bar) / sageru (lower it).

items.use: A modest way to say a role or job is too much for you, often when turning down a position like leader or speaker: watashi ni wa ni ga omoi. Not ki ga omoi, which is dreading something.

example.romaji: riidaa nante, ore ni wa ni ga omoi yo
example.ja: リーダーなんて、俺には荷が重いよ
example.english: Me, team leader? That's too much for me.

examplePolite.romaji: riidaa nante, watashi ni wa ni ga omoi desu
examplePolite.ja: リーダーなんて、私には荷が重いです
examplePolite.english: Me, team leader? That's too much for me.

items.notes: Relief when it's lifted: kata no ni ga oriru.

items.english: be no match for, can't crack it
items.use: Said when an opponent or problem is too strong or too hard for you, usually with zenzen and in the past: ani ni wa zenzen ha ga tatanai, shiken, ha ga tatanakatta. Not te ni oenai, which is something out of your control.

example.romaji: shiken, zenzen ha ga tatanakatta
example.ja: 試験、全然歯が立たなかった
example.english: The exam was way beyond me.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken, zenzen ha ga tachimasen deshita
examplePolite.ja: 試験、全然歯が立ちませんでした
examplePolite.english: The exam was way beyond me.

items.notes: Close: X ni wa kanawanai (can't beat X).

items.english: can't compete with, can't stand up to
items.use: Said of a pro, a rival or a big competitor you can't hope to match, usually as X ni wa tachiuchi dekinai: puro ni wa tachiuchi dekinai, oote no yasusa ni wa tachiuchi dekinai (can't compete with the big chains' low prices). With the means it takes ja: ima no jitsuryoku ja tachiuchi dekinai (at my level I'm no match), and of a champion, dare mo tachiuchi dekinai. Close to ha ga tatanai, which also covers a test or problem too hard to crack; tachiuchi dekinai is about competing.

example.romaji: puro ni wa tachiuchi dekinai yo
example.ja: プロには太刀打ちできないよ
example.english: There's no competing with a pro.

examplePolite.romaji: puro ni wa tachiuchi dekimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: プロには太刀打ちできませんよ
examplePolite.english: There's no competing with a pro.

items.notes: Plain alternative: kanawanai (puro ni wa kanawanai yo, can't beat a pro).

blocks.label: In a group
blocks.rationale: What someone is like with other people: the loner, the generous one, the forgiving one, the fun one, the carer.
blocks.interference: kimae ga ii (open-handed with money) and kokoro ga hiroi (forgiving) both translate as 'generous'. kimae, nori and mendoumi all take ga ii.

items.english: a loner who goes their own way
items.use: About a coworker or classmate who works alone and keeps out of groups, said neutrally or with a little admiration: kare wa ippiki ookami da kara. Often softened with tte kanji (kind of a lone wolf). Also said of yourself, usually half-joking: watashi, ippiki ookami taipu da kara.

example.romaji: kare tte, ippiki ookami tte kanji da yo ne.
example.ja: 彼って、一匹狼って感じだよね。
example.english: He's kind of a lone wolf, isn't he?

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa ippiki ookami tte kanji desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は一匹狼って感じですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's a bit of a lone wolf, isn't he?

items.notes: Plain way: hitori de iru no ga suki (likes being on their own).

items.use: Said when someone pays for everyone, tips big or hands out treats: kimae ii ne! or, as an adverb, kimae yoku ogotte kureta (treated us generously). It's about money and gifts (a kind person is yasashii), and politely it's said about a third party, not to a senior who is treating you.

example.romaji: kyou wa ogori? kimae ii ne!
example.ja: 今日はおごり？気前いいね！
example.english: Your treat today? That's generous!

examplePolite.romaji: buchou tte, kimae ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 部長って、気前がいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: The boss is really generous, isn't he?

items.notes: Opposite single word: kechi (stingy); casual: futoppara (open-handed).

items.use: Praise for someone who forgives mistakes or lets things go, like a partner who laughs off a forgotten anniversary: kokoro hiroi ne. Also said of yourself, half joking, when letting something slide: ore wa kokoro ga hiroi kara. The opposite kokoro ga semai (petty) is a common jab.

example.romaji: sore de yurushita no? kokoro hiroi ne.
example.ja: それで許したの？心広いね。
example.english: And you forgave him? You're so big-hearted.

examplePolite.romaji: sore de yurushita n desu ka? kokoro ga hiroi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それで許したんですか？心が広いですね。
examplePolite.english: And you forgave him? You're very forgiving.

items.notes: Opposite: kokoro ga semai (petty, narrow-minded).

items.english: game for anything, fun to be around
items.use: About a friend or coworker who joins in jokes, karaoke and last-minute plans: nori ii ne! The opposite nori ga warui (no fun, a wet blanket) is just as common; nori is the mood and rhythm of a group, written ノリ.

example.romaji: suzuki-san tte, nori ii yo ne.
example.ja: 鈴木さんって、ノリいいよね。
example.english: Suzuki's always up for anything.

examplePolite.romaji: suzuki-san tte, nori ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 鈴木さんって、ノリがいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: Suzuki's always a good sport, isn't she?

items.notes: Opposite: nori ga warui (no fun); nori de = on a whim.

items.english: caring, good at looking after people
items.use: Top praise for a senpai, boss, older sibling or teacher who takes care of juniors and newcomers: senpai, mendoumi ii yo ne. It names the trait; looking after someone in the moment is mendou o miru.

example.romaji: tanaka-senpai, honto mendoumi ii yo ne.
example.ja: 田中先輩、ほんと面倒見いいよね。
example.english: Tanaka's such a caring senpai.

examplePolite.romaji: tanaka-senpai wa hontou ni mendoumi ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 田中先輩は本当に面倒見がいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: Tanaka really looks after us, doesn't she?

items.notes: The act itself: mendou o miru (look after someone).

blocks.label: Comes back on you
blocks.rationale: Bad outcomes you brought on yourself: your own fault, the bill coming due, digging your own grave, punishment, a plan backfiring.
blocks.interference: jigou jitoku (your own fault) vs bachi ga ataru (punished from above) vs tsuke ga mawatte kuru (it catches up later); boketsu o horu (you make it worse for yourself) vs urame ni deru (a plan has the opposite effect).

items.literal: one's own deeds, one's own receiving (of their result)
items.use: Said, often bluntly, when someone's trouble is their own fault, like a hangover or a failed test after no studying: jigou jitoku da yo. It can sound cold, so use it with friends or about other people, not to a superior's face.

example.romaji: are wa jigou jitoku da yo
example.ja: あれは自業自得だよ
example.english: He brought that on himself.

examplePolite.romaji: are wa jigou jitoku desu yo
examplePolite.ja: あれは自業自得ですよ
examplePolite.english: He really brought that on himself.

items.notes: Plain alternative: jibun no sei (your own fault).

items.english: past neglect or excess catches up with you
items.use: Said when skipped study, lost sleep, overspending or cut corners catch up with you, usually in the past: tsuke ga mawatte kita. tsuke is a bar tab, and tsuke o harau (pay the price) uses the same picture.

example.romaji: nebusoku no tsuke ga mawatte kita
example.ja: 寝不足のツケが回ってきた
example.english: The lack of sleep is catching up with me.

examplePolite.romaji: nebusoku no tsuke ga mawatte kimashita
examplePolite.ja: 寝不足のツケが回ってきました
examplePolite.english: The lack of sleep is catching up with me.

items.notes: Same image: tsuke o harau (pay the price for it).

items.english: dig your own grave, shoot yourself in the foot
items.use: Said when someone brings trouble on themselves through their own words or actions, very often by saying too much and giving themselves away: jibun de boketsu hotta. Common as a self-mocking groan.

example.romaji: yokei na koto itte boketsu hotta.
example.ja: 余計なこと言って墓穴掘った。
example.english: I said too much and dug my own grave.

examplePolite.romaji: yokei na koto o itte, boketsu o hotte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 余計なことを言って、墓穴を掘ってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I said too much and dug myself a hole.

items.notes: Same idea: jibun no kubi o shimeru (tighten the noose on yourself).

items.english: be punished by heaven, get bad karma
items.use: A half-joking warning to someone who wastes food, is ungrateful or disrespects something sacred: bachi ga ataru yo. People also say it about themselves when life feels too good, as in konna ni shiawase de bachi ga ataranai kana.

example.romaji: gohan nokoshitara bachi ga ataru yo
example.ja: ご飯残したらバチが当たるよ
example.english: Leave food and heaven will punish you.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan o nokoshitara bachi ga atarimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: ご飯を残したらバチが当たりますよ
examplePolite.english: Leaving food will bring bad karma.

items.notes: Written 罰 but read bachi here; an ungrateful person is a bachiatari.

items.literal: the back face (of the die) comes up
items.use: Said when a plan or a kind gesture produces the opposite of what you wanted, mostly in the past: yokare to omotte shita koto ga urame ni deta (I meant well, but it backfired). Sometimes a warning: urame ni deru zo.

example.romaji: yokare to omotte yatta noni, urame ni deta.
example.ja: 良かれと思ってやったのに、裏目に出た。
example.english: I meant well, but it backfired.

examplePolite.romaji: yokare to omotte shita koto ga urame ni demashita.
examplePolite.ja: 良かれと思ってしたことが裏目に出ました。
examplePolite.english: What I did with good intentions backfired.

items.notes: Plain alternative: gyaku kouka (counterproductive).

blocks.label: Being a burden
blocks.rationale: Being the one who holds others back, or the one who has to put up with it.
blocks.interference: ashi o hipparu (drag down) vs ashidematoi ni naru (be dead weight) both involve legs; sewa ga yakeru describes the handful, shirinugui o suru is cleaning up after them.

items.english: hold others back, let the team down; (deliberately) drag someone down
items.use: The team, club and work apology ashi hippatte gomen, and also deliberate sabotage of a rival: hito no ashi bakkari hipparu (always dragging others down). A false friend: English 'pull someone's leg' means tease. ashidematoi ni naru is being a burden just by being there.

example.romaji: minna no ashi hippatte, gomen ne.
example.ja: みんなの足引っ張って、ごめんね。
example.english: Sorry for holding everyone back.

examplePolite.romaji: minasan no ashi o hippatte shimatte, sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 皆さんの足を引っ張ってしまって、すみません。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry for holding everyone back.

items.english: be a handful, need constant looking after
items.use: Fond grumbling about a child, partner, junior or pet who keeps needing help: mattaku, sewa ga yakeru na. There's affection in it; mendokusai is plain annoyance.

example.romaji: mattaku, sewa ga yakeru na.
example.ja: まったく、世話が焼けるな。
example.english: Honestly, you're such a handful.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no musuko wa, hontou ni sewa ga yakeru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちの息子は、本当に世話が焼けるんです。
examplePolite.english: My son is such a handful.

items.notes: Also sewa no yakeru yatsu (what a handful). Plainer: te ga kakaru (takes a lot of looking after). sewa o yaku = fuss over someone; a born fusser is a sewayaki.

items.english: be a burden, slow others down
items.literal: become a tangle round hands and feet
items.use: Mostly said about yourself when refusing help or staying behind: ashidematoi ni naritakunai (I don't want to slow you down); said to others it's harsh. Unlike ashi o hipparu (dragging a result down), it's being a burden just by being there.
items.politeJa: 足手まといになります

example.romaji: ashidematoi ni naritakunai kara, saki itte.
example.ja: 足手まといになりたくないから、先行って。
example.english: I don't want to slow you down, go on ahead.

examplePolite.romaji: ashidematoi ni naritakunai node, saki ni itte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 足手まといになりたくないので、先に行ってください。
examplePolite.english: I don't want to slow you down, so please go ahead.

items.use: A work and family complaint about fixing what someone else messed up: mata ore ga ano hito no shirinugui ka yo. Often shirinugui o saserareru (get stuck cleaning up); ashi o hipparu is dragging the others down.

example.romaji: mata ore ga ano hito no shirinugui ka yo.
example.ja: また俺があの人の尻拭いかよ。
example.english: So I'm cleaning up his mess again?

examplePolite.romaji: mata watashi ga ano hito no shirinugui o suru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: また私があの人の尻拭いをするんですか？
examplePolite.english: So I'm cleaning up his mess again?

blocks.label: Feeling better
blocks.rationale: Relief and the gloom lifting: satisfied, at ease, distracted, refreshed, burden lifted.
blocks.interference: ki ga hareru (gloom lifts) vs ki ga magireru (mind taken off it); ki ga sumu (satisfied) vs ki ga raku (at ease).

items.englishIdiom: get it out of one's system
items.use: You'll hear ki ga sumu made (as much as you need), ki ga sumanai (won't rest until) and the exasperated kore de ki ga sunda? (happy now?). It's about getting an urge or grudge out, not being pleased with a result (manzoku).

example.romaji: ki ga sumu made naite ii yo.
example.ja: 気が済むまで泣いていいよ。
example.english: Cry as much as you need to.

examplePolite.romaji: ki ga sumu made yatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 気が済むまでやってください。
examplePolite.english: Go ahead until you're satisfied.

items.notes: Not sumu 'live'; plain word for satisfied: manzoku.

items.use: Said when pressure lifts or something feels less daunting, most often as ki ga raku ni naru: sou kiku to ki ga raku ni natta. Also for low pressure in general (hitori no hou ga ki ga raku). Kiraku (carefree) is a separate single word for a person or lifestyle.

example.romaji: sou itte kureru to ki ga raku ni naru.
example.ja: そう言ってくれると気が楽になる。
example.english: It's a relief to hear you say that.

examplePolite.romaji: sou itte itadakeru to ki ga raku ni narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: そう言っていただけると気が楽になります。
examplePolite.english: It puts my mind at ease to hear that.

items.notes: Plain alternative: hotto suru (feel relieved); kiraku = carefree.

items.use: Said of whatever helps you forget a worry for a while: hataraiteru to ki ga magireru. Ki ga chiru is the opposite kind of distraction, an unwanted loss of focus, and ki ga hareru is when the gloom actually lifts.

example.romaji: hanashitara sukoshi ki ga magireta.
example.ja: 話したら少し気が紛れた。
example.english: Talking took my mind off it a bit.

examplePolite.romaji: hanashitara sukoshi ki ga magiremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 話したら少し気が紛れました。
examplePolite.english: Talking helped take my mind off things a little.

items.notes: Transitive: ki o magirawasu (distract yourself on purpose).

items.literal: the mind clears up (like the sky)
items.use: Said after venting, a good cry or a change of scene (hanashitara ki ga hareta), as advice (sanpo demo shitara ki ga hareru yo), or in sore de ki ga hareru nara (if that makes you feel better). Ki ga magireru only takes your mind off a worry for a while; ki ga hareru means it actually lifts.

example.romaji: omoikkiri naitara, chotto ki ga hareta.
example.ja: 思いっきり泣いたら、ちょっと気が晴れた。
example.english: I had a good cry and feel a bit better.

examplePolite.romaji: hanashi o kiite moratte, sukoshi ki ga haremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 話を聞いてもらって、少し気が晴れました。
examplePolite.english: Having you listen made me feel a little better.

items.notes: Everyday swap: sukkiri shita. Pick-me-up: kibarashi. Variant: kibun ga hareru.

items.literal: the load comes off the shoulders
items.use: Said after handing over or finishing a duty you carried for a long time, nearly always in the past: yatto kata no ni ga orita. It's a bigger, longer-felt relief than ki ga raku ni naru.

example.romaji: hikitsugi mo owatte, yatto kata no ni ga orita.
example.ja: 引き継ぎも終わって、やっと肩の荷が下りた。
example.english: The handover's done, so that's finally a weight off my shoulders.

examplePolite.romaji: purojekuto ga owatte, kata no ni ga orimashita.
examplePolite.ja: プロジェクトが終わって、肩の荷が下りました。
examplePolite.english: With the project finished, it's a weight off my shoulders.

items.notes: Plain alternative: hotto suru (feel relieved).

blocks.label: Not right now
blocks.rationale: Whether you are free at this moment: tied up, hands full, no time for that, or finally free.
blocks.interference: te ga hanasenai (can't step away) and te ga aku (be free) use the same te ga frame with opposite meanings; te ippai is about overall capacity, not this one moment.

items.english: be tied up, can't step away now
items.use: The stock excuse when someone calls or asks for help mid-task: ima te ga hanasenai kara ato de ne. It is about this moment only; for being swamped in general say te ippai, and once you're free again, te ga aku.

example.romaji: gomen, ima te ga hanasenai
example.ja: ごめん、今手が離せない
example.english: Sorry, I'm tied up right now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima chotto te ga hanasenakute
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今ちょっと手が離せなくて
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm a bit tied up right now.

items.notes: In speech the ga often drops: ima te hanasenai.

items.english: have your hands full, at full capacity
items.use: Turning down more work or responsibility, usually as X de te ippai: jibun no shigoto de te ippai. Unlike te ga hanasenai (busy this minute), it means your plate is full in general.

example.romaji: gomen, ima jibun no shigoto de te ippai nan da
example.ja: ごめん、今自分の仕事で手一杯なんだ
example.english: Sorry, I've got my hands full with my own work right now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima jibun no shigoto de te ippai nan desu
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今自分の仕事で手一杯なんです
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I've got my hands full with my own work right now.

items.notes: Slangier: ippai ippai (at my absolute limit).

items.english: no time for that; far from it
items.literal: it's not that place (not the point for that)
items.use: The brush-off when you're swamped or something more urgent is going on: ima sore dokoro ja nai! It also corrects someone, 'far from it' (tanoshikatta? sore dokoro ja nai yo, saiaku datta).
items.politeJa: それどころじゃありません

example.romaji: gomen, ima sore dokoro ja nai n da
example.ja: ごめん、今それどころじゃないんだ
example.english: Sorry, I've got no time for that right now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima sore dokoro ja nai n desu
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今それどころじゃないんです
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I've got no time for that right now.

items.notes: Formal: sore dokoro de wa nai.

items.english: be free (not tied up), have a spare moment
items.use: Asking or saying whether someone is free to help right now: te aiteru? (got a sec?), te ga aitara onegai (when you're free). At work the stock promise is te ga aki shidai (as soon as I'm free): te ga aki shidai orikaeshimasu (I'll call you back as soon as I'm free). The opposite of te ga hanasenai; it is a free moment at work or home, not a free day.

example.romaji: te ga aitara chotto tetsudatte
example.ja: 手が空いたらちょっと手伝って
example.english: When you've got a free moment, give me a hand.

examplePolite.romaji: te ga aitara chotto tetsudatte moraemasu ka
examplePolite.ja: 手が空いたらちょっと手伝ってもらえますか
examplePolite.english: When you've got a free moment, could you give me a hand?

items.notes: Plain alternative: ima chotto ii? (got a sec?); hima? is free time in general and can sound like they're idle. To a boss or client: otesuki no toki ni (when you have a moment).

blocks.label: Letting things go
blocks.rationale: Forgiving or overlooking after a falling-out, and the no-hard-feelings line.
blocks.interference: nakatta koto ni suru (pretend it never happened), oome ni miru (let it slide) and mizu ni nagasu (forgive and forget) are near-synonyms; mizu ni nagasu vs mizu o sasu (spoil the mood) share mizu.

items.literal: make it a thing that wasn't
items.use: After an awkward moment, a confession or a slip: ima no, nakatta koto ni shite (forget I said that); also for burying a mistake or a deal. It erases rather than forgives, unlike mizu ni nagasu.
items.politeJa: なかったことにします

example.romaji: ima no, nakatta koto ni shite.
example.ja: 今の、なかったことにして。
example.english: Forget I said that.

examplePolite.romaji: ima no wa, nakatta koto ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今のは、なかったことにしてください。
examplePolite.english: Please forget I said that.

items.english: let it slide, go easy on someone
items.literal: look at it by a generous measure
items.use: Asking for or granting leniency over a small offence, usually kondo dake oome ni mite (just this once). A boss, parent or teacher does it; mizu ni nagasu is forgiving after a real fight.

example.romaji: kondo dake, oome ni mite yo.
example.ja: 今度だけ、大目に見てよ。
example.english: Just this once, let it slide.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo dake, oome ni mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今度だけ、大目に見てください。
examplePolite.english: Just this once, please let it slide.

items.literal: wash it away in the water
items.use: Making up after a fight or a grudge, usually as mizu ni nagasou (let's put it behind us). Different from nakatta koto ni suru, which pretends it never happened rather than forgiving it. Not mizu o nagasu (flush, run the water) or mizu o sasu (put a damper on).

example.romaji: mou mukashi no koto da shi, mizu ni nagasou yo.
example.ja: もう昔のことだし、水に流そうよ。
example.english: It's all in the past, let's put it behind us.

examplePolite.romaji: mou mukashi no koto desu shi, mizu ni nagashimashou.
examplePolite.ja: もう昔のことですし、水に流しましょう。
examplePolite.english: It's all in the past, let's put it behind us.

items.use: Said before janken, a draw, a bet or a vote so the loser won't sulk: uramikko nashi ne. Also after the result, to keep things friendly.

example.romaji: janken de kimeyou. uramikko nashi ne.
example.ja: じゃんけんで決めよう。恨みっこなしね。
example.english: Let's settle it with rock-paper-scissors. No hard feelings.

examplePolite.romaji: dou natte mo, uramikko nashi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: どうなっても、恨みっこなしですよ。
examplePolite.english: Whatever happens, no hard feelings.

blocks.label: Getting carried away
blocks.rationale: Losing your restraint: getting cocky, going overboard, getting full of yourself, a sudden lapse.
blocks.interference: choushi ni noru (cocky, can be playful) vs ii ki ni naru (smug, a sharper rebuke); ma ga sashita (a lapse) vs ma ga warui (bad timing) in A rough time.

items.englishIdiom: let it go to one's head
items.use: Usually a tease or a scolding (choushi ni noranaide yo, choushi notteru), or an apology (choushi ni notchatta). There is a rarer positive sense, 'get on a roll'. Don't confuse it with choushi ga warui (feel off).

example.romaji: gomen, choushi ni notchatta
example.ja: ごめん、調子に乗っちゃった
example.english: Sorry, I got carried away.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, choushi ni notte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: すみません、調子に乗ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I got carried away.

items.notes: Casual: choushi notteru (ni dropped); a person who does this is an ochoushimono.

items.use: Said about parties, trips and celebrations, usually as a caution: hame o hazushisuginaide ne (don't go too wild). It's fine for a well-earned blowout and negative only when it goes too far.

example.romaji: hame hazushisuginai you ni ne
example.ja: 羽目外しすぎないようにね
example.english: Don't go too wild, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: hame o hazushisuginai you ni shite kudasai ne
examplePolite.ja: 羽目を外しすぎないようにしてくださいね
examplePolite.english: Please don't go too overboard.

items.notes: Unrelated to hame ni naru (end up stuck doing) despite the shared word hame.

items.englishIdiom: get too big for one's boots
items.use: The standard rebuke for someone smug after a little success or praise: ii ki ni naru na yo. naru na is blunt; the softer form is ii ki ni naranai de. It sounds sharper than choushi ni noru, which can be playful. Don't confuse it with ki ni naru (be on one's mind).

example.romaji: chotto homerareta kurai de ii ki ni naru na yo.
example.ja: ちょっと褒められたくらいでいい気になるなよ。
example.english: Don't get full of yourself over a little praise.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto ii ki ni natte imashita.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっといい気になっていました。
examplePolite.english: I was getting a bit full of myself.

items.notes: Sarcastic cousin: ii ki na mon da (must be nice).

items.english: something came over me (a sudden lapse)
items.use: The set excuse for an out-of-character lapse, like cheating, pocketing something or a cruel remark, often softened with tsui or chotto (tsui ma ga sashite, chotto ma ga sashita). Said about yourself, or to excuse someone else (ma ga sashita n deshou).

example.romaji: gomen, tsui ma ga sashita n da.
example.ja: ごめん、つい魔が差したんだ。
example.english: Sorry, something just came over me.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui ma ga sashite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: つい魔が差してしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I gave in to temptation for a moment.

items.notes: Unrelated to ma ga warui (bad timing) despite the shared sound ma.

blocks.label: Secrets
blocks.rationale: Sharing a secret, letting it slip, playing dumb, and keeping it for life.
blocks.interference: kuchi ga suberu (let it slip) vs shira o kiru (play dumb about what you know); koko dake no hanashi shares a secret, hakaba made motte iku keeps one forever.

items.use: The usual opener before a secret or a frank opinion: koko dake no hanashi, ... It quietly asks the listener not to spread it.

example.romaji: koko dake no hanashi, kare kekkon suru n da tte.
example.ja: ここだけの話、彼結婚するんだって。
example.english: Between you and me, I hear he's getting married.

examplePolite.romaji: koko dake no hanashi, kare, kekkon suru rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ここだけの話、彼、結婚するらしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Between you and me, apparently he's getting married.

items.use: Mostly in the past, as an apology or excuse for blurting out a secret or a careless remark: tsui kuchi ga subetchatta (it just slipped out). Also heard as kuchi o suberaseru (let it slip).

example.romaji: gomen, tsui kuchi ga subetchatta.
example.ja: ごめん、つい口が滑っちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, it just slipped out.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, tsui kuchi ga suberimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、つい口が滑りました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, it just slipped out.

items.english: play dumb, pretend not to know
items.literal: put on a not-knowing act (shira; kiru as in mie o kiru, strike a pose)
items.use: Accusing someone of acting ignorant about something they clearly know, usually their own wrongdoing: shira kitte mo muda da yo (no use playing dumb). Mostly said to someone else, as shira o kiru na or shira kiranaide. Finally telling under pressure is the opposite, kuchi o waru.

example.romaji: shira kitte mo muda da yo, miteta n da kara.
example.ja: しら切っても無駄だよ、見てたんだから。
example.english: No use playing dumb, I saw you.

examplePolite.romaji: shira o kitte mo muda desu yo, mite ita n desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: しらを切っても無駄ですよ、見ていたんですから。
examplePolite.english: There's no point playing dumb. I saw you.

items.notes: Everyday alternatives: tobokenaide yo (don't play dumb), shirabakkureru.

items.english: keep a secret to the grave
items.literal: carry it as far as the graveyard
items.use: Promising never to tell anyone, as a solemn vow or half-jokingly about something embarrassing: kono koto wa hakaba made motte iku (I'm taking this to the grave). It's also said of a regret or humiliation you'll carry all your life: kono kutsujoku wa hakaba made motte iku.
items.kana: はかばまでもっていく
items.politeJa: 墓場まで持っていきます

example.romaji: kono hanashi wa hakaba made motteku yo.
example.ja: この話は墓場まで持ってくよ。
example.english: I'm taking this one to the grave.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hanashi wa hakaba made motte ikimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この話は墓場まで持っていきますよ。
examplePolite.english: I'll take this one to the grave.

items.notes: Casual: hakaba made motteku. Also: haka made motte iku.

blocks.label: Looking away
blocks.rationale: Choosing not to see something, plus missing what's right under your nose.
blocks.interference: me o tsuburu (let it slide) vs me o somukeru (refuse to face it) vs mite minu furi (pretend you didn't see); toudai moto kurashi is overlooking by accident, not by choice.

items.use: Said by someone in charge who lets a small fault slide: konkai dake me o tsuburu (I'll overlook it this once). It also means accepting a downside you can live with: tashou no ketten ni wa me o tsuburu. The same words literally mean close your eyes, so context decides; mite minu furi is the disapproving version, ignoring something that's wrong.

example.romaji: konkai dake wa me o tsuburu yo.
example.ja: 今回だけは目をつぶるよ。
example.english: I'll overlook it just this once.

examplePolite.romaji: konkai dake wa me o tsuburimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 今回だけは目をつぶりましょう。
examplePolite.english: I'll overlook it just this once.

items.notes: Also said me o tsumuru.

items.english: look away from, refuse to face
items.use: Said about avoiding an unpleasant truth or sight: genjitsu kara me o somukenaide. It's also literal, turning your eyes from something painful to see. Mite minu furi is pretending not to see so you needn't get involved; me o somukeru is not facing something because it hurts to look.

example.romaji: genjitsu kara me o somukenaide.
example.ja: 現実から目を背けないで。
example.english: Don't close your eyes to reality.

examplePolite.romaji: genjitsu kara me o somukenaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 現実から目を背けないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't close your eyes to reality.

items.notes: More everyday: me o sorasu (genjitsu kara me o sorasanaide), which is also looking away from someone's gaze.

items.english: pretend not to see, look the other way
items.literal: seeing, yet putting on not seeing
items.use: Disapproving: ignoring bullying, cheating or someone in trouble because getting involved is a hassle. Mite minu furi wa dekinai means I can't just look the other way, and o is often dropped. Me o tsuburu is the forgiving version, letting a small fault go on purpose.
items.politeJa: 見て見ぬふりをします

example.romaji: sonna no, mite minu furi dekinai yo.
example.ja: そんなの、見て見ぬふりできないよ。
example.english: I can't just look the other way.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa mite minu furi dekimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: それは見て見ぬふりできませんよ。
examplePolite.english: I can't just look the other way.

items.notes: Casual alternative: shiranpuri suru (act like you don't know).

items.english: you overlook what's right next to you
items.literal: below the lamp stand is dark
items.use: Said when a lost thing turns up somewhere obvious (keys in your pocket, glasses on your head), or when the answer was close by all along. Toudai here is an old oil-lamp stand, not a lighthouse, though many people picture a lighthouse.

example.romaji: megane, atama no ue ni atta. toudai moto kurashi da.
example.ja: メガネ、頭の上にあった。灯台下暗しだ。
example.english: My glasses were on my head. Right under my nose!

examplePolite.romaji: megane, atama no ue ni arimashita. toudai moto kurashi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: メガネ、頭の上にありました。灯台下暗しですね。
examplePolite.english: My glasses were on my head. Right under my nose!

blocks.label: Stubborn
blocks.rationale: Won't bend: won't listen, won't give up, proud, won't make exceptions, rigid thinking.
blocks.interference: atama ga katai (rigid) can be confused with kuchi ga katai (discreet). iji o haru (out of pride) can be confused with mie o haru (showing off). kiku mimi o motanai (won't listen) and yuuzuu ga kikanai (won't bend) share kiku/kikanai.

items.polite: kiku mimi o motanai n desu
items.english: refuse to listen, won't hear a word of it
items.use: A complaint about a parent, partner or boss who won't hear any advice or objection; o is often dropped in casual talk: nani itte mo kiku mimi motanai. Almost always negative, or wished for (sukoshi wa kiku mimi motte yo, have some ears for once); it's refusing to listen, not being unable to hear (kikoenai).
items.politeJa: 聞く耳を持たないんです

example.romaji: nani itte mo kiku mimi motanai n da yo.
example.ja: 何言っても聞く耳持たないんだよ。
example.english: Whatever I say, he just won't listen.

examplePolite.romaji: nani o itte mo kiku mimi o motanai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 何を言っても聞く耳を持たないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: No matter what I say, he won't listen.

items.notes: Plain way: zenzen kiite kurenai (just won't listen to me).

items.english: won't give up, can't let go
items.use: About someone who keeps trying or can't move on, like an ex who keeps texting or a rival who won't concede; also about yourself, half proud: akirame ga warui kara. Less often the opposite, akirame ga ii / hayai (lets go easily). Oujougiwa ga warui is narrower: refusing to admit you've lost.

example.romaji: watashi, akirame ga warui kara ne.
example.ja: 私、諦めが悪いからね。
example.english: I don't give up that easily.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, akirame ga warui n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 私、諦めが悪いんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I'm not one to give up easily.

items.notes: Verb: akirameru (give up).

items.use: Said to someone refusing help or refusing to apologise out of pride (iji haranaide yo), or about yourself after a fight: tsui iji hatchatta. Atama ga katai is about rigid ideas; this is about pride. Not mie o haru (show off).

example.romaji: tsui iji hatchatta.
example.ja: つい意地張っちゃった。
example.english: I let my pride get in the way.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui iji o hatte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: つい意地を張ってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I ended up being stubborn about it.

items.notes: Noun: ijippari (a stubborn person).

items.use: The staple complaint about a boss, clerk or system that won't make an exception: yuuzuu kikanai na. Mostly negative; yuuzuu ga kiku (flexible) is praise. Atama ga katai is about ideas; this is about rules and requests.

example.romaji: uchi no buchou, honto yuuzuu kikanai n da yo.
example.ja: うちの部長、ほんと融通利かないんだよ。
example.english: My boss just won't bend the rules.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no buchou wa hontou ni yuuzuu ga kikanai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: うちの部長は本当に融通が利かないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: Our manager really won't make any exceptions.

items.notes: Opposite: yuuzuu ga kiku (flexible, accommodating).

items.use: The usual complaint about bosses, parents or teachers who won't accept new ideas: atama katai na, with ga dropped. It means closed-minded, not stupid (that's atama ga warui); it also teases someone stuck on a riddle or a new way of doing things: atama katai naa.

example.romaji: uchi no oya, atama katai n da yo.
example.ja: うちの親、頭固いんだよ。
example.english: My parents are so set in their ways.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no oya wa atama ga katai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: うちの親は頭が固いんですよ。
examplePolite.english: My parents are rather old-fashioned in their thinking.

items.notes: Opposite: atama ga yawarakai (flexible); single word: ganko (stubborn).

blocks.label: Cooling off
blocks.rationale: Getting worked up versus calming down and loosening up; a natural three.
blocks.interference: atama o hiyasu (cool off) vs atama ni kuru in Getting angry; kata no chikara o nuku vs kata no ni ga oriru in Feeling better.

items.use: Said after an argument, either as an order (atama hiyashite koi, go cool your head) or about yourself (chotto atama hiyashite kuru). It can also literally mean cooling a feverish head.
