example.romaji: chotto soto de atama hiyashite kuru.
example.ja: ちょっと外で頭冷やしてくる。
example.english: I'm going outside to cool off.

examplePolite.romaji: sukoshi atama o hiyashite kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 少し頭を冷やしてきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll go cool off for a bit.

items.notes: Plain alternative: ochitsuku (calm down).

items.english: get worked up, take it too seriously
items.use: Mostly teasing someone who overreacts to a joke or a small thing (nani muki ni natteru no?), or owning up yourself (tsui muki ni natchatta). It isn't plain anger. It means taking something trivial too seriously.

example.romaji: sonna muki ni naranaide yo.
example.ja: そんなムキにならないでよ。
example.english: Don't get so worked up.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni muki ni naranaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなにムキにならないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: There's no need to get so worked up.

items.literal: take the strength out of the shoulders
items.use: Advice to someone nervous or trying too hard, mostly as kata no chikara nuite: it doesn't have to be perfect. Kata no chikara ga nuketeru also praises a relaxed, natural manner. The same words are the literal 'relax your shoulders' at a massage or in yoga.

example.romaji: kanpeki ni yaranakute ii n da kara, motto kata no chikara nuitara?
example.ja: 完璧にやらなくていいんだから、もっと肩の力抜いたら？
example.english: You don't have to be perfect, so why not stop trying so hard?

examplePolite.romaji: hajimete na n desu kara, kata no chikara o nuite daijoubu desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 初めてなんですから、肩の力を抜いて大丈夫ですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's your first time, so there's no need to try so hard.

items.notes: Opposite: kata ni chikara ga hairu (tense up); plain word: rirakkusu suru.

blocks.label: Keeping your nerve
blocks.rationale: Motivation rising and falling: warming to it, 'you can do it', talking of quitting, and finally giving up inside.
blocks.interference: yowane o haku means saying aloud that you can't take it, while kokoro ga oreru means the will itself giving way inside.

items.english: warm to the idea; get carried away, take it seriously
items.literal: come into that frame of mind
items.use: Most heard as sono ki ni nareba dekiru (you can if you put your mind to it), sono ki ni natte kita (I'm warming to it) and sono ki ni saseru (talk someone into it, or lead someone on). It is also taking praise or a joke at face value: homeraretara sugu sono ki ni naru (gets carried away as soon as he's praised), sono ki ni naru na yo (don't take it seriously). Not ki ni naru, which is being curious or bothered.

example.romaji: nanka sono ki ni natte kita
example.ja: なんかその気になってきた
example.english: I'm kind of warming to the idea.

examplePolite.romaji: nandaka sono ki ni natte kimashita
examplePolite.ja: なんだかその気になってきました
examplePolite.english: I'm kind of warming to the idea.

items.notes: No intention at all: sono ki wa nai.

items.english: you can do it if you try
items.literal: if you do it, you can
items.use: Encouragement (yareba dekiru yo) and praise after a success, often a little teasing: yareba dekiru jan (see, you CAN do it). The bookish source naseba naru is rarely said.

example.romaji: hora, yareba dekiru jan
example.ja: ほら、やればできるじゃん
example.english: See, you can do it when you try!

examplePolite.romaji: hora, yareba dekiru ja nai desu ka
examplePolite.ja: ほら、やればできるじゃないですか
examplePolite.english: See, you can do it when you try!

items.notes: Stock praise: yareba dekiru ko (a kid who can do it when they try).

items.english: say you can't take it, talk of giving up
items.use: Admitting out loud that you're struggling or want to quit, often in the negative (yowane o haku na, no whining) or as a self-aware confession. Not monku o iu, which is complaining about others or things.

example.romaji: yowane hakitakunai kedo, mou genkai
example.ja: 弱音吐きたくないけど、もう限界
example.english: I don't want to whine, but I'm at my limit.

examplePolite.romaji: yowane wa hakitakunai n desu kedo, mou genkai desu
examplePolite.ja: 弱音は吐きたくないんですけど、もう限界です
examplePolite.english: I don't want to whine, but I'm at my limit.

items.english: lose the will to keep going
items.use: A modern casual staple for giving up after setbacks or strain, mostly as kokoro oreta (that broke me) or kokoro oresou (about to give up), often without ga. Stronger than ki o otosu (be disappointed), and not romantic heartbreak, which is shitsuren.

example.romaji: are de kanzen ni kokoro oreta
example.ja: あれで完全に心折れた
example.english: That completely broke me.

examplePolite.romaji: are de kanzen ni kokoro ga oremashita
examplePolite.ja: あれで完全に心が折れました
examplePolite.english: That completely broke me.

items.notes: Transitive: kokoro o oru (crush someone's spirit).

blocks.label: Bad blood
blocks.rationale: Rubbing people the wrong way, from offence to a new enemy or a lasting grudge.
blocks.interference: ki o waruku suru (they take offence) vs ki ni sawaru (it grates on them) differ in who is hurt; don't merge ki ni sawaru with ki ni suru / ki ni naru; ne ni motsu (hold a grudge) is the opposite of mizu ni nagasu in Letting things go.

items.use: Almost always a softener before blunt words: ki o waruku shinaide (no offense, but...). The subject is the person who might feel hurt; ki ni sawaru is the remark that does the hurting.

example.romaji: ki o waruku shinaide kiite ne.
example.ja: 気を悪くしないで聞いてね。
example.english: Don't take this the wrong way, but hear me out.

examplePolite.romaji: ki o waruku shinaide kiite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 気を悪くしないで聞いてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please don't take this the wrong way.

items.use: Most often in the apology ki ni sawattara gomen (sorry if that upset you), or about a grating manner (ano iikata ga ki ni sawaru). The subject is the remark, not the hurt person (that's ki o waruku suru); not ki ni naru (be on your mind).

example.romaji: nanka ki ni sawatta nara, gomen ne.
example.ja: なんか気に障ったなら、ごめんね。
example.english: Sorry if I said something that upset you.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika oki ni sawattara, moushiwake arimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 何かお気に障ったら、申し訳ありません。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry if anything I said upset you.

items.english: make an enemy of, turn (someone) against you
items.use: A warning about someone powerful or vindictive: ano hito o teki ni mawasu to kowai yo. Also about taking on many at once (minna o teki ni mawashite mo); mikata ni tsukeru (win someone over) is the opposite.

example.romaji: ano hito o teki ni mawasu to kowai yo.
example.ja: あの人を敵に回すと怖いよ。
example.english: You don't want to make an enemy of her.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito o teki ni mawasu to kowai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの人を敵に回すと怖いですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't want to make an enemy of her.

items.use: Usually teasing or defensive, in the -teru form: mada ne ni motteru no? (still sore about that?). The opposite of mizu ni nagasu.

example.romaji: mada ano koto ne ni motteru no?
example.ja: まだあのこと根に持ってるの？
example.english: You're still holding a grudge about that?

examplePolite.romaji: mada ano koto o ne ni motte iru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: まだあのことを根に持っているんですか？
examplePolite.english: Are you still holding a grudge about that?

blocks.label: Closing the matter
blocks.rationale: Bringing a matter to an end: settling it, declaring it done, owning it properly.
blocks.interference: keri o tsukeru (finish it off) vs kejime o tsukeru (take responsibility, draw a line) share o tsukeru; ikken rakuchaku is said once it's done.

items.english: settle it, put an end to it
items.literal: attach a keri (the classical verb ending that closed poems and tales)
items.use: Said when you decide to end something for good: a feud or rivalry (aitsu to keri o tsukeru), or a relationship or job that has dragged on. It has a showdown flavour, so in everyday talk it is often half-joking. The intransitive keri ga tsuku (it got settled) exists but is much rarer.

example.romaji: sorosoro keri o tsukenai to
example.ja: そろそろケリをつけないと
example.english: Time I settled this once and for all.

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro keri o tsukenai to ikemasen ne
examplePolite.ja: そろそろケリをつけないといけませんね
examplePolite.english: We need to settle this soon.

items.notes: Near-synonym: kecchaku o tsukeru (settle a contest).

items.use: Said, often half-jokingly, the moment a problem or squabble gets sorted: kore de ikken rakuchaku. It echoes the magistrate's closing line in old samurai dramas but is used for small everyday fixes.

example.romaji: yoshi, kore de ikken rakuchaku da ne
example.ja: よし、これで一件落着だね
example.english: Right, that's that sorted.

examplePolite.romaji: kore de ikken rakuchaku desu ne
examplePolite.ja: これで一件落着ですね
examplePolite.english: That settles it, then.

items.notes: Plain alternative: kaiketsu (solved).

items.english: take proper responsibility; draw a clear line
items.use: Two everyday uses: owning up to a mess properly, often by apologising or resigning (kejime o tsukenai to), and keeping things clearly apart, like work and private life (koushi no kejime). In dramas it's often a demand or vow to settle accounts: ore ga kejime o tsukeru (I'll settle this myself). keri o tsukeru ends a matter; kejime is about doing it properly.

example.romaji: kono ken wa chanto kejime tsukenai to.
example.ja: この件はちゃんとけじめつけないと。
example.english: I need to take proper responsibility for this.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ken wa kichinto kejime o tsukemasu.
examplePolite.ja: この件はきちんとけじめをつけます。
examplePolite.english: I'll take proper responsibility for this matter.

items.notes: kejime o tsukero! is a rough demand (in yakuza dramas, a threat). koushi no kejime: keeping work and private life apart.

blocks.label: Conversation flow
blocks.rationale: Moments inside a conversation: butting in, derailing, the subject walking in, awkward silence.
blocks.interference: kuchi o hasamu (butt in) vs hanashi no koshi o oru (derail someone mid-story); ma ga motanai is running out of things to say, not interrupting.

items.english: butt in, put in one's two cents (in talk or matters that aren't yours)
items.use: Butting into other people's conversation or business, heard as kuchi hasamanaide (stay out of this) or the polite preface kuchi o hasamu you desu ga (sorry to cut in). kuchi o dasu is close but stronger, actively meddling; cutting someone off mid-sentence is hanashi no koshi o oru, and kuchi ni dasu is just saying something out loud.

example.romaji: ima daiji na hanashi da kara, kuchi hasamanaide.
example.ja: 今大事な話だから、口挟まないで。
example.english: This is important, so don't butt in.

examplePolite.romaji: ima daiji na hanashi na node, kuchi o hasamanaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今大事な話なので、口を挟まないでください。
examplePolite.english: We're discussing something important, so please don't interrupt.

items.use: Said the moment the person you were talking about walks in or calls: a, uwasa o sureba! People clip the full saying uwasa o sureba kage ga sasu (talk of someone and their shadow appears).

example.romaji: a, uwasa o sureba kita yo.
example.ja: あ、噂をすれば来たよ。
example.english: Oh, speak of the devil, here he comes.

examplePolite.romaji: a, uwasa o sureba kimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: あ、噂をすれば来ましたね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, speak of the devil, here he is.

items.notes: Full saying: uwasa o sureba kage ga sasu.

items.english: interrupt and derail what someone is saying
items.literal: break the waist of the talk
items.use: Cutting in so the speaker loses their thread, as a complaint (hanashi no koshi oranaide) or an apology (hanashi no koshi o otte gomen). kuchi o hasamu is butting in with your own remark; this is derailing what someone was in the middle of saying.

example.romaji: chotto, hanashi no koshi oranaide yo.
example.ja: ちょっと、話の腰折らないでよ。
example.english: Hey, don't cut me off.

examplePolite.romaji: ohanashi no koshi o oru you de sumimasen ga, hitotsu dake ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お話の腰を折るようですみませんが、一つだけいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry to interrupt, but could I just say one thing?

items.notes: Politely the talk becomes ohanashi, since it's the listener's; the stock preface is ohanashi no koshi o oru you desu ga...

items.english: can't fill the silence, run out of things to say
items.literal: the pause can't be held up
items.use: Said of a silence you can't fill: on a first date, in a lift with your boss, at a table where nobody talks. Usually about yourself or a situation, as futarikiri da to ma ga motanai (just the two of us, I run out of things to say). Also about killing time: sumaho ga nai to ma ga motanai.

example.romaji: futarikiri da to ma ga motanai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 二人きりだと間が持たないんだよね。
example.english: When it's just the two of us, I run out of things to say.

examplePolite.romaji: futarikiri da to ma ga motanai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 二人きりだと間が持たないんですよね。
examplePolite.english: When it's just the two of us, I never know how to fill the silence.

blocks.label: Hunches and surprises
blocks.rationale: Feelings about what's coming: it's nothing, a premonition, never saw it coming, a revelation.
blocks.interference: ki no sei (just your imagination) vs mushi no shirase (a feeling that proved right); omoi mo yoranai and yume ni mo omowanakatta both mean 'never imagined'.

items.use: The stock reply when someone thinks they heard or saw something: ki no sei da yo (you're imagining it). About your own hunch it's ki no sei kana (maybe it's just me), often paired with ki ga suru.

example.romaji: ki no sei da yo. nanimo kikoenai.
example.ja: 気のせいだよ。何も聞こえない。
example.english: It's just your imagination. I can't hear anything.

examplePolite.romaji: ki no sei desu yo. nanimo kikoemasen.
examplePolite.ja: 気のせいですよ。何も聞こえません。
examplePolite.english: It's just your imagination. I can't hear anything.

items.notes: Hedge form: ki no sei kana (maybe it's just me).

items.use: Mostly in the past, omoi mo yoranakatta (I never imagined), or before a noun, omoi mo yoranai tenkai (a turn nobody saw coming). It's a touch more neutral than yume ni mo omowanakatta and works in work talk too.
items.politeJa: 思いもよりませんでした

example.romaji: konna koto ni naru nante, omoi mo yoranakatta.
example.ja: こんなことになるなんて、思いもよらなかった。
example.english: I never imagined it would come to this.

examplePolite.romaji: konna koto ni naru to wa, omoi mo yorimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: こんなことになるとは、思いもよりませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I never imagined it would come to this.

items.notes: Plain alternative: omoi mo shinakatta (never even thought of it).

items.literal: didn't think it even in a dream
items.use: Said in the past, as ... nante yume ni mo omowanakatta (I never dreamed ...). It's for a big surprise, good or bad: running into a star, a friend getting married, a betrayal. Don't confuse it with yume o miru (have a dream while asleep).
items.kana: ゆめにもおもわなかった
items.politeJa: 夢にも思いませんでした

example.romaji: konna tokoro de au nante yume ni mo omowanakatta.
example.ja: こんなところで会うなんて夢にも思わなかった。
example.english: I never dreamed I'd run into you here.

examplePolite.romaji: konna tokoro de au nante yume ni mo omoimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: こんなところで会うなんて夢にも思いませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I never dreamed I'd run into you here.

items.notes: Plain alternative: masaka (no way); casual: omoi mo shinakatta.

items.use: A hunch that turned out right, usually about bad news or someone close, often named afterwards: mushi no shirase datta no kana. The mushi is the old idea of a bug inside you that senses things. Ki no sei is the opposite: a feeling that turns out to be nothing.

example.romaji: mushi no shirase datta no kana. kyuu ni kaasan ni denwa shitara, nyuuin shiteta n da.
example.ja: 虫の知らせだったのかな。急に母さんに電話したら、入院してたんだ。
example.english: Maybe it was a premonition. I called Mum out of the blue, and she was in hospital.

examplePolite.romaji: mushi no shirase datta n deshou ka. kyuu ni haha ni denwa shitara, nyuuin shiteta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 虫の知らせだったんでしょうか。急に母に電話したら、入院してたんです。
examplePolite.english: Maybe it was a premonition. I called my mother out of the blue, and she was in hospital.

items.notes: Plain alternative: iya na yokan (a bad feeling).

items.english: a revelation that changes your view
items.use: Said after a tip, a fact or a trick that changes how you see something: kore wa me kara uroko datta (that was a real eye-opener). It's casual and a TV favourite. The full saying, me kara uroko ga ochiru, is rarer in talk.

example.romaji: kono urawaza, maji de me kara uroko datta.
example.ja: この裏技、マジで目からウロコだった。
example.english: This trick was a real eye-opener.

examplePolite.romaji: kono urawaza, hontou ni me kara uroko deshita.
examplePolite.ja: この裏技、本当に目からウロコでした。
examplePolite.english: This trick was a real eye-opener.

items.notes: Full form: me kara uroko ga ochiru.

blocks.label: Hidden side
blocks.rationale: The person behind the surface: not what they look like, a different person, scheming, faking sweetness, good at heart.
blocks.interference: hara ga kuroi (secretly scheming) vs neko o kaburu (faking innocence). ne wa ii can be mixed up with hito ga ii. hito ga kawaru (become a different person) vs ki ga kawaru (change your mind).

items.english: not what you'd guess from looks
items.englishIdiom: you can't judge a book by its cover
items.use: Said when someone turns out different from how they look, like a gentle-looking guy who boxes: hito wa mikake ni yoranai ne. Always negative; as an adverb, mikake ni yorazu (despite looks): mikake ni yorazu yoku taberu.
items.politeJa: 見かけによらないです

example.romaji: ano hito ga? mikake ni yoranai ne.
example.ja: あの人が？見かけによらないね。
example.english: Him? You'd never guess from looking.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito ga desu ka? hito wa mikake ni yoranai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人がですか？人は見かけによらないですね。
examplePolite.english: Him? You really can't judge people by their looks.

items.notes: Full saying: hito wa mikake ni yoranai; plain word: igai (unexpected).

items.use: About someone who changes completely when drunk, angry or behind the wheel (nomu to hito ga kawaru), or someone who has changed for good or bad: hito ga kawatta mitai. Mostly with -to or in the past. With a modifier it's literal: tantou no hito ga kawaru (the person in charge changes).

example.romaji: kare, osake nomu to hito ga kawaru n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、お酒飲むと人が変わるんだよ。
example.english: He turns into a different person when he drinks.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa osake o nomu to hito ga kawaru n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はお酒を飲むと人が変わるんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He becomes a different person when he drinks.

items.notes: Like a different person: hito ga kawatta you ni / mitai ni.

items.use: About someone who smiles sweetly but is calculating underneath, often half-joking, about a coworker, a celebrity or a friend's new partner. It is fused from hara ga kuroi, which people hardly ever say in full. Neko o kaburu is only the sweet act, without the scheming.

example.romaji: ano ko, jitsu wa haraguroi yo.
example.ja: あの子、実は腹黒いよ。
example.english: She's actually a schemer.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, jitsu wa haraguroi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの人、実は腹黒いですよ。
examplePolite.english: She's actually quite calculating.

items.notes: Noun: haraguro (a schemer).

items.english: put on a sweet, innocent act
items.use: About someone acting sweet, shy or well-behaved to hide their real self, in front of a boss, a date or the in-laws; usually neko kabutteru with o dropped. Close to haraguroi, but this is only the act, not scheming.

example.romaji: ano ko, kachou no mae da to neko kabutteru yo.
example.ja: あの子、課長の前だと猫かぶってるよ。
example.english: She acts all sweet in front of the boss.

examplePolite.romaji: ano ko, kachou no mae da to neko kabuttemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの子、課長の前だと猫かぶってますよ。
examplePolite.english: She puts on an innocent act in front of the manager.

items.notes: Noun: nekokaburi (someone putting on an act).

items.englishIdiom: one's heart is in the right place
items.use: Defending someone who seems rude, scary or lazy, nearly always as ne wa ii yatsu or ne wa ii hito. Ne (root) is someone's true nature: ne wa majime (serious at heart), ne wa yasashii (kind at heart).

example.romaji: kuchi warui kedo, ne wa ii yatsu da yo.
example.ja: 口悪いけど、根はいいやつだよ。
example.english: He's mouthy, but he's a good guy at heart.

examplePolite.romaji: kuchi wa warui desu kedo, ne wa ii hito desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 口は悪いですけど、根はいい人ですよ。
examplePolite.english: He can be blunt, but he's a good person at heart.

items.notes: Same pattern: ne wa majime, ne wa yasashii.

blocks.label: Pride, envy, gloating
blocks.rationale: Feelings about other people: proud of them, jealous over them, glad they got what they deserved.
blocks.interference: zamaa miro (to their face) vs ii kimi (about them); ii kimi shares kimi with kimi ga warui.

items.literal: look at the state of you
items.use: The stock gloat at someone getting their comeuppance, often said jokingly among friends or muttered at a rival; zamaa! on its own is common too. Ii kimi da is the cooler, more grown-up 'serves them right'.

example.romaji: sakki warikonde kita kuruma, tsukamatteru. zamaa miro.
example.ja: さっき割り込んできた車、捕まってる。ざまあみろ。
example.english: That car that cut in on us got pulled over. Ha, serves him right.

items.notes: Also: zamaa!, zama miro.

items.use: Pride in a child, friend or team member whose success reflects on you: watashi mo hana ga takai yo. It can also literally mean a prominent nose. Don't mix it up with tengu ni naru (get conceited).

example.romaji: yuushou shita nante, watashi mo hana ga takai yo.
example.ja: 優勝したなんて、私も鼻が高いよ。
example.english: You won? I'm so proud of you.

examplePolite.romaji: buka ga homerarete, watashi mo hana ga takai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 部下が褒められて、私も鼻が高いです。
examplePolite.english: My team member got praised, and I'm proud too.

items.notes: Plain alternative: jiman (something to be proud of).

items.use: Spiteful satisfaction when someone who had it coming gets hurt, usually ii kimi da, said about them or to their face. It's cooler and more grown-up than the taunting zamaa miro. The kimi here is 'feeling' (as in kimi ga warui), not kimi 'you'.

example.romaji: itsumo ibatteta kara, ii kimi da yo.
example.ja: いつも威張ってたから、いい気味だよ。
example.english: He was always so full of himself, so serves him right.

items.literal: grill rice cakes (yaku is also the word for being jealous)
items.use: Jealousy over someone's affection or attention, whether a partner, a child about a new sibling or a friend, with yakimochi yaiteru no? as the classic tease. Shitto suru is the heavier plain word, and urayamashii is envy of what someone has.

example.romaji: moshikashite, yakimochi yaiteru no?
example.ja: もしかして、やきもち焼いてるの？
example.english: Wait, are you jealous?

examplePolite.romaji: kare, sugu yakimochi o yaku n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼、すぐやきもちを焼くんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He gets jealous so easily.

items.notes: Single words: yakimochi (jealousy), shitto; envious: urayamashii.

blocks.label: Slacking off
blocks.rationale: The opposite of effort: half-hearted, easing off, and cutting corners.
blocks.interference: ki o nuku and te o nuku differ by one word: ki means letting your attention slip (often a warning), while te means cutting corners on purpose.

items.use: Criticises half-finished work or half-hearted commitment (chuuto hanpa ni yaru nara yamero, chuuto hanpa na kimochi), and describes anything stuck awkwardly in between (chuuto hanpa na jikan, an awkward time). Na before nouns, ni before verbs.

example.romaji: nanka chuuto hanpa ni owatchatta
example.ja: なんか中途半端に終わっちゃった
example.english: It kind of ended up half-finished.

examplePolite.romaji: nandaka chuuto hanpa ni owatte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: なんだか中途半端に終わってしまいました
examplePolite.english: It kind of ended up half-finished.

items.notes: Slang hanpa nai (from hanpa ja nai) means insane, incredible.

items.english: let your guard down, ease off
items.use: Mostly a warning to stay sharp until it's over (ki o nuku na, ki o nukanaide), or about a slip: chotto ki o nuita suki ni (the moment I let my guard down). It can also be easing off on purpose (tama ni wa ki o nuku no mo daiji). Not te o nuku, which is deliberately doing less.

example.romaji: saigo made ki o nuku na yo
example.ja: 最後まで気を抜くなよ
example.english: Don't let up till the very end.

examplePolite.romaji: saigo made ki o nukanaide kudasai ne
examplePolite.ja: 最後まで気を抜かないでくださいね
examplePolite.english: Please don't let up until the very end.

items.notes: Intransitive ki ga nukeru: feel deflated; (drinks) go flat.

items.use: Doing a task with less effort than it deserves, about chores, cooking, work or a game: kyou wa ryouri te o nuichatta, te o nuku na. Not ki o nuku, which is losing focus rather than deliberately doing less.

example.romaji: kyou wa bangohan te nuichatta
example.ja: 今日は晩ご飯手抜いちゃった
example.english: I cut corners on dinner tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no bangohan wa chotto te o nuichaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 今日の晩ご飯はちょっと手を抜いちゃいました
examplePolite.english: I cut corners on dinner tonight.

items.notes: Noun: tenuki (tenuki ryouri = a lazy meal).

blocks.label: At a get-together
blocks.rationale: Showing up to a gathering, dampening the mood and wrapping it up.
blocks.interference: kao o dasu (show up) vs te o dasu / kuchi o dasu in Butting in; mizu o sasu (spoil the mood) vs mizu ni nagasu (forgive and forget) share mizu.

items.use: Popping into a party, club, office or someone's home, often briefly: chotto kao dasu ne. Not te o dasu or kuchi o dasu, which are about interfering.

example.romaji: nomikai, chotto dake kao dasu yo.
example.ja: 飲み会、ちょっとだけ顔出すよ。
example.english: I'll show my face at the drinks for a bit.

examplePolite.romaji: nomikai ni wa, chotto dake kao o dashimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 飲み会には、ちょっとだけ顔を出します。
examplePolite.english: I'll show my face at the drinks for a bit.

items.notes: Also kao o miseru, the usual one for visiting: tama ni wa kao misete ne (come and see us sometimes).

items.english: call it a night, wrap up (a party)
items.use: How a party, drinking session or wedding gets ended, since owaru is avoided at celebrations: jaa, sorosoro ohiraki ni shiyou ka. When telling what happened: ohiraki ni natta (it broke up).

example.romaji: jaa, sorosoro ohiraki ni shiyou ka.
example.ja: じゃあ、そろそろお開きにしようか。
example.english: OK, shall we call it a night?

examplePolite.romaji: sore de wa, sorosoro ohiraki ni shitai to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: それでは、そろそろお開きにしたいと思います。
examplePolite.english: Well, I think it's about time we wrapped up.

items.notes: Often just ohiraki: kore de ohiraki (that's a wrap); the host's formal line is ohiraki to sasete itadakimasu.

items.english: put a damper on, spoil the mood
items.use: Mostly the apology before bad news or an objection: mizu sasu you de warui kedo (sorry to be a downer, but). Also coming between a happy couple or friends (futari no naka ni mizu o sasu). Not mizu ni nagasu (forgive and forget).

example.romaji: mizu sasu you de warui kedo, sono hi ame rashii yo.
example.ja: 水差すようで悪いけど、その日雨らしいよ。
example.english: Sorry to be a downer, but it's supposed to rain that day.

examplePolite.romaji: mizu o sasu you de moushiwake nai n desu ga, sono hi wa ame rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 水を差すようで申し訳ないんですが、その日は雨らしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Sorry to be a downer, but it's supposed to rain that day.

blocks.label: All for nothing
blocks.rationale: Effort or chances that are lost, progress wiped out, and being too late to fix it.
blocks.interference: mizu no awa (effort comes to nothing) vs bou ni furu (you throw something away yourself); torikaeshi ga tsukanai (can't be undone) vs ato no matsuri (too late to act).

items.use: Said when effort, time or savings are wiped out in one go, usually as zenbu mizu no awa da or mizu no awa ni natta. People say it about their own wasted work far more often than about anyone else's.

example.romaji: kore de zenbu mizu no awa da yo
example.ja: これで全部水の泡だよ
example.english: Now it's all gone down the drain.

examplePolite.romaji: kore de zenbu mizu no awa desu yo
examplePolite.ja: これで全部水の泡ですよ
examplePolite.english: Now it's all been for nothing.

items.notes: Plain alternative: muda ni natta (went to waste).

items.use: A warning before damage that can't be fixed (torikaeshi no tsukanai koto ni naru) or regret afterwards (torikaeshi no tsukanai koto o shita). It mostly appears in the no form before koto.
items.kana: とりかえしがつかない
items.politeJa: 取り返しがつきません

example.romaji: torikaeshi no tsukanai koto shichatta
example.ja: 取り返しのつかないことしちゃった
example.english: I've done something I can't undo.

examplePolite.romaji: torikaeshi no tsukanai koto o shite shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 取り返しのつかないことをしてしまいました
examplePolite.english: I've done something that can't be undone.

items.notes: Before a noun it's torikaeshi no tsukanai; torikaesu alone means get back, win back.

items.english: throw away (a chance, a career, years)
items.use: Said about wasting something big through one bad choice: jinsei o bou ni furu (throw your life away), chansu o bou ni furu. Often a warning: sonna koto de jinsei bou ni furu na yo. For effort that simply comes to nothing, say mizu no awa.

example.romaji: sonna koto de jinsei bou ni furu na yo.
example.ja: そんなことで人生棒に振るなよ。
example.english: Don't throw your life away over that.

examplePolite.romaji: sekkaku no chansu o bou ni futte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: せっかくのチャンスを棒に振ってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I threw away a golden chance.

items.notes: Plain alternative: muda ni suru (waste).

items.literal: go back to the starting square (of a board game)
items.use: Said when a setback wipes out all progress on a plan, a search or a negotiation, mostly in the past: mata furidashi ni modotta. Often clipped to furidashi da or mata furidashi ka. furidashi ni modoru is what happens to you; ichi kara yarinaosu is what you then choose to do.

example.romaji: kore de mata furidashi ni modotchatta.
example.ja: これでまた振り出しに戻っちゃった。
example.english: Great, now we're back to square one again.

examplePolite.romaji: kore de mata furidashi ni modorimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: これでまた振り出しに戻りましたね。
examplePolite.english: So we're back to square one again.

items.notes: Scrapping a plan on purpose is hakushi ni modosu.

items.use: Said when regret or a fix comes too late, usually about a missed chance, often your own: imasara itte mo ato no matsuri da (no use saying it now).

example.romaji: imasara itte mo ato no matsuri da yo
example.ja: 今さら言っても後の祭りだよ
example.english: No use saying that now, it's too late.

examplePolite.romaji: imasara itte mo ato no matsuri desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 今さら言っても後の祭りですよ
examplePolite.english: It's too late to say that now.

items.notes: Plain alternative: mou osoi (it's too late).

blocks.label: Fair point
blocks.rationale: Granting that someone's reaction or guess makes sense.
blocks.interference: muri mo nai (no wonder, understandable) vs ichiri aru (you have a point); ii sen itteru means close to the right answer, not agreement.

items.use: Said in sympathy once you hear why someone is tired, upset or angry, usually as X no mo muri (wa) nai: okoru no mo muri nai (no wonder she's angry). Don't confuse it with muri on its own (impossible, too much) or muri shinaide (don't overdo it).

example.romaji: tetsuya? nemui no mo muri nai ne.
example.ja: 徹夜？眠いのも無理ないね。
example.english: An all-nighter? No wonder you're sleepy.

examplePolite.romaji: tetsuya desu ka? nemui no mo muri wa arimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 徹夜ですか？眠いのも無理はありませんね。
examplePolite.english: An all-nighter? No wonder you're sleepy.

items.notes: Also muri wa nai. Close: douri de (no wonder: douri de nemui wake da).

items.literal: there is a grain of reason
items.use: Used to concede part of someone's argument without fully agreeing: tashika ni, sore mo ichiri aru ne. It's said of the opinion, not the person: kimi no iken ni mo ichiri aru.

example.romaji: tashika ni, sore mo ichiri aru ne.
example.ja: 確かに、それも一理あるね。
example.english: True, you've got a point there.

examplePolite.romaji: tashika ni, sore mo ichiri arimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 確かに、それも一理ありますね。
examplePolite.english: True, you've got a point there.

items.notes: Plain alternative: tashika ni (fair enough).

items.use: Said about a guess that's nearly right (ii sen itteru kedo, chigau) or an attempt that's pretty good but not quite there, and sometimes about a person who's a decent prospect. It's light and a little playful, and you'll hear it in the -teru form.

example.romaji: oshii! ii sen itteru kedo, chigau.
example.ja: 惜しい！いい線いってるけど、違う。
example.english: So close! You're on the right track, but no.

examplePolite.romaji: oshii desu ne! ii sen itte imasu kedo, chigaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 惜しいですね！いい線いっていますけど、違います。
examplePolite.english: So close! You're on the right track, but no.

items.notes: Plain alternative: oshii (so close).

blocks.label: Close and distant
blocks.rationale: Who is inside your circle and how far you let them in.
blocks.interference: aka no tanin (a complete stranger) vs tanin gyougi (too formal with someone close) share tanin; kokoro o hiraku (open up) is the opposite of kyori o oku (keep your distance).

items.use: About a shy child, a new colleague, a rescued pet or a guarded partner finally trusting you: yatto kokoro o hiraite kureta, or nakanaka kokoro o hirakanai. kyori o oku is the opposite move.

example.romaji: ano ko, yatto kokoro hiraite kureta.
example.ja: あの子、やっと心開いてくれた。
example.english: She's finally opened up to me.

examplePolite.romaji: ano ko, yatto kokoro o hiraite kureta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの子、やっと心を開いてくれたんです。
examplePolite.english: She's finally opened up to me.

items.notes: Close: kokoro o yurusu / ki o yurusu (trust someone, let your guard down).

items.english: keep your distance, take time apart
items.use: Relationship talk: shibaraku kyori o okitai (I want some time apart), or stepping back from a draining friend or group. Softer than wakareru: it's a break, not a breakup.

example.romaji: shibaraku kyori oita hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: しばらく距離置いたほうがいいよ。
example.english: You two should take some time apart.

examplePolite.romaji: shibaraku kyori o oita hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: しばらく距離を置いたほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You'd be better off taking some time apart.

items.use: Stresses there's no connection at all, often bitterly: after a breakup, mou aka no tanin. Aka here means 'complete', not the colour.

example.romaji: wakaretara, mou aka no tanin da yo.
example.ja: 別れたら、もう赤の他人だよ。
example.english: Once you break up, you're total strangers.

examplePolite.romaji: wakaretara, mou aka no tanin desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 別れたら、もう赤の他人ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Once you break up, you're total strangers.

items.notes: Plain alternative: tanin (outsider, someone not family).

items.use: A complaint about being the last to know or shut out of a decision: nande ore dake kaya no soto na no? Heard at work, among friends and in families, often as kaya no soto ni sareta (got shut out).

example.romaji: nande ore dake kaya no soto na no?
example.ja: なんで俺だけ蚊帳の外なの？
example.english: Why am I the only one left out?

examplePolite.romaji: watashi dake kaya no soto datta n desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私だけ蚊帳の外だったんですね。
examplePolite.english: So I was the only one left out of the loop.

items.use: Said to a friend, partner or relative who's being too polite or reserved with you: tanin gyougi da na (why so formal?). Often about keigo, over-thanking or refusing help; aka no tanin is an actual stranger.

example.romaji: keigo nante yamete yo. tanin gyougi ja n.
example.ja: 敬語なんてやめてよ。他人行儀じゃん。
example.english: Drop the keigo. You're being so formal with me.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna tanin gyougi na koto iwanaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんな他人行儀なこと言わないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Don't be so formal with me.

items.notes: Close: mizukusai na (why didn't you just ask me? / don't be a stranger), said when a friend keeps things to themselves.

items.romaji: yoso wa yoso, uchi wa uchi
items.english: other families do as they like; we do it our way
items.literal: elsewhere is elsewhere, home is home
items.use: Every parent's reply to 'but everyone else has one / is allowed': yoso wa yoso, uchi wa uchi. Also more widely, that other people's choices aren't yours to copy.
items.ja: よそはよそ、うちはうち
items.kana: よそはよそ、うちはうち

example.romaji: minna motteru tte? yoso wa yoso, uchi wa uchi desho.
example.ja: みんな持ってるって？よそはよそ、うちはうちでしょ。
example.english: Everyone has one? Other families can do what they like; this is our house.

examplePolite.romaji: yoso wa yoso, uchi wa uchi desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: よそはよそ、うちはうちですから。
examplePolite.english: Other places do things their way; we do ours.

items.notes: Also said the other way round: uchi wa uchi, yoso wa yoso.

blocks.label: Bound to happen
blocks.rationale: Remarks about what is sure to come, or come again: a matter of time, a repeat failure, threes, experts slipping.
blocks.interference: nido aru koto wa sando aru (bad luck repeats) vs sandome no shoujiki (the third try works) predict opposite thirds; ni no mai is repeating one particular past failure.

items.use: Said when something is bound to happen sooner or later, most often being found out, caught or a collapse: bareru no wa jikan no mondai da, mou jikan no mondai da.

example.romaji: bareru no wa jikan no mondai da yo
example.ja: バレるのは時間の問題だよ
example.english: It's only a matter of time before they find out.

examplePolite.romaji: bareru no wa jikan no mondai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: バレるのは時間の問題ですよ
examplePolite.english: It's only a matter of time before they find out.

items.english: a repeat of an earlier failure (someone else's, or last time's)
items.literal: the second dance (a clown copying the first dancer)
items.use: Almost always X no ni no mai, where X is the person or event whose failure you'd repeat: a groan (kore ja zenkai no ni no mai da, it's last time all over again), a refusal (X no ni no mai wa gomen da, I'm not going through X again) or a warning (senpai no ni no mai ni naranai you ni). Don't confuse it with ni no ashi o fumu (hesitate).

example.romaji: senpai no ni no mai ni naranai you ni ne.
example.ja: 先輩の二の舞にならないようにね。
example.english: Don't end up like your senpai, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: zenkai no ni no mai ni naranai you ni shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 前回の二の舞にならないようにしましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's not repeat what happened last time.

items.notes: Written form: ni no mai o enjiru. You'll also hear ni no mai o fumu, a blend with ni no ashi o fumu that dictionaries call a mistake.

items.romaji: nido aru koto wa sando aru
items.english: if it happened twice, it'll happen again
items.literal: what happens twice happens three times
items.use: Quoted after a second mishap, like losing an umbrella again or a second breakdown, as a half-joking warning that a third one is coming. The comeback is sandome no shoujiki (third time lucky).
items.ja: 二度あることは三度ある
items.kana: にどあることはさんどある

example.romaji: nido aru koto wa sando aru tte iu shi, ki o tsukete ne
example.ja: 二度あることは三度あるって言うし、気をつけてね
example.english: They say what happens twice happens again, so be careful.

examplePolite.romaji: nido aru koto wa sando aru tte iimasu kara ne
examplePolite.ja: 二度あることは三度あるって言いますからね
examplePolite.english: They do say what happens twice happens again.

items.notes: Comeback: sandome no shoujiki (third time's the charm).

items.english: the third try will be the one
items.use: Said before a third attempt at an exam, a confession or a game, or after it finally works: kondo koso sandome no shoujiki da. It is the hopeful answer to nido aru koto wa sando aru.
items.kana: さんどめのしょうじき

example.romaji: kondo koso sandome no shoujiki da!
example.ja: 今度こそ三度目の正直だ！
example.english: Third time's the charm!

examplePolite.romaji: sandome no shoujiki de, yatto goukaku shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 三度目の正直で、やっと合格しました。
examplePolite.english: Third time lucky, I finally passed.

items.use: Said kindly or teasingly when someone skilled slips up. It calls the person a monkey, so never say it to or about a superior (koubou ni mo fude no ayamari is the respectful version). Said about yourself, it's a joke that casts you as the expert. For ordinary mistakes say dare ni demo aru (it happens to everyone).

example.romaji: saru mo ki kara ochiru tte yatsu da ne
example.ja: 猿も木から落ちるってやつだね
example.english: Even the pros slip up, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: puro demo misu suru n desu ne. saru mo ki kara ochiru tte iimasu kara ne
examplePolite.ja: プロでもミスするんですね。猿も木から落ちるって言いますからね
examplePolite.english: So even pros make mistakes. Even monkeys fall from trees, as they say.

items.notes: Plain alternative: dare ni demo machigai wa aru (anyone can make a mistake).

blocks.label: Comes to mind
blocks.rationale: Ideas and pictures surfacing, or almost surfacing.
blocks.interference: atama ni ukabu (an idea comes to mind) vs me ni ukabu (you can picture it); pin to kuru means it clicks or rings a bell, and pin to konai means it doesn't grab you.

items.english: it clicks, it rings a bell
items.use: Said when something clicks, like a hunch, a name or the right answer: pin to kita (it clicked). The negative pin to konai is just as common, for a name that doesn't ring a bell or an idea or design that doesn't grab you (imaichi pin to konai).

example.romaji: sono namae, imaichi pin to konai.
example.ja: その名前、いまいちピンとこない。
example.english: That name doesn't really click for me.

examplePolite.romaji: sono namae wa, imaichi pin to kimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: その名前は、いまいちピンときませんね。
examplePolite.english: That name doesn't really click for me.

items.use: For ideas, faces or words that pop into your head: ii aidea ga ukanda. It's very often negative, nanimo ukabanai (nothing comes to mind), and atama ni is often dropped. It differs from omoidasu (remember on purpose), and me ni ukabu is picturing a scene.

example.romaji: ii namae ga zenzen atama ni ukabanai.
example.ja: いい名前が全然頭に浮かばない。
example.english: I can't think of a good name at all.

examplePolite.romaji: ii namae ga zenzen atama ni ukabimasen.
examplePolite.ja: いい名前が全然頭に浮かびません。
examplePolite.english: I can't think of a good name at all.

items.notes: Plain alternative: omoitsuku (think of, hit on).

items.use: For a scene you can see in your mind, usually someone's face: a reaction you can already picture (okaasan no okoru kao ga me ni ukabu) or a memory that's still vivid (ima demo ano hi no koto ga me ni ukabu). Atama ni ukabu is an idea or word popping up; me ni ukabu is a picture.

example.romaji: kanojo no yorokobu kao ga me ni ukabu yo.
example.ja: 彼女の喜ぶ顔が目に浮かぶよ。
example.english: I can just picture how happy she'll be.

examplePolite.romaji: okusan no yorokobu kao ga me ni ukabimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 奥さんの喜ぶ顔が目に浮かびますね。
examplePolite.english: I can just picture how happy your wife will be.

items.english: on the tip of my tongue
items.literal: it's half out, up to the throat
items.englishIdiom: on the tip of my tongue
items.use: Said while you're straining to remember a name or word, usually after are, nan datta kke..., about yourself and in the -teru form. In the past, nodo made dekakatta is something you nearly said and held back: nodo made dekakatta kedo, iwanakatta.
items.kana: のどまででかかってる
items.politeJa: 喉まで出かかっています

example.romaji: are, nan datta kke... nodo made dekakatteru n da kedo.
example.ja: あれ、何だったっけ…喉まで出かかってるんだけど。
example.english: What was it... it's on the tip of my tongue.

examplePolite.romaji: are, nan deshita kke... nodo made dekakatteru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、何でしたっけ…喉まで出かかってるんですけど。
examplePolite.english: What was it... it's on the tip of my tongue.

items.notes: Also koko made dekakatteru (with a hand at the throat).

blocks.label: Feeling down
blocks.rationale: Low spirits: depressed, brooding, discouraged, dreading it.
blocks.interference: ki ga meiru (depressing) vs ki ga omoi (dread it); particles differ: ki o otosu, ki ni yamu.

items.use: Grumbling about grey days, bad news or a draining situation, usually naming the cause: ame bakkari de ki ga meiru. Ki ga omoi is dread of something ahead, and ochikomu is feeling down after a setback.

example.romaji: ame bakkari de ki ga meiru ne.
example.ja: 雨ばっかりで気が滅入るね。
example.english: All this rain really gets you down.

examplePolite.romaji: ame bakari de ki ga meirimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 雨ばかりで気が滅入りますね。
examplePolite.english: All this rain is so depressing.

items.notes: Plain alternatives: ochikomu, yuuutsu.

items.english: fret over it, take it to heart
items.literal: fall ill in the mind over it
items.use: Mostly as comfort to someone blaming themselves: ki ni yamu koto nai yo, ki ni yamanaide, ki ni yamanakute ii yo (don't let it eat at you). It sounds more serious and grown-up than ki ni shinaide. Ki ni suru is everyday minding; ki ni yamu is brooding until it hurts.

example.romaji: anata no sei ja nai n da kara, ki ni yamanaide.
example.ja: あなたのせいじゃないんだから、気に病まないで。
example.english: It's not your fault, so don't beat yourself up over it.

examplePolite.romaji: amari ki ni yamanaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: あまり気に病まないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please don't let it weigh on you too much.

items.notes: Everyday version: ki ni shinaide.

items.use: Almost always the comfort line ki o otosanaide (don't let it get you down), or sonna ni ki o otosu na. To describe yourself feeling down, people say ochikomu instead.

example.romaji: sonna ni ki o otosanaide yo.
example.ja: そんなに気を落とさないでよ。
example.english: Don't let it get you down so much.

examplePolite.romaji: amari ki o otosanaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: あまり気を落とさないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please don't be too discouraged.

items.notes: Plain word for being down: ochikomu.

items.english: dread it, not look forward to it
items.use: What you say before a task or conversation you're dreading: ashita no mensetsu, ki ga omoi naa. It's the opposite of ki ga raku. Ki ga meiru is general gloom, not dread of something ahead.

example.romaji: ashita no kaigi, ki ga omoi naa.
example.ja: 明日の会議、気が重いなあ。
example.english: I'm dreading tomorrow's meeting.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no kaigi, chotto ki ga omoi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の会議、ちょっと気が重いですね。
examplePolite.english: I'm not looking forward to tomorrow's meeting.

items.notes: Single-word alternative: yuuutsu (gloomy, dreading it).

blocks.label: Taking a gamble
blocks.rationale: Taking a chance: trying with nothing to lose, betting everything, risky moves, offers that look too good.
blocks.interference: dame moto (nothing to lose) vs ichi ka bachi ka (all or nothing); its bachi is unrelated to bachi ga ataru (punishment) in Comes back on you.

items.literal: if it fails, back to where you started
items.use: Said before trying a long shot: damemoto de kiite miru (I'll ask anyway, nothing to lose). It is also a common softener before a cheeky request (damemoto na n da kedo ...), even at work.

example.romaji: damemoto de kiite miru yo
example.ja: ダメ元で聞いてみるよ
example.english: I'll ask anyway, nothing to lose.

examplePolite.romaji: damemoto de kiite mimasu
examplePolite.ja: ダメ元で聞いてみます
examplePolite.english: I'll ask anyway; it's worth a shot.

items.notes: Short for dame de motomoto.

items.english: take the gamble, all or nothing
items.use: Said before a risky, all-out attempt, nearly always as ichi ka bachi ka yatte miru (I'll just risk it). It works like an adverb and goes before the verb.

example.romaji: ichi ka bachi ka yatte miyou
example.ja: 一か八かやってみよう
example.english: Let's just risk it and go for it.

examplePolite.romaji: ichi ka bachi ka yatte mimashou
examplePolite.ja: 一か八かやってみましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's take the gamble and try.

items.notes: Plain alternative: kake (a gamble), as in kake da ne.

items.use: Said about taking a risk that could land you in trouble, usually over money or bending rules rather than physical danger. Often about a risk already taken (kimi no tame ni abunai hashi o watatta, I stuck my neck out for you; kanari abunai hashi o watatteru, you're skating on thin ice) or someone's habits (abunai hashi o wataru taipu), and also to refuse one: sonna abunai hashi wa wataranai.
items.kana: あぶないはしをわたる

example.romaji: sonna abunai hashi, wataritakunai yo.
example.ja: そんな危ない橋、渡りたくないよ。
example.english: I don't want to take a risk like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna abunai hashi wa wataremasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんな危ない橋は渡れませんよ。
examplePolite.english: I can't take a risk like that.

items.notes: Plain alternative: risuku ga takai (it's too risky).

items.english: a sweet deal, an easy-money offer (usually doubted)
items.use: Said about deals, jobs and investments that promise easy gain. The person pitching says it straight (umai hanashi nan da yo), and everyone else usually doubts it: sonna umai hanashi aru wake nai (there's no way that's real), or umai hanashi ni wa ura ga aru (every sweet deal has a catch).

example.romaji: sonna umai hanashi, aru wake nai jan.
example.ja: そんなうまい話、あるわけないじゃん。
example.english: There's no way a deal that good is real.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna umai hanashi wa nai to omoimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなうまい話はないと思いますよ。
examplePolite.english: I doubt a deal that good really exists.

items.notes: Same thing, very common casually: oishii hanashi. Saying: umai hanashi ni wa ura ga aru (a sweet deal always has a catch).

blocks.label: Who you know
blocks.rationale: Ties, networks and the small-world saying.
blocks.interference: en o kiru (cut ties) vs en ga aru (be meant to be) share en; kao ga hiroi (know lots of people) is not kao o dasu (show up).

items.use: Said admiringly about someone with a big network, often when you need a contact: kare, kao ga hiroi kara. Nothing to do with a big face (kao ga ookii).

example.romaji: kare, kao ga hiroi kara kiite miru yo.
example.ja: 彼、顔が広いから聞いてみるよ。
example.english: He knows everyone, I'll ask him.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa kao ga hiroi node, kiite mimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は顔が広いので、聞いてみますね。
examplePolite.english: He knows everyone, so I'll ask him.

items.use: Breaking off for good with family, an ex, a toxic friend or a gang, often oya to en o kitta or ano hito to wa mou en o kitta. Far stronger than kyori o oku (keeping your distance).

example.romaji: ano hito to wa mou en kitta kara.
example.ja: あの人とはもう縁切ったから。
example.english: I've cut ties with her.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito to wa, mou en o kirimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの人とは、もう縁を切りました。
examplePolite.english: I've cut ties with her.

items.notes: Also te o kiru (break off with a partner or associate).

items.english: be meant to be, have a connection
items.use: Heard most in the negative to soften a breakup, rejection or failed job hunt: en ga nakatta n da yo (it just wasn't meant to be). Polite speech says goen, as in the business goodbye mata goen ga areba (if our paths cross again). Also en ga nai for things that never come your way: okane ni wa en ga nai.

example.romaji: kanojo to wa en ga nakatta n da yo.
example.ja: 彼女とは縁がなかったんだよ。
example.english: It just wasn't meant to be with her.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo to wa, goen ga nakatta n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女とは、ご縁がなかったんですよ。
examplePolite.english: It just wasn't meant to be with her.

items.notes: On a chance meeting: kore mo nanika no en (this must be fate).

items.use: Said on finding a mutual friend or bumping into someone unexpectedly, almost always with ne. Younger speakers also say sekai wa semai.

example.romaji: e, kare to shiriai na no? seken wa semai ne.
example.ja: え、彼と知り合いなの？世間は狭いね。
example.english: Wait, you know him? Small world.

examplePolite.romaji: e, kare to oshiriai na n desu ka? seken wa semai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: え、彼とお知り合いなんですか？世間は狭いですね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, you know him? Small world.

items.notes: Variant: sekai wa semai.

blocks.label: Obvious or hidden
blocks.rationale: Things in plain sight vs things below the surface.
blocks.interference: me ni mieteru (the outcome is predictable) vs ichimoku ryouzen (clear at a glance) vs kao ni kaite aru (your feelings show); ura ga aru (a hidden catch, negative) vs oku ga fukai (hidden depth, positive).

items.english: there's a catch, a hidden motive
items.use: Said with suspicion about an offer that seems too good or kindness that's out of character: nanka ura ga aru n ja nai? It's also said of a person with a hidden side (ura ga aru hito). Oku ga fukai is the admiring 'there's more to it'.

example.romaji: sonna umai hanashi, zettai ura ga aru yo.
example.ja: そんなうまい話、絶対裏があるよ。
example.english: A deal that good definitely has a catch.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna umai hanashi wa, zettai ura ga arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなうまい話は、絶対裏がありますよ。
examplePolite.english: A deal that good definitely has a catch.

items.notes: Set phrase: umai hanashi ni wa ura ga aru.

items.use: Used to predict a bad outcome you can already see coming: okorareru no wa me ni mieteru (it's obvious we'll get told off). It's always about a future result and always in the -teru form. Don't confuse it with me ni miete (visibly: me ni miete yaseta = noticeably thinner) or plain me ni mieru (literally visible).

example.romaji: sonna koto shitara okorareru no me ni mieteru yo.
example.ja: そんなことしたら怒られるの目に見えてるよ。
example.english: Do that and you'll obviously get told off.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna koto o shitara, okorareru no wa me ni miete imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなことをしたら、怒られるのは目に見えていますよ。
examplePolite.english: If you do that, you'll obviously get told off.

items.notes: Short form: kekka wa mieteru (we know how it ends).

items.english: has real depth, more to learn
items.use: Said with admiration about a hobby, craft, language or field that keeps getting deeper the more you learn: nihongo tte oku ga fukai ne. It's said about things, not people. Ura ga aru is the suspicious 'there's more to it'.

example.romaji: koohii tte, oku ga fukai ne.
example.ja: コーヒーって、奥が深いね。
example.english: There's more to coffee than you'd think.

examplePolite.romaji: koohii wa oku ga fukai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: コーヒーは奥が深いですね。
examplePolite.english: There's more to coffee than you'd think.

items.notes: Adjective form: okubukai (deep, profound).

items.use: Said when a comparison, a chart or a before-and-after makes the answer instantly clear, often after mireba (if you look). It's used with da or desu.

example.romaji: narabete mireba ichimoku ryouzen da yo.
example.ja: 並べてみれば一目瞭然だよ。
example.english: Put them side by side and it's obvious.

examplePolite.romaji: narabete mireba ichimoku ryouzen desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 並べてみれば一目瞭然ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Put them side by side and it's obvious.

items.notes: Plain alternative: mireba wakaru (you'll see if you look).

items.english: it's written all over your face
items.use: Teasing someone whose thoughts are obvious, like boredom, a lie or a crush: kao ni kaite aru yo. It's usually said to the person, about what they think or want. Kao ni deru is broader: any feeling showing on someone's face (sugu kao ni deru = can't hide feelings); kao ni kaite aru reads a specific thought as if it were spelled out.

example.romaji: tsumannai tte kao ni kaite aru yo.
example.ja: つまんないって顔に書いてあるよ。
example.english: 'I'm bored' is written all over your face.

examplePolite.romaji: tsumaranai tte kao ni kaite arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: つまらないって顔に書いてありますよ。
examplePolite.english: 'I'm bored' is written all over your face.

items.notes: Plain alternative: miemie (so obvious).

blocks.label: Hard work or easy
blocks.rationale: How much effort a task takes, from hard work, high-maintenance and elaborately made to 'happy to help' and child's play.
blocks.interference: te ga kakaru (needs a lot of looking after) and te ga komu (made with real care) share te ga; oyasui goyou is a reply to a request, while asameshi mae describes a task.

items.english: be hard work, take a lot of effort
items.use: Said of a job or task that takes real effort and patience, physical or not: kare o settoku suru no wa hone ga oreru, hone no oreru shigoto. The same words literally mean a bone broke, so context decides; casual talk often just says taihen.

example.romaji: kore zenbu katazukeru no, hone ga oreru na
example.ja: これ全部片付けるの、骨が折れるな
example.english: Tidying all this up is going to be hard work.

examplePolite.romaji: kore zenbu katazukeru no wa hone ga oremasu ne
examplePolite.ja: これ全部片付けるのは骨が折れますね
examplePolite.english: Tidying all this up is going to be hard work.

items.notes: Plain alternative: taihen.

items.english: need a lot of looking after
items.use: Mostly about kids, pets or people who need constant looking after, often as te no kakaru ko (a handful of a kid). For a fiddly task people usually say tema ga kakaru instead; jikan ga kakaru is just taking time.

example.romaji: uchi no ko, honto te ga kakaru n da yo
example.ja: うちの子、ほんと手がかかるんだよ
example.english: My kid is such a handful.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no ko, hontou ni te ga kakaru n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: うちの子、本当に手がかかるんですよ
examplePolite.english: My kid is such a handful.

items.notes: Opposite: te ga kakaranai (low-maintenance).

items.english: be elaborate, made with real care
items.use: Praise for cooking, gifts, crafts or plans that clearly took a lot of work, and also for elaborate pranks or scams. You hear te no konda before nouns and te ga konderu at the end, almost never the dictionary form te ga komu.

example.romaji: kore, sugoi te ga konderu ne
example.ja: これ、すごい手が込んでるね
example.english: Wow, a lot of work went into this.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, sugoku te ga konde imasu ne
examplePolite.ja: これ、すごく手が込んでいますね
examplePolite.english: Wow, a lot of work went into this.

items.notes: Plain alternative: kotteru (kotta ryouri, elaborate cooking).

items.use: The cheerful yes when a friend, family member or junior asks a favour, said by the helper about the favour: oyasui goyou da yo; also X kurai oyasui goyou (that much is no trouble at all). It sounds a little old-fashioned and jokey, and to a boss or customer it can sound breezy, as if the request were trivial: say yorokonde or kashikomarimashita there. Not asameshi mae, which says how easy a task is rather than agreeing to a favour.

example.romaji: oyasui goyou da yo, makasete
example.ja: お安い御用だよ、任せて
example.english: No problem, leave it to me.

examplePolite.romaji: oyasui goyou desu yo, makasete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: お安い御用ですよ、任せてください
examplePolite.english: No problem, leave it to me.

items.notes: Plainer: ii yo, makasete (sure, leave it to me).

items.use: A playful boast that something is easy for you, mostly about your own ability: sonna no asameshi mae da. It sounds a little old-fashioned and jokey (younger speakers more often say yoyuu or rakushou); not oyasui goyou, which is the cheerful yes to a favour.

example.romaji: sonna no asameshi mae da yo
example.ja: そんなの朝飯前だよ
example.english: That's a piece of cake.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna no asameshi mae desu yo
examplePolite.ja: そんなの朝飯前ですよ
examplePolite.english: That's a piece of cake.

items.notes: Plain alternative: kantan.

blocks.label: Warned you
blocks.rationale: Warning ahead, telling someone again and again, and 'I told you so' afterwards.
blocks.interference: nen o osu (remind to make sure) vs kugi o sasu (stern warning in advance); mimi ni tako ga dekiru is the listener's complaint, kuchi o suppaku shite iu the speaker's.

items.english: make sure by telling someone again, stress, remind firmly
items.use: Saying something again to make sure the other person has really understood or will really do it: ichiou nen oshitoku kedo... (just to be sure...). kugi o sasu is the stronger move, a warning not to do something.

example.romaji: ichiou nen oshitoku kedo, ashita juuji da yo.
example.ja: 一応念押しとくけど、明日十時だよ。
example.english: Just to be sure: it's ten o'clock tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ichiou nen o oshite okimasu ga, ashita juuji desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 一応念を押しておきますが、明日十時ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Just to make sure, it's ten o'clock tomorrow.

items.notes: Related: nen no tame (just in case).

items.literal: it's not as if I didn't say it
items.use: Said when things go wrong after someone ignored your warning: hora, iwan kotcha nai (see, I told you). It's a contraction of iwanai koto ja nai and sounds a bit parental. Friends also say dakara itta desho.

example.romaji: hora, iwan kotcha nai. nomisugi da yo.
example.ja: ほら、言わんこっちゃない。飲みすぎだよ。
example.english: See, I told you so. You drank too much.

items.notes: Everyday alternative: dakara itta desho.

items.use: Warning someone ahead of time not to do something, like telling, being late or overspending. It's often heard in the passive, kugi o sasareta (I was warned). nen o osu only double-checks; kugi o sasu is a warning.

example.romaji: dare ni mo iu na tte, kugi sasareta.
example.ja: 誰にも言うなって、釘刺された。
example.english: I got warned not to tell anyone.

examplePolite.romaji: dare ni mo iu na tte, kugi o sasaremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 誰にも言うなって、釘を刺されました。
examplePolite.english: I was told in no uncertain terms not to tell anyone.

items.literal: a callus forms on your ears
items.use: The tired reply to advice or a story you've heard over and over, usually as mimi ni tako ga dekiru hodo kiita. The tako is a callus, not an octopus, though people joke about it. kuchi o suppaku shite iu is the same thing from the speaker's side.

example.romaji: sono hanashi, mimi ni tako ga dekiru hodo kiita yo.
example.ja: その話、耳にタコができるほど聞いたよ。
example.english: I've heard that one a million times.

examplePolite.romaji: sono hanashi, mimi ni tako ga dekiru hodo kikimashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: その話、耳にタコができるほど聞きましたよ。
examplePolite.english: I've heard that story more times than I can count.

items.notes: Slangy short form: mimitako (mimitako da yo).

items.literal: make one's mouth sour saying it
items.englishIdiom: till I'm blue in the face
items.use: A parent's or teacher's exasperation at a warning repeated many times, usually in the past: kuchi o suppaku shite itta desho. mimi ni tako ga dekiru is the same thing from the listener's side.
items.ja: 口を酸っぱくして言う
items.kana: くちをすっぱくしていう
items.politeJa: 口を酸っぱくして言います

example.romaji: are hodo kuchi o suppaku shite itta noni.
example.ja: あれほど口を酸っぱくして言ったのに。
example.english: And I told you over and over!

examplePolite.romaji: are hodo kuchi o suppaku shite iimashita yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あれほど口を酸っぱくして言いましたよね。
examplePolite.english: I told you again and again, didn't I?

blocks.label: Tastes and likeness
blocks.rationale: What suits whom and who is alike: to one's taste, suits one's nature, alike in character, identical, everyone differs.
blocks.interference: kuchi ni au (suits one's palate) and shou ni au (suits one's nature) both end in ni au. nita mono doushi (alike in character) vs uri futatsu (alike in looks).

items.use: The host's line when serving food or drink, politely with o: okuchi ni au ka wakarimasen kedo; the question every visitor to Japan gets: nihon no tabemono, kuchi ni au? (politely okuchi ni aimasu ka?); and a soft way to say you don't like something: chotto kuchi ni awanakute. Shou ni au is for activities, not food.

example.romaji: kore, kuchi ni au ka wakannai kedo, tabete mite.
example.ja: これ、口に合うかわかんないけど、食べてみて。
example.english: Not sure you'll like it, but give it a try.

examplePolite.romaji: okuchi ni au ka wakarimasen ga, douzo.
examplePolite.ja: お口に合うかわかりませんが、どうぞ。
examplePolite.english: I'm not sure it'll be to your taste, but please have some.

items.notes: Polite with o: okuchi ni au; plain way: suki ka wakannai (not sure you'll like it).

items.english: suit one's nature, be one's thing
items.use: About jobs, lifestyles and ways of doing things, mostly in the negative: jimu shigoto wa shou ni awanai. It's for activities; food that suits you is kuchi ni au, and clicking with a person is ki ga au.

example.romaji: jimu shigoto wa shou ni awanai n da.
example.ja: 事務仕事は性に合わないんだ。
example.english: Office work just isn't me.

examplePolite.romaji: jimu shigoto wa shou ni awanai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 事務仕事は性に合わないんです。
examplePolite.english: Office work doesn't really suit me.

items.notes: Plainer: watashi ni wa muitenai (not suited to me), or nigate.

items.use: Teasing two friends or a couple who share the same quirks or faults: futari tte nita mono doushi da yo ne. About character and habits, not looks; looking alike is uri futatsu or sokkuri.

example.romaji: futari tte, nita mono doushi da yo ne.
example.ja: 二人って、似た者同士だよね。
example.english: You two are two of a kind.

examplePolite.romaji: ofutari wa nita mono doushi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: お二人は似た者同士ですね。
examplePolite.english: You two are very much alike.

items.notes: Related saying, said aloud too: rui wa tomo o yobu (birds of a feather), for a group drawn together; clipped to ruitomo.

items.use: Said about a child and parent, siblings or a celebrity lookalike: okaasan to uri futatsu da ne. Only about looks; the everyday single word sokkuri is said more often, and nita mono doushi is about personality.

example.romaji: okaasan to uri futatsu da ne!
example.ja: お母さんと瓜二つだね！
example.english: You're the spitting image of your mum!

examplePolite.romaji: okaasan to uri futatsu desu ne!
examplePolite.ja: お母さんと瓜二つですね！
examplePolite.english: You look exactly like your mother!

items.notes: Single word: sokkuri (just like), far more common in speech.

items.use: Ends a debate about taste, opinions or how to do something: konomi wa juunin toiro da kara ne. It sounds a little proverbial; hito sorezore is the plain everyday way.

example.romaji: konomi wa juunin toiro da kara ne.
example.ja: 好みは十人十色だからね。
example.english: Everyone's got their own taste.

examplePolite.romaji: konomi wa juunin toiro desu kara ne.
examplePolite.ja: 好みは十人十色ですからね。
examplePolite.english: Tastes differ from person to person.

items.notes: Plain everyday way: hito sorezore (it depends on the person).

blocks.label: Embarrassment
blocks.rationale: Self-conscious feelings: it shows on your face, sheepish, it stings to hear, want to disappear.
blocks.interference: kimari ga warui (sheepish) vs the other '... warui' idioms (kimi ga warui, munakuso warui).

items.english: your feelings show on your face
items.literal: it comes out on the face
items.use: Feelings leaking onto your face in spite of you. It's used about yourself (sugu kao ni deru taipu) and to tease others (kao ni deteru yo). Kao ni kaite aru is the stronger 'it's written all over your face'.

example.romaji: watashi, sugu kao ni deru n da yo ne.
example.ja: 私、すぐ顔に出るんだよね。
example.english: My face always gives me away.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, sugu kao ni deru n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 私、すぐ顔に出るんですよ。
examplePolite.english: Everything I feel shows on my face.

items.notes: Keep it hidden: kao ni dasanai. Of drink: sugu kao ni deru (go red).

items.use: The awkward feeling of being caught out or having to face people after a slip, often in the past: uso ga barete kimari ga warukatta. Batsu ga warui means the same but is said less, and in everyday talk most people just say kimazui; hazukashii is plain embarrassment.

example.romaji: uso ga barete, sugoku kimari ga warukatta.
example.ja: 嘘がバレて、すごくきまりが悪かった。
example.english: My lie got found out and I felt so sheepish.

examplePolite.romaji: ima kara okurete hairu no wa, chotto kimari ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今から遅れて入るのは、ちょっときまりが悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: It's a bit awkward to walk in late now.

items.notes: Also said without ga: kimari warui. Everyday word: kimazui (what younger speakers say). Same meaning, rarer: batsu ga warui.

items.english: it stings to hear (because it's true)
items.use: Said ruefully, often with a wry laugh, when criticism or advice applies to you: sore wa mimi ga itai, or mimi ga itai hanashi. It can also mean a literal earache, so context decides.

example.romaji: sore iwareru to mimi ga itai na.
example.ja: それ言われると耳が痛いな。
example.english: Ouch, that hits close to home.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa mimi ga itai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは耳が痛いですね。
examplePolite.english: That one stings a bit.

items.notes: Literal sense too: an earache.

items.english: so embarrassed I want to disappear
items.literal: if there were a hole, I'd want to get in it
items.englishIdiom: I wish the ground would swallow me up
items.use: The stock reaction after embarrassing yourself, often half-joking: hazukashikute ana ga attara hairitai. It's a fixed form and only used for your own feelings.
items.ja: 穴があったら入りたい
items.kana: あながあったらはいりたい
items.politeJa: 穴があったら入りたいです

example.romaji: hazukashikute, ana ga attara hairitai.
example.ja: 恥ずかしくて、穴があったら入りたい。
example.english: I'm so embarrassed I want to crawl into a hole.

examplePolite.romaji: hazukashikute, ana ga attara hairitai kimochi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 恥ずかしくて、穴があったら入りたい気持ちです。
examplePolite.english: I'm so embarrassed I could just disappear.

items.notes: Partner phrase: kao kara hi ga deru (face burning with shame).

blocks.label: Whatever happens
blocks.rationale: Taking outcomes calmly, before or after they happen.
blocks.interference: sono toki wa sono toki (before the fact: deal with it then) vs kekka oorai (after the fact: it worked out); naru you ni naru is a general shrug.

items.polite: sono toki wa sono toki desu
items.english: we'll deal with it if it happens
items.englishIdiom: cross that bridge when we come to it
items.use: The everyday shrug at a what-if worry: dame dattara sono toki wa sono toki (if it fails, we'll deal with it then). You say it to calm yourself or someone else, often with maa in front.

example.romaji: maa, sono toki wa sono toki da yo
example.ja: まあ、その時はその時だよ
example.english: Eh, we'll cross that bridge when we come to it.

examplePolite.romaji: maa, sono toki wa sono toki desu yo
examplePolite.ja: まあ、その時はその時ですよ
examplePolite.english: Well, we'll deal with it if it happens.

items.notes: Rougher casual form: son toki wa son toki.

items.literal: it becomes the way it becomes
items.use: A relaxed shrug about something out of your hands, usually maa, naru you ni naru sa. It sounds comforting rather than defeated; naru you ni shika naranai (it'll go how it goes) is more resigned.

example.romaji: maa, naru you ni naru tte
example.ja: まあ、なるようになるって
example.english: Eh, it'll work out somehow.

examplePolite.romaji: maa, naru you ni narimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: まあ、なるようになりますよ
examplePolite.english: Well, things will work out somehow.

items.notes: Plain alternative: nantoka naru (it'll work out).

items.english: it worked out in the end, so fine
items.use: Said when luck covered a mistake or a messy process: maa, kekka oorai jan. Casual and a bit cheeky, often used to brush off criticism of how you got there.

example.romaji: maa, kekka oorai jan.
example.ja: まあ、結果オーライじゃん。
example.english: Well, it worked out in the end.

examplePolite.romaji: kekka oorai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 結果オーライですね。
examplePolite.english: Well, it all worked out.

items.notes: oorai is 'all right', the fielder's call in baseball.

blocks.label: Couples
blocks.rationale: Romantic relationships, from crossing the line to bickering like an old married couple.
blocks.interference: issen o koeru (sleep together, go too far) vs yori o modosu (get back together); kenka suru hodo naka ga ii vs kenka o uru (pick a fight) in Squaring up.

items.english: cross the line, go too far; (of two people) sleep together
items.use: Two senses, both everyday: going too far in a fight, a joke or a job (sore wa issen o koeteru, that's crossing the line) and, in gossip, two people becoming lovers (ano futari, issen koeta rashii yo). The famous affair denial is issen wa koete imasen.

example.romaji: ano futari, mou issen koeta rashii yo.
example.ja: あの二人、もう一線越えたらしいよ。
example.english: Apparently those two have already slept together.

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari, mou issen o koeta rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの二人、もう一線を越えたらしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Apparently those two have already slept together.

items.notes: issen o hiku = draw a line, keep a boundary.

items.literal: put the twist back in the strands
items.use: Dating gossip about exes: motokare to yori modoshita (she got back with her ex). Only for couples; friends making up is nakanaori.

example.romaji: ano futari, mata yori modoshita rashii yo.
example.ja: あの二人、またより戻したらしいよ。
example.english: Apparently those two got back together again.

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari, mata yori o modoshita rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの二人、またよりを戻したらしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Apparently those two got back together again.

items.notes: Noun in gossip: fukuen (getting back together).

items.english: two-time, date two people at once
items.use: Dating gossip and accusations, often passive: futamata kakerareteta (I was being two-timed). Mostly romance; it can also mean hedging between two options (two job offers).

example.romaji: kare ni futamata kakerareteta no.
example.ja: 彼に二股かけられてたの。
example.english: He was two-timing me.

examplePolite.romaji: kare ni futamata o kakerarete ita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼に二股をかけられていたんです。
examplePolite.english: He was two-timing me.

items.notes: Casual: futamata suru.

items.romaji: kenka suru hodo naka ga ii
items.english: fighting just shows how close you are
items.literal: on such good terms that they fight
items.use: Said about a bickering couple, siblings or friends, half teasing: kenka suru hodo naka ga ii tte iu shi ne. Also a consolation after you've argued with someone you love.
items.ja: 喧嘩するほど仲がいい
items.kana: けんかするほどなかがいい

example.romaji: mata kenka shiteru no? maa, kenka suru hodo naka ga ii tte iu shi ne.
example.ja: また喧嘩してるの？まあ、喧嘩するほど仲がいいって言うしね。
example.english: Fighting again? Well, they say the more you fight, the closer you are.

examplePolite.romaji: kenka suru hodo naka ga ii tte iimasu kara ne.
examplePolite.ja: 喧嘩するほど仲がいいって言いますからね。
examplePolite.english: They do say the more you fight, the closer you are.

blocks.label: Believing it
blocks.rationale: How much of what you hear you believe, from swallowing it whole to not falling for it.
blocks.interference: ma ni ukeru (take it seriously) vs unomi ni suru (swallow it uncritically); sono te ni wa noranai rejects a trick outright, while hanshin hangi only half believes.

items.english: take it at face value, take it seriously
items.use: It's mostly negative and said after a joke or a flattering line: joudan da yo, ma ni ukenaide (I'm kidding, don't take it seriously). People also say it with regret: ma ni uketa watashi ga baka datta. It's about believing words that weren't meant literally; unomi ni suru is swallowing information or rumours whole.

example.romaji: joudan da yo, ma ni ukenaide.
example.ja: 冗談だよ、真に受けないで。
example.english: I'm kidding, don't take it seriously.

examplePolite.romaji: joudan desu yo, ma ni ukenaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 冗談ですよ、真に受けないでください。
examplePolite.english: I'm only joking, please don't take it seriously.

items.notes: Plain alternative: honki ni suru (take seriously).

items.use: About information: rumours, something online, what an expert or a salesperson says. It's mostly advice in the negative: unomi ni shinai hou ga ii. Ma ni ukeru is believing a joke or a line that wasn't meant seriously.

example.romaji: netto no uwasa, unomi ni shinai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: ネットの噂、鵜呑みにしないほうがいいよ。
example.english: Don't believe every rumour you read online.

examplePolite.romaji: netto no uwasa wa unomi ni shinai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ネットの噂は鵜呑みにしないほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Don't believe every rumour you read online.

items.use: A playful or wary comeback when you see through a trick, flattery or bait. Te here means a trick or move, as in a game.
items.politeJa: その手には乗りません

example.romaji: mata sore? sono te ni wa noranai yo.
example.ja: またそれ？その手には乗らないよ。
example.english: That again? I'm not falling for it.

examplePolite.romaji: mata sore desu ka? sono te ni wa norimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: またそれですか？その手には乗りませんよ。
examplePolite.english: That again? I'm not falling for it.

items.notes: Rough: sono te ni noru ka! (as if I'd fall for that!) or sono te ni wa noran. Also sono te ga atta! (oh, that's an option!).

items.use: Said about how you felt at first about news, a rumour or a too-good offer, usually in the past: saisho wa hanshin hangi datta. It works like a na-adjective: hanshin hangi de kiku.

example.romaji: saisho wa hanshin hangi datta kedo, hontou datta n da yo.
example.ja: 最初は半信半疑だったけど、本当だったんだよ。
example.english: I only half believed it at first, but it turned out to be true.

examplePolite.romaji: saisho wa hanshin hangi deshita kedo, hontou datta n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 最初は半信半疑でしたけど、本当だったんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I only half believed it at first, but it turned out to be true.

blocks.label: Swamped
blocks.rationale: Overloaded for days: can't keep it up, can't get around to things, crazy busy, desperate for any help.
blocks.interference: te ga mawaranai and me ga mawaru both use mawaru: te means you can't get around to it, while me means dizzy or crazy busy.

items.english: (my) body can't take it, I won't last at this rate
items.use: The standard complaint about overtime, late nights, drinking or training you can't sustain, usually after kono mama ja, konna peesu ja or a -tara clause: kono mama ja karada ga motanai. Also a warning to someone else (sonna ni hataraitara karada motanai yo) and, in hospital talk, a patient who can't take more. The ga often drops, and mi ga motanai means the same.

example.romaji: konna ni zangyou tsuzuitara karada motanai yo
example.ja: こんなに残業続いたら体もたないよ
example.english: If all this overtime keeps up, I won't last.

examplePolite.romaji: konna ni zangyou ga tsuzuitara karada ga mochimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: こんなに残業が続いたら体がもちませんよ
examplePolite.english: If all this overtime keeps up, I won't last.

items.notes: Plain alternative: mou genkai (I'm at my limit).

items.use: Said when you're too stretched to deal with one more part of your duties, usually as X made te ga mawaranai: isogashikute souji made te ga mawaranai. Not te ga hanasenai (tied up this minute).

example.romaji: isogashikute souji made te ga mawaranai
example.ja: 忙しくて掃除まで手が回らない
example.english: I'm too busy to get around to cleaning.

examplePolite.romaji: isogashikute souji made te ga mawarimasen
examplePolite.ja: 忙しくて掃除まで手が回りません
examplePolite.english: I'm too busy to get around to cleaning.

items.notes: The positive te ga mawaru is rare in talk; in dramas keisatsu no te ga mawaru means the police are closing in.

items.use: Literally feeling dizzy (me ga mawatta), and figuratively in the set exaggeration me ga mawaru hodo isogashii for a hectic day. The busy sense almost always comes with isogashii.

example.romaji: kyou, me ga mawaru hodo isogashikatta
example.ja: 今日、目が回るほど忙しかった
example.english: Today was so busy my head was spinning.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa me ga mawaru hodo isogashikatta desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日は目が回るほど忙しかったです
examplePolite.english: Today was so busy my head was spinning.

items.notes: Plain word for dizzy: memai (memai ga suru).

items.polite: neko no te mo karitai kurai desu
items.literal: I'd borrow even a cat's paws
items.use: A half-joking way to say a workplace or season is frantic, usually followed by kurai or hodo isogashii: nenmatsu wa neko no te mo karitai kurai. Said at work and at home, not only in writing.
items.politeJa: 猫の手も借りたいくらいです

example.romaji: ima, neko no te mo karitai kurai da yo
example.ja: 今、猫の手も借りたいくらいだよ
example.english: We're so busy we'd take any help.

examplePolite.romaji: ima, neko no te mo karitai kurai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 今、猫の手も借りたいくらいですよ
examplePolite.english: We're so busy we'd take any help.

items.notes: Plain alternative: sugoku isogashii.

blocks.label: Lies and big talk
blocks.rationale: Lying, bragging and stretching the truth, from flat lies to fudged ages.
