blocks.interference: makka na uso (a flat lie) vs uso mo houben (a white lie is sometimes fine); hanashi o moru pads a story, ooguchi o tataku brags about what you'll do, saba o yomu fudges a number.

items.english: talk big, brag about what you'll do
items.literal: bang out a big mouth (tataku: hit, here spout, as in kageguchi o tataku)
items.use: Bragging about what you can or will do, usually as a put-down or a warning: ooguchi tataku na (stop talking big). It's about the boast itself; kuchi dake is about never following through. Politely, people say it of themselves before a bold promise: ooguchi o tataku you desu ga, kanarazu katsu tsumori desu (I may be talking big, but I fully intend to win).

example.romaji: ooguchi tataku no wa katte kara ni shite.
example.ja: 大口叩くのは勝ってからにして。
example.english: Save the big talk for after you win.

examplePolite.romaji: ooguchi o tataku no wa katte kara ni shite kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大口を叩くのは勝ってからにしてくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Save the big talk until you've actually won.

items.notes: Rougher, mostly male: dekai kuchi (o) tataku, as in dekai kuchi tataku na.

items.use: Calls a rumour, an excuse or a claim totally untrue: sore, makka na uso da yo. The 'bright red' just means total and obvious.

example.romaji: ano uwasa? makka na uso da yo.
example.ja: あの噂？真っ赤な嘘だよ。
example.english: That rumour? It's a complete lie.

examplePolite.romaji: ano uwasa desu ka? makka na uso desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの噂ですか？真っ赤な嘘ですよ。
examplePolite.english: That rumour? It's an outright lie.

items.notes: Plain alternatives: oouso, zenbu uso.

items.english: a white lie is sometimes needed
items.literal: a lie is also an expedient
items.use: Justifies a kind or convenient fib, such as telling a nervous friend they'll be fine: maa, uso mo houben da yo. Houben is a Buddhist word for a means to an end.

example.romaji: maa, uso mo houben tte iu shi.
example.ja: まあ、嘘も方便って言うし。
example.english: Well, sometimes a white lie is for the best.

examplePolite.romaji: maa, uso mo houben tte iimasu shi ne.
examplePolite.ja: まあ、嘘も方便って言いますしね。
examplePolite.english: Well, they do say a white lie can be necessary.

items.literal: heap up the story (like food on a plate)
items.use: Modern casual way to say someone is puffing up a story to make it funnier or more impressive: sore, motteru desho (you're exaggerating). Moru alone is enough, and morisugi (way overdone) also covers heavy makeup or edited photos.

example.romaji: sore, zettai hanashi motteru desho.
example.ja: それ、絶対話盛ってるでしょ。
example.english: You're totally exaggerating that.

examplePolite.romaji: sore, zettai hanashi mottemasu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: それ、絶対話盛ってますよね。
examplePolite.english: You're definitely exaggerating that, right?

items.notes: Plain alternative: oogesa (exaggerated).

items.use: Mostly about age, height or weight, often as a joke: gosai saba yonderu desho (you're knocking five years off). It works in either direction, knocking years off or adding a few centimetres, and casual speech drops the o. The image is fishmongers counting mackerel in a hurry and getting the count conveniently wrong.

example.romaji: nijuu hassai? zettai saba yonderu desho.
example.ja: 二十八歳？絶対サバ読んでるでしょ。
example.english: Twenty-eight? You're definitely knocking a few years off.

examplePolite.romaji: jitsu wa, chotto saba yondemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 実は、ちょっとサバ読んでました。
examplePolite.english: Actually, I knocked a few years off.

blocks.label: Proud or humble
blocks.rationale: Ego in three: talking down, showing off, staying humble.
blocks.interference: ue kara mesen (looking down from above) is the opposite of koshi ga hikui (keeping your hips low). mie o haru can be confused with iji o haru in Stubborn.

items.use: The modern catch-all for a condescending tone, from a boss, a know-it-all friend or a customer: nani sono ue kara mesen? Used as a noun (ue kara mesen da) or with de (ue kara mesen de iwanaide).

example.romaji: ano hito, itsumo ue kara mesen da yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、いつも上から目線だよね。
example.english: He always talks down to people.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa itsumo ue kara mesen desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人はいつも上から目線ですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's always rather condescending, isn't he?

items.notes: Single word: erasou (bossy, full of yourself).

items.english: put on a front, try to look better off than you are
items.use: About spending or pretending beyond your means to look good, like a pricey date or a brand bag on credit: mie hatte takai mise ni shichatta, with o dropped. Bragging about something real is jiman suru, not this. Iji o haru is pride that won't back down, not putting on a front.

example.romaji: mie hatte takai mise yoyaku shichatta.
example.ja: 見栄張って高い店予約しちゃった。
example.english: I wanted to look good, so I went and booked a pricey place.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui mie o hatte, takai mise o yoyaku shichaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: つい見栄を張って、高い店を予約しちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I wanted to look good, so I booked a pricey restaurant.

items.notes: Noun: mieppari (someone vain who always puts on a front).

items.use: Praise for someone important who still treats everyone modestly and politely: shachou na noni koshi ga hikui. The opposite attitude is erasou or ue kara mesen; not koshi ga itai (my back hurts).

example.romaji: ano hito, shachou na noni koshi hikui yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、社長なのに腰低いよね。
example.english: He's the boss, yet he's so humble.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa shachou na noni koshi ga hikui desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は社長なのに腰が低いですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's the company president, yet so modest.

items.notes: Single word: kenkyo (modest).

blocks.label: Moved
blocks.rationale: Strong feelings in the chest: heartache, being moved, overwhelmed; a natural three.
blocks.interference: mune ga itamu (it pains me) vs mune ga ippai (overwhelmed): same opening, opposite tone.

items.english: it pains me, it breaks my heart
items.use: Said about sad news, someone's hardship, or guilt at hurting someone: aa iu nyuusu o miru to mune ga itamu. Kokoro ga itamu means the same and is said about three times as often; mune ga itamu sounds a little more formal. For guilt, English says 'I feel bad' or 'it pains me' rather than 'it breaks my heart'. Mune ga itai can also be literal chest pain.

example.romaji: aa iu nyuusu o miru to, mune ga itamu yo ne.
example.ja: ああいうニュースを見ると、胸が痛むよね。
example.english: News like that really breaks your heart.

examplePolite.romaji: hisaichi no eizou o miru to, mune ga itamimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 被災地の映像を見ると、胸が痛みます。
examplePolite.english: It breaks my heart to see the footage from the disaster area.

items.notes: Same meaning, said more: kokoro ga itamu. Casual: mune ga itai (included in the count; can also be literal chest pain). Written: mune o itameru.

items.english: be moved, it really gets you
items.use: A reaction to a moving scene, song, line or gesture, mostly in the past: ano serifu, gutto kita. It's also used for being charmed by someone: sono shigusa, gutto kuru. Pin to kuru is the same pattern, but it means something clicked in your understanding, not your feelings.

example.romaji: saigo no shiin, gutto kita.
example.ja: 最後のシーン、グッときた。
example.english: The last scene really got me.

examplePolite.romaji: saigo no supiichi, gutto kimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 最後のスピーチ、グッときましたね。
examplePolite.english: That last speech was really moving.

items.notes: Plain word: kandou suru (be moved).

items.use: Said at graduations, farewells, reunions and big thank-yous, usually when you're too moved to get the words out: mune ga ippai de nanimo ienai. Mune ga ippai de taberarenai is being too emotional to eat, and onaka ga ippai is a full stomach.

example.romaji: nanka mune ga ippai de, umaku kotoba ni dekinai.
example.ja: なんか胸がいっぱいで、うまく言葉にできない。
example.english: I'm so overwhelmed I can't find the words.

examplePolite.romaji: minasan no kotoba de mune ga ippai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 皆さんの言葉で胸がいっぱいです。
examplePolite.english: Your kind words fill my heart.

blocks.label: Close calls
blocks.rationale: Coming through danger: the worst passing, a near miss, a razor-thin margin, the one lucky part of a bad situation.
blocks.interference: kiki ippatsu (a near disaster) vs kami hitoe (a razor-thin gap, often between winning and losing); yama o kosu is the crisis passing, not a near miss.

items.use: Said about an illness, a crunch period or a crisis once the hardest part is behind you, usually in the past: yama o koeta, yama wa koeta (the worst is over). The crunch point itself is the yama (koko ga yama da).

example.romaji: shigoto, yatto yama koeta yo
example.ja: 仕事、やっと山越えたよ
example.english: Work's finally over the hump.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto mo yatto yama o koemashita
examplePolite.ja: 仕事もやっと山を越えました
examplePolite.english: Work is finally past the worst.

items.notes: Literal twin: crossing a real mountain. For an illness people also say touge o koeta (past the crisis).

items.use: Said right after a narrow escape from real danger, like nearly being hit by a car or a bike: kiki ippatsu datta. It sounds a bit dramatic; abunakatta (that was close) is the everyday version. For just making it in time, say girigiri or kan ippatsu de maniatta: kan ippatsu means 'by a hair', kiki ippatsu 'a moment of danger'.

example.romaji: ima no, kiki ippatsu datta ne
example.ja: 今の、危機一髪だったね
example.english: That was a close shave.

examplePolite.romaji: ima no wa kiki ippatsu deshita ne
examplePolite.ja: 今のは危機一髪でしたね
examplePolite.english: That was a really close call.

items.notes: Everyday alternative: abunakatta! (that was close). Near-twin: kan ippatsu (by a hair).

items.use: Said when two things are separated by almost nothing, most often as A to B wa kami hitoe, like the set line tensai to baka wa kami hitoe (genius and idiot are a hair apart). Also for a razor-thin margin: kami hitoe no sa de maketa (lost by a hair).

example.romaji: tensai to baka wa kami hitoe tte iu yo ne.
example.ja: 天才とバカは紙一重って言うよね。
example.english: They say there's a fine line between genius and idiot.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou ni kami hitoe deshita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 本当に紙一重でしたね。
examplePolite.english: That was a really close one.

items.notes: Near-twin: kan ippatsu (by a hair).

items.english: the one lucky part of a bad situation
items.literal: good fortune in the middle of misfortune
items.use: Said after an accident or setback about the one thing that went right, such as nobody getting hurt or the data being backed up: kega ga nakatta no wa fukouchuu no saiwai datta. Heard often from sympathetic listeners.
items.kana: ふこうちゅうのさいわい

example.romaji: kega nakute fukouchuu no saiwai datta ne
example.ja: 怪我なくて不幸中の幸いだったね
example.english: At least nobody got hurt.

examplePolite.romaji: kega ga nakute fukouchuu no saiwai deshita ne
examplePolite.ja: 怪我がなくて不幸中の幸いでしたね
examplePolite.english: It's lucky nobody was hurt, at least.

items.notes: Plain alternative: ... dake de yokatta (lucky it was only ...).

blocks.label: Reading people
blocks.rationale: Sensing what others feel or want without being told.
blocks.interference: kuuki o yomu (read the room) vs kaoiro o ukagau (anxiously watch one person's mood); aite no mi ni naru is empathy, ishin denshin is understanding each other without words.

items.english: put yourself in the other person's place
items.use: Two shapes: advice, aite no mi ni natte kangaete (think how they'd feel), and, heard even more, the complaint about yourself: chotto wa watashi no mi ni mo natte yo (try being in my shoes for once). Anyone can fill the slot: kodomo no mi ni natte. It's imagining one person's side; kuuki o yomu is sensing the room.

example.romaji: aite no mi ni natte kangaete mina yo.
example.ja: 相手の身になって考えてみなよ。
example.english: Try seeing it from their side.

examplePolite.romaji: aite no mi ni natte kangaete mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 相手の身になって考えてみてください。
examplePolite.english: Please try to see it from their side.

items.notes: Rough complaint: ore no mi ni mo natte miro! (try being in my shoes!). Also aite no tachiba ni natte (from their position).

items.english: read the mood, pick up on the vibe
items.use: Mostly a complaint about someone who doesn't: kuuki yomenai (he can't read the room), kuuki yome yo (read the room!). It's sensing the mood; ki o tsukau is actively being considerate.

example.romaji: ano hito, honto kuuki yomenai yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、ほんと空気読めないよね。
example.english: He really can't read the room, can he?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, hontou ni kuuki yomenai desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人、本当に空気読めないですよね。
examplePolite.english: He really can't read the room, can he?

items.english: watch someone's mood, anxiously try to stay on their good side
items.use: Mostly a complaint about someone always checking how a boss, parent or partner will react: joushi no kaoiro bakkari ukagatteru. Close to kuuki o yomu, but fixed on one person's mood and the fear of upsetting them.

example.romaji: ano hito, itsumo joushi no kaoiro bakkari ukagatteru.
example.ja: あの人、いつも上司の顔色ばっかりうかがってる。
example.english: All he ever does is watch the boss's mood.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, itsumo joushi no kaoiro bakari ukagattemasu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人、いつも上司の顔色ばかりうかがってますよね。
examplePolite.english: He's always watching the boss's mood, isn't he?

items.notes: Literal kaoiro ga warui = look pale.

items.use: A playful comment when a friend or partner reads your mind: ishin denshin da ne. Said about couples, close friends or a well-tuned team.

example.romaji: sore iou to omotteta! ishin denshin da ne.
example.ja: それ言おうと思ってた！以心伝心だね。
example.english: I was just about to say that! You read my mind.

examplePolite.romaji: sore, ima iou to omotte imashita. ishin denshin desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それ、今言おうと思っていました。以心伝心ですね。
examplePolite.english: I was just about to say that. You read my mind.

blocks.label: Can't resist
blocks.rationale: Desire, greed and curiosity pulling at your attention.
blocks.interference: me ga nai (crazy about it, fondly) vs me ga kuramu (blinded by greed): both start me ga, and the character list's miru me ga nai (poor judge) sounds alike; kuse ni naru describes the moreish thing, me ga nai describes you.

items.use: Always used with ni, usually about yourself, to confess a weakness for a food or hobby: amai mono ni me ga nai (I can't resist sweets). Don't confuse it with miru me ga nai (bad judgement of people) or me ga warui (poor eyesight).

example.romaji: amai mono ni wa me ga nai n da.
example.ja: 甘いものには目がないんだ。
example.english: I can't resist sweets.

examplePolite.romaji: amai mono ni wa me ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 甘いものには目がないんです。
examplePolite.english: I can't resist sweets.

items.notes: Plain alternative: daisuki (love it).

items.use: Said mostly in the past about someone who did something wrong for money or a prize: okane ni me ga kuranda. It also literally means dazzled by light, or dizzy.

example.romaji: kare, okane ni me ga kuranda n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、お金に目がくらんだんだよ。
example.english: He was blinded by the money.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa okane ni me ga kuranda n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はお金に目がくらんだんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He was blinded by the money.

items.use: Said about food, music, a game or a feeling you can't get enough of. It's variety TV's favourite food verdict (kuse ni naru aji). It also warns that something will turn into a bad habit: amayakasu to kuse ni naru yo. Kuse on its own just means a habit or a quirk.

example.romaji: kono karasa, kuse ni naru ne.
example.ja: この辛さ、クセになるね。
example.english: This spiciness is addictive.

examplePolite.romaji: kono karasa, kuse ni narimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この辛さ、クセになりますね。
examplePolite.english: This spiciness is addictive.

items.notes: Close: hamaru (get hooked on).

items.use: Describes someone, often a crowd or kids, who's intensely curious and leaning in about gossip, a new gadget or someone's love life: minna kyoumi shinshin datta. It works like a na-adjective, with da, na or de.

example.romaji: minna, atarashii buchou ni kyoumi shinshin da yo.
example.ja: みんな、新しい部長に興味津々だよ。
example.english: Everyone's dying to know about the new manager.

examplePolite.romaji: minna, atarashii buchou ni kyoumi shinshin desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: みんな、新しい部長に興味津々ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Everyone's dying to know about the new manager.

items.notes: Plain alternative: sugoku kyoumi ga aru.

blocks.label: Comebacks and digs
blocks.rationale: Verbal sparring: sniping, winning and losing the exchange.
blocks.interference: ippon torareta (you got me) vs guu no ne mo denai (no comeback at all); aa ieba kou iu (always has a retort) vs hitokoto ooi (always one remark too many); kechi o tsukeru is not the single word kechi (stingy).

items.literal: stick a bad omen on it
items.use: Criticising or nitpicking something, often unfairly or out of spite: nan ni demo kechi tsukeru (finds fault with everything). Often as a hedge: kechi tsukeru wake ja nai kedo (not to nitpick, but...). Kechi here keeps its old sense of a bad omen (also in kechi ga tsuku, things start going wrong); 'stingy' grew out of the same word later.

example.romaji: hito no ryouri ni kechi tsukenaide yo.
example.ja: 人の料理にケチつけないでよ。
example.english: Don't knock my cooking.

examplePolite.romaji: hito no ryouri ni kechi o tsukenaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: 人の料理にケチをつけないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Please don't criticise my cooking.

items.use: A good-humoured concession when someone outwits you with a clever reply or trick: kore wa ippon torareta na (well, you got me there). It's a fixed passive past; the ippon is a winning point in kendo or judo. It sounds a little old-fashioned, the kind of thing a good-humoured senior says; among younger friends yarareta is the everyday equivalent.

example.romaji: naruhodo ne. kore wa ippon torareta na.
example.ja: なるほどね。これは一本取られたな。
example.english: Ha, fair enough. You got me there.

examplePolite.romaji: naruhodo, kore wa ippon toraremashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: なるほど、これは一本取られましたね。
examplePolite.english: I see. You've got me there.

items.english: always says one thing too many
items.use: A complaint about someone who can't resist adding one needless, annoying remark: itsumo hitokoto ooi n da yo. People say it about partners, bosses and parents, and about themselves when they regret a remark. The remark itself is yokei na hitokoto.

example.romaji: kare, itsumo hitokoto ooi n da yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、いつも一言多いんだよね。
example.english: He always has to add one comment too many.

examplePolite.romaji: kare, itsumo hitokoto ooi n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼、いつも一言多いんですよね。
examplePolite.english: He always says one thing too many.

items.notes: The remark itself: yokei na hitokoto.

items.literal: not even a 'guu' sound comes out
items.use: Admitting that someone's point is so right you can't argue back: seiron sugite guu no ne mo denai. Also said about someone else who lost an argument: kare, guu no ne mo denakatta.

example.romaji: sou iwaretara, guu no ne mo denai yo.
example.ja: そう言われたら、ぐうの音も出ないよ。
example.english: When you put it like that, I've got nothing.

examplePolite.romaji: sou iwaretara, guu no ne mo demasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: そう言われたら、ぐうの音も出ませんね。
examplePolite.english: Put like that, I can't argue.

items.literal: say it that way and they say it this way
items.use: An exasperated complaint about someone who argues back to everything, typically a parent about a child: hontou ni aa ieba kou iu n da kara. It's said about others, never about yourself.

example.romaji: mou, aa ieba kou iu n da kara.
example.ja: もう、ああ言えばこう言うんだから。
example.english: Honestly, you've got an answer for everything.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no ko, hontou ni aa ieba kou iu n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: うちの子、本当にああ言えばこう言うんですよ。
examplePolite.english: My kid has an answer for everything.

blocks.label: Temper
blocks.rationale: The ki ga set for temperament: feisty, hasty, timid, short-tempered, plus caving under pressure.
blocks.interference: ki ga hayai (jumping the gun) vs ki ga mijikai (impatient). ki ga tsuyoi and ki ga yowai are opposites. ki ga yowai (timid) vs oshi ni yowai (caves when pushed).

items.use: About someone who speaks their mind and won't back down, often said of a woman or a child: kanojo, ki ga tsuyoi kara. Praise or complaint depending on tone; the opposite is ki ga yowai (timid).

example.romaji: uchi no imouto, ki ga tsuyoi n da yo.
example.ja: うちの妹、気が強いんだよ。
example.english: My little sister's pretty feisty.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no imouto wa ki ga tsuyoi n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: うちの妹は気が強いんですよ。
examplePolite.english: My younger sister is quite strong-willed.

items.notes: Before a noun: ki no tsuyoi hito.

items.english: jumping the gun, getting ahead of oneself
items.use: A light tease for someone planning or celebrating too early, like booking the honeymoon before the proposal: mada ki ga hayai yo. Not ki ga mijikai (short-tempered).

example.romaji: mou kurisumasu no junbi? ki ga hayai ne.
example.ja: もうクリスマスの準備？気が早いね。
example.english: Getting ready for Christmas already? You're getting ahead of yourself!

examplePolite.romaji: mou kurisumasu no junbi desu ka? ki ga hayai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: もうクリスマスの準備ですか？気が早いですね。
examplePolite.english: Preparing for Christmas already? You're certainly keen!

items.notes: Also about yourself: chotto ki ga hayai kedo (it's early, but...).

items.use: About someone shy and timid who can't refuse or speak up, very often yourself: ki ga yowakute kotowarenai. The opposite of ki ga tsuyoi; oshi ni yowai is narrower (caves when pushed).

example.romaji: watashi, ki ga yowai kara kotowarenai n da.
example.ja: 私、気が弱いから断れないんだ。
example.english: I'm too timid to say no.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, ki ga yowai node kotowarenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 私、気が弱いので断れないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm too timid to turn people down.

items.notes: Close: ki ga chiisai (faint-hearted); single word: okubyou (cowardly).

items.use: About someone who loses patience or temper fast, such as a parent, a boss or yourself. Not ki ga hayai, which means jumping the gun.

example.romaji: kare, chotto ki ga mijikai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、ちょっと気が短いんだよね。
example.english: He's a bit short-tempered.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa chotto ki ga mijikai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はちょっと気が短いんですよね。
examplePolite.english: He can be a little short-tempered.

items.notes: Single word people say more: tanki (short-tempered); plainest: sugu okoru (gets angry fast).

items.use: About someone who gives in when asked insistently, by a salesperson, a persistent admirer or a friend begging a favour; constant in dating talk (kanojo, oshi ni yowai kara). Narrower than ki ga yowai (timid in general).

example.romaji: watashi, oshi ni yowai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 私、押しに弱いんだよね。
example.english: I always cave if someone pushes.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, oshi ni yowai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私、押しに弱いんですよね。
examplePolite.english: I tend to give in when people push.

items.notes: Opposite: oshi ga tsuyoi (pushy).

blocks.label: Worth the money
blocks.rationale: Money and value: not worth it, costs adding up, getting your money back, a pitiful sum.
blocks.interference: wari ni awanai (doesn't pay) vs moto o toru (get your money's worth); baka ni naranai (costs add up) vs suzume no namida (a tiny amount).

items.use: A grumble when the reward doesn't cover the effort or risk, like low pay for a hard job: kono kyuuryou ja wari ni awanai. It's nearly always negative; the positive wari ni au (it pays) is rare.

example.romaji: kono jikyuu ja wari ni awanai yo
example.ja: この時給じゃ割に合わないよ
example.english: It's not worth it for this hourly pay.

examplePolite.romaji: kono jikyuu ja wari ni aimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: この時給じゃ割に合いませんよ
examplePolite.english: It doesn't pay at this hourly rate.

items.notes: Plain alternative: son (a loss), as in son da yo.

items.literal: doesn't become foolish (= can't be laughed off as trivial)
items.use: Said mostly about money that seems small but adds up, like train fares, coffee or phone bills: koutsuuhi mo baka ni naranai. Don't confuse it with baka ni suru (make fun of) or baka o miru (end up the loser).

example.romaji: koutsuuhi mo baka ni naranai yo
example.ja: 交通費もバカにならないよ
example.english: Train fares really add up too.

examplePolite.romaji: koutsuuhi mo baka ni narimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: 交通費もバカになりませんよ
examplePolite.english: Travel costs really add up as well.

items.notes: Variant: baka ni dekinai; plain alternative: kekkou kakaru (costs quite a bit).

items.use: Said about buffets, gym memberships, passes and pricey gadgets: tabehoudai de moto o toru (eat enough to make the buffet worth it). The negative moto ga torenai (it won't pay for itself) is just as common.

example.romaji: tabehoudai da kara moto toranakya
example.ja: 食べ放題だから元取らなきゃ
example.english: It's all-you-can-eat, gotta get our money's worth.

examplePolite.romaji: tabehoudai desu kara, moto o toranai to ikemasen ne
examplePolite.ja: 食べ放題ですから、元を取らないといけませんね
examplePolite.english: It's all-you-can-eat, so we should get our money's worth.

items.notes: Intransitive: moto ga toreru (it pays for itself).

items.english: a pitifully small amount (usually of money)
items.use: The stock complaint about pay, bonuses, pensions or interest, often as suzume no namida hodo: boonasu wa suzume no namida hodo datta. Mostly about money, though any tiny amount can qualify.

example.romaji: boonasu, suzume no namida datta yo.
example.ja: ボーナス、雀の涙だったよ。
example.english: My bonus was a pittance.

examplePolite.romaji: boonasu wa suzume no namida deshita.
examplePolite.ja: ボーナスは雀の涙でした。
examplePolite.english: The bonus was next to nothing.

items.notes: Plain alternative: hon no sukoshi (just a tiny bit).

blocks.label: Under someone's thumb
blocks.rationale: Deferring to someone with power over you: flattering, humouring, unable to push back.
blocks.interference: goma o suru (suck up for gain) vs kigen o toru (keep someone in a good mood); atama ga agaranai (can't stand up to them) vs shiri ni shikareru (bossed around by your wife).

items.use: Office and school talk about someone flattering the boss or teacher: buchou ni goma sutteru. The suru is 擂る (grind), so it's sutteru and surimasu, not shiteru or shimasu.

example.romaji: ano hito, itsumo buchou ni goma sutteru yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、いつも部長にごますってるよね。
example.english: He's always sucking up to the boss, isn't he?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, itsumo buchou ni goma suttemasu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人、いつも部長にごますってますよね。
examplePolite.english: He's always sucking up to the boss, isn't he?

items.notes: Noun: gomasuri (a suck-up).

items.use: Smoothing things over with a sulking partner, child or grumpy boss, often as gokigen o toru. It's about soothing a mood; goma o suru is flattery to curry favour.

example.romaji: kanojo no kigen toru no, taihen na n da yo.
example.ja: 彼女の機嫌取るの、大変なんだよ。
example.english: Keeping my girlfriend happy is hard work.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo no kigen o toru no, taihen na n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女の機嫌を取るの、大変なんですよ。
examplePolite.english: Keeping my girlfriend happy is hard work.

items.notes: Also gokigen o toru; noun gokigentori.

items.english: owe someone too much to stand up to them
items.use: About a wife, older sibling, mentor or boss who's done so much for you that you can never argue back: ane ni wa atama ga agaranai. Always negative and said with fond resignation; shiri ni shikareru is being bossed around without the gratitude.

example.romaji: ane ni wa atama ga agaranai n da yo.
example.ja: 姉には頭が上がらないんだよ。
example.english: I owe my sister too much to ever argue with her.

examplePolite.romaji: ane ni wa, hontou ni atama ga agarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 姉には、本当に頭が上がりません。
examplePolite.english: I owe my sister so much, I can never argue with her.

items.english: be bossed around by your wife
items.literal: be laid under (someone's) bottom like a cushion
items.use: Light teasing about a husband or boyfriend, almost always in the -teru form: okusan no shiri ni shikareteru. Rarely a real insult.

example.romaji: kare, kanzen ni okusan no shiri ni shikareteru yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、完全に奥さんの尻に敷かれてるよね。
example.english: He's totally under his wife's thumb.

examplePolite.romaji: kare, kanzen ni okusan no shiri ni shikaretemasu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼、完全に奥さんの尻に敷かれてますよね。
examplePolite.english: He's totally under his wife's thumb.

notes: Kanyouku plus the sayings (kotowaza) and four-character phrases (yojijukugo) people really say; chosen on how common they are in Japanese, whether or not English has an equivalent.

Out of scope by design: literal noun + verb sets (they are in 21-list-collocations.json); single words, even slangy ones (rakushou, yabai) — mentioned in notes where they are the plain alternative; bookish sayings people rarely say aloud.

Built by two workflows: a harvest by source (ki and the inner body, head and face, mouth and ears, hands, legs and body, animals and objects, modern set phrases) with gap hunts, a count of every candidate in the subtitle corpus, then a second, wider gap hunt (sayings, four-character phrases, idioms without body parts, everyday situations, the corpus), a three-judge selection on commonness, writing, four reviews per topic (native naturalness, meaning and literal sense, register and real-life use, romaji and data), chunking and course order.
The corpus is mostly subtitles for foreign films, so dramatic lines are over-counted and casual Japanese talk is under-counted; judged commonness corrects for both.

cuts.english: look after, take care of (kids, pets, juniors)
cuts.reason: Already in 21-list-collocations.json (c-mendou-o-miru); all four reviewers cut it as a repeated collocation. ki ni kakeru and sewa ga yakeru now cover looking after people.

cuts.english: make fun of, look down on
cuts.reason: Already in 21-list-collocations.json (c-baka-ni-suru); all four reviewers cut it as a repeated collocation.

cuts.english: come to your senses
cuts.reason: The figurative 'me o samase!' (snap out of it, wake up to reality) is a stock line, but most of its 525 hits are literal waking up.

cuts.english: disappear, vanish, go missing
cuts.reason: Vanish; 367 hits but mostly plot narration (people say inaku naru).

cuts.english: have an idea (kentou mo tsukanai = no idea at all)
cuts.reason: Same idiom; it is almost always said in the negative, kept as kentou mo tsukanai.

cuts.english: have no idea, can't even guess
cuts.reason: A variant of kentou mo tsukanai (no idea at all), which is kept.

cuts.english: fall in love
cuts.reason: Plain 'fall in love'; a film-heavy collocation, cut from that list.

cuts.english: risk one's life, stake everything on
cuts.reason: 'Stake your life on it', also used loosely (inochi kakete). The top count here (215 to 270, including inochigake), though drama inflates it.

cuts.english: listen closely, heed
cuts.reason: Formal, speech-style version of the kept mimi o kasu (listen to someone).

cuts.english: pull out, back off, quit
cuts.reason: Common (about 150 hits): back off, pull out of a deal (kono ken kara te o hike).

cuts.english: reliable, dependable (tayori ni suru = count on someone)
cuts.reason: Plain 'be reliable' (179 hits); a collocation (cut from that list), not an idiom.

cuts.english: not so fast; that won't work (this time)
cuts.reason: Not so fast (142), but plain words: it doesn't go that way.

cuts.english: turn away from, refuse to face
cuts.reason: Mostly the literal 'turn your back'; the figurative 'turn away from reality' is narration more than talk.

cuts.english: embarrass oneself, be humiliated
cuts.reason: All four reviewers: already a kept collocation (c-haji-o-kaku) with the same example, and the brief says never repeat collocations. alsoIn now points to it from ana ga attara hairitai.

cuts.english: faint, pass out
cuts.reason: Just 'faint'. ishiki o ushinau is already in the collocation list.

cuts.english: bow; apologise; humbly ask
cuts.reason: Literally bow your head to apologise or ask; cut from the collocation list, not figurative.

cuts.english: show your face, come and visit
cuts.reason: Show your face, come visit; the kept kao o dasu says the same.

cuts.english: the person who saved one's life (often jokingly)
cuts.reason: Common, often as a joke (138 hits): you saved my life.

cuts.english: look the part, look natural doing it
cuts.literal: it takes on a proper form
cuts.reason: 'Look the part' (sama ni natteru); common praise, though the true count is hard to separate from 'you ni naru'.

cuts.english: team up, join forces
cuts.reason: Team up, mostly in crime-plot talk (judged 2); te o kasu and chikara ni naru cover everyday help.

cuts.english: meet (humble): ome ni kakarete kouei desu = an honour to meet you
cuts.reason: Humble keigo for 'meet'; learn it with keigo.

cuts.english: pay someone back (a favour); get even
cuts.reason: Paying back a favour is part of the kept kari ga aru family (kari wa kaesu).

cuts.english: be within reach; afford; nearly (an age)
cuts.reason: Reach, afford, or nearly hit an age (yonjuu ni te ga todoku); common (52) and nothing kept says it.

cuts.english: settle it once and for all (kecchaku ga tsuku = be settled)
cuts.reason: Settle it once and for all; keri o tsukeru says the same.

cuts.english: are you out of your mind?
cuts.reason: Its 112 hits are mostly dubbing of 'are you crazy?'; real talk says dou ka shiteru or shouki?

cuts.english: step away (from one's desk or the room); give people some privacy
cuts.reason: Mostly the office phone formula (seki o hazushite orimasu).

cuts.english: to tell the truth, actually
cuts.reason: Means just what it says; the versatility list's jitsu wa already does this job.

cuts.english: confess, spill the secret
cuts.reason: Strong count (95-104): 'finally talks' about a suspect, also joked about friends who won't spill (nakanaka kuchi o waranai).

cuts.english: have a drink (together)
cuts.reason: Just 'have a drink'; the collocation list already has ippai nomu.

cuts.english: news to me, first I've heard
cuts.reason: One word (hatsumimi = news to me), very common (98) and worth learning as vocabulary.

cuts.english: cut ties with, break off with
cuts.reason: Cut ties, mostly in crime and business plots (judged 2); en o kiru is the everyday one.

cuts.english: unimaginable, I can't even imagine
cuts.reason: Literally 'can't even imagine'; transparent, like souzou dekinai.

cuts.english: someone owes you one
cuts.reason: The other side of the kept kari ga aru (you owe me one).
